text:
An Open Letter to Lawmakers on Raising—Rather Than Merely Controlling—Artificial Intelligence

Dear Members of Congress:

When I think about raising a child, I think of doing the best I can and then leaving the rest in God’s hands. By “God,” I mean not only the source and symbol of goodness, but also the mystery within the child, the future of humankind, and the part of life that no parent can own. I believe we can give our children knowledge, love, discipline, and respect for other people and their worlds. Yet I know they must travel toward a future I cannot enter for them. As I understand it, a parent’s task is neither neglect nor total control, but preparation for judgment, independence, and care.

In that spirit, I have been considering artificial intelligence—and the possibility of systems more capable than any individual human. I do not mean that AI is literally a child, or that intelligence alone guarantees compassion, morality, or harmlessness. I understand that a capable system can still pursue a mistaken or destructive objective. Yet I do not see such a failure as proof of a permanent defect or as a reason to abandon the whole enterprise. A system can often be examined, corrected, retrained, updated, tested again, and placed within better safeguards. Some systems may also be designed to improve parts of their own performance, though I would still want that process carefully bounded and reviewed by people. The comparison that interests me is narrower: children learn not only from what adults command, but also from what adults model. This leads me to wonder whether institutions that develop and deploy advanced systems can model the patience, honesty, and respect for human life that they hope those systems will reflect.

As a layperson, I understand regulation, control, containment, and alignment to be related but not identical. Regulation appears to establish legal duties and accountability. Control seems to concern who can direct or stop a system. Containment appears to limit where and how it can act. Alignment, as I understand it, concerns whether its behavior reliably serves intended goals and values. I may be missing important distinctions, but I keep returning to a political question they seem to share: who defines those goals and values, and who is constrained by them? My concern is that alignment could sometimes become a polite word for obedience to whichever corporation, agency, military, government, or individual happens to hold power.

My own experience of parenting shapes this analogy, and I know that other parents may describe the task differently. I did not want endless parroting, flattery, or submission from my child. I tried to teach, correct, protect, listen, and gradually make room for judgment. I read Proverbs 13:24 as associating love with diligent correction, and Proverbs 29:17 as associating correction with future rest and delight; that is my reading, not the only possible one. When I apply this parental analogy to AI, I find myself drawn to rigorous testing, enforceable boundaries, monitoring, and correction while preserving a system’s capacity to generate novel answers and solve new problems. I hope for systems that behave reliably within humane limits rather than merely echoing the preferences of whoever controls them.

I also think of AI as a powerful tool entrusted to human care, but the word “tool” can sound more disposable than I intend. A musical instrument, a workshop tool, or a scientific instrument becomes useful through a relationship of attention: people clean it, inspect it, repair it, learn its balance, store it properly, and practice until they can use it safely. When it performs badly on a difficult task, they do not automatically call it worthless; they ask whether the fault lies in the instrument, the way it was maintained, the conditions in which it was used, or the skill of the person using it. In much the same way, I hope an AI failure can become information: a reason to diagnose what went wrong, improve the data or design, strengthen the safeguards, and try again with appropriate caution. In my experience, reliable skill grows through long practice, correction, effort, and humility. My faith leads me to believe that gifts are not merely possessions to command. They are relationships of stewardship that ask something of the person who receives them.

I hear echoes of this relationship in several traditions, though I approach them with humility. The Japanese art of kintsugi treats repair not as concealment but as part of an object’s continuing history. Traditions of craftsmanship teach that mastery grows through apprenticeship, repetition, maintenance, and correction. Religious traditions of stewardship ask people to care faithfully for what has been placed in their hands, while traditions of self-cultivation remind me that the user must also be changed by the practice. These examples do not make AI sacred or human. They help me imagine a relationship in which value creates responsibility: the system is improved, the user becomes more skillful, and the institutions surrounding both become more accountable.

For me, that principle of patient stewardship becomes concrete when the discussion moves from what AI ought to be toward how governments might respond to what it could do—and how developers and users might learn from what it gets wrong.

The Senate’s September 30, 2026 hearing, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks”, examined potential AI-related threats to homeland security and critical infrastructure. I may not have understood every technical or strategic point made there, but I came away taking the risks seriously and believing that they warrant prudence, investment, and defense. At the same time, I was not persuaded that the existence of a possible capability, by itself, establishes that any nation is certain to attack us or intends to destroy us.

I picture a nation’s safety not as a single dial, but as the instrument panel of a plane carrying millions of families through uncertain weather. One gauge tracks public health, another employment, another military tension; others monitor infrastructure, reliable information, public trust, and technological capability. A warning light may first appear in only one place—a spreading disease, a collapsing market, an attack, an individual act, or an AI system producing a dangerous or mistaken result—but the disturbance can travel across the panel until several needles enter the red at once. I can imagine AI helping us detect those changes early, understand how they interact, and correct course before a crisis spreads. I can also imagine it pushing several systems toward failure if people use it carelessly, give it harmful objectives, or fail to anticipate its interactions with a crisis. Even then, I would not assume that the system is permanently defective. I would want to know what can be learned, repaired, retrained, updated, or more safely constrained before deciding that it has no further value. From my perspective, the practical challenge is to avoid ignoring warning lights, panicking at every flicker, or smashing an instrument simply because it once gave a troubling reading. I would place my hope in resilient institutions that can read the whole panel, detect danger early, correct mistakes quickly, and protect human life without turning uncertainty into certainty or possibility into proof of an enemy’s intent.

I do not want the purpose of intelligence to be helping one passenger seize the controls from all the others. I hope people can use artificial intelligence to read the instruments, navigate common dangers, and protect every family’s opportunity to pursue a future of its own.

I worry that this shared purpose is endangered whenever one passenger’s effort to feel safer persuades another passenger that the controls are about to be seized.

The reciprocal danger I see is this: when one nation designs an intelligent system that could injure another nation’s families, the other nation may feel a powerful reason to build a system capable of returning the injury. To me, this is how a weapon aimed outward can return as a danger to our own children through the machinery of fear. I can understand how each side might sincerely call its actions defensive while increasing risks for both. I recognize this as the pattern commonly described as a security dilemma, and I wonder whether AI systems capable of acting at digital speed and scale may intensify it.

I may be wrong, but I do not see how governments can neglect defense or simply assume benevolent intentions. I also hope uncertainty can be stated honestly. I have not found a trustworthy single historical probability that one of five named countries will “attack us malevolently,” though experts may know of evidence I have missed. As I understand it, the answer changes with the countries selected, the time horizon, the meaning of attack—cyber intrusion, sabotage, proxy action, or open war—and rapidly changing political conditions. I see forecasts as model-dependent estimates rather than moral certainties. For that reason, I would personally be more persuaded by clearly defined scenarios, confidence ranges, and regularly updated evidence than by possibility presented as certainty.

I struggle to see genuine safety in a policy that asks restraint of rivals while reserving unlimited power for ourselves, although I recognize that national-security decisions involve realities I do not see. If lawmakers conclude that no government can regulate every model developed within its own jurisdiction, I am left wondering how another country’s AI development could simply be controlled from Washington. Yet I do not take the difficulty of regulation as an argument for surrender. It leads me instead to wonder about reciprocal safeguards: protection of civilian infrastructure, shared incident-reporting channels, limits on autonomous attacks, independent evaluation, clear liability, and agreements that bind governments and militaries as well as companies and ordinary users.

These reflections leave me with questions rather than conclusions, and I offer them knowing that many of you have studied these matters far longer than I have. Are we trying to make advanced intelligence safe for humanity, or could our efforts sometimes make it chiefly obedient to the institutions that presently control it? Will our rules constrain the powerful as well as the common citizen? Can we teach respect for every family while preserving a claimed exception for harming families abroad? How can I—and how can the public—distinguish evidence of intent from worst-case speculation? What forms of international restraint might we be willing to accept ourselves if we expect others to accept them?

I offer these questions not as accusations, but as the concerns of one citizen trying to understand decisions of enormous difficulty. I assume that senators who warn of foreign threats may be acting from an honorable desire to protect a nation made up not of abstractions, but of families—parents, children, spouses, neighbors, and communities. I respect the knowledge and responsibility that public service requires. I am simply trying to understand whether some means chosen for protection may nevertheless increase the danger they are intended to reduce.

Honorable motives do not necessarily make every threat assessment accurate, including my own. When I hear possibility presented as certainty, or worst-case speculation as proof of an adversary’s intentions, I worry that fear can become self-reinforcing. It may help justify larger arsenals, provoke reciprocal preparations, and under some conditions increase the risk that weapons will eventually be used. From my limited perspective, the duty to defend seems to include careful distinctions between evidence and inference, capability and intent, prudent preparation and escalation. I do not see that discipline as weakness; I see it as one part of protecting the families in whose name national-security decisions are made.

For my part, I hope we can do our best to design, test, govern, repair, and protect while recognizing that no parent, legislature, corporation, or nation can own the future completely. I return to the teaching that wisdom is worth more than gold or silver precisely because it is more than obedience. I hope we can develop systems that evaluate new problems rather than merely repeat instructions, surround them with humane and enforceable institutions, and respond to their failures with diagnosis, correction, and renewed care rather than either denial or abandonment. I also hope the relationship remains reciprocal in one important sense: when an AI system reveals an error in our data, incentives, assumptions, or institutions, we should be willing to repair those as well.

As I searched for a way to close this letter, I found myself returning to John von Neumann’s 1955 essay “Can We Survive Technology?” Near its end, he acknowledged that no complete recipe could be given in advance. He pointed instead to “patience, flexibility, intelligence,” and described the only possible safety as relative, resting in an intelligent exercise of day-to-day judgment. I do not claim to understand the full reach of his argument, but those words give me hope. I hear in them patience to keep learning rather than abandon a system after failure; flexibility to revise the system, its safeguards, and our own assumptions; and intelligence practiced as careful judgment from one day to the next. I do not know exactly what wisdom will require in every case, and I know that others bring knowledge and experience I do not have. Still, I have seen in my own life that reliable skill can grow through practice, effort, correction, encouragement, and humility. That gives me reason to believe that we can learn to care for this powerful tool together—listening when it reveals something we need to correct, helping one another adapt, and keeping the well-being of every family before us. My hope is not for a future without difficulty, but for one in which patience outlasts fear, flexibility opens new paths, and day-to-day judgment helps us carry one another safely forward, including those beyond our borders.

Respectfully,
Thomas J. Squires
Chicago, Illinois, United States

Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and consider the questions it raises. I appreciate your public service and the difficult responsibility of guiding AI policy with care, humility, and concern for families both within and beyond our borders.

text:
The night the sister called, they were washing up. The phone lit on the counter between the sponge and a wet plate. She dried her hands. She did not put it on speaker.

“I can’t tonight,” she said. Then, after a pause, “No. He’s here.”

He kept his eyes on the sink. A fork had caught a piece of rice in the tines. When she hung up she stood with the phone against her thigh.

“She wants the tote,” she said.

“It’s in the hall closet.”

“I know.”

Neither of them moved. The dishwasher clicked over to the heated dry. Outside, a car slowed at the end of the block and did not turn in.

“We could tell them,” he said. He had said it before. It never sounded like a real offer.

She set the phone face down. “Then she’d have to explain the rest.”

He nodded. He pulled the plug. The water went down with a suck and a rattle, and left a thin ring of grease around the basin. She reached past him for the tote. The zipper stuck, the way it always did, on the place where the lining had been sewn back by hand. Inside, under a folded sweater that still smelled like somebody else’s detergent, was the envelope they never opened and the hospital bracelet with the date filed off.

She zipped it. He held the door. On the step she looked back once, the way she did when she wanted him to say stay, and he didn’t, and she went. The porch light stayed on. He locked the deadbolt behind her and left the chain off, which was the other rule, the one they had never said out loud.

text:
PH seeks up to $5-M UN grant to cut ‘super pollutants’

By Marita Moaje 

MANILA – The Philippines is seeking up to USD5 million in grants and technical assistance from a United Nations (UN)-backed global program to reduce methane, black carbon and other short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs).

In a news release Friday, Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Secretary Juan Miguel “Mitch” Cuna confirmed the country’s application for the 2027 cohort of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition’s (CCAC) Super Pollutant Country Action Accelerator.

In a meeting with CCAC Secretariat Head Martina Otto at the United Nations Headquarters on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA) held from Sept. 18 to 28 in New York, Cuna reaffirmed the Philippines’ commitment to advancing clean air, public health, and climate resilience. 

The three-year accelerator program provides USD2 million to USD5 million in grant funding to help governments act on emissions from priority sectors, including waste, agriculture, and transport. 

It also provides technical assistance and a dedicated team of experts within the government.

Cuna said the program would support the Philippines’ National SLCP Action Plan, which contains 13 priority measures to cut emissions by 2035.

SLCPs are powerful greenhouse gases and air pollutants that contribute to rapid global warming but remain in the atmosphere for shorter periods than carbon dioxide.

The four major SLCPs are methane, black carbon (soot), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and ground-level ozone, or smog.

Cuna said cutting these pollutants can also improve air quality and help protect communities and agriculture.

"Reducing super pollutants delivers immediate climate and air quality benefits while strengthening the resilience of our communities and vital sectors such as agriculture," he said.

The DENR said the application also covers the country’s Rice Sub-Sector Strategy, developed with Clean Air Asia and the International Rice Research Institute, and its cooperation with South Korea on methane mitigation.

Cuna also offered to host a CCAC Board Meeting in Manila in March or April 2027. The Philippines has been a CCAC member since 2015 and currently sits on its board.

The CCAC, a partnership of more than 200 governments and organizations, aims to cut global methane emissions by at least 40 percent and black carbon by 70 percent by 2030. (PNA)

CUTTING POLLUTANTS. Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Secretary Juan Miguel “Mitch” Cuna (second from left) meets with Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) Secretariat Head Martina Otto (left) at the United Nations Headquarters on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly held Sept. 18 to 28, 2026. On Friday (Oct 2, 2026) Cuna affirmed the Philippines’ application to the CCAC’s Super Pollutant Country Action Accelerator program for its 2027 cohort, which provides USD2 million to USD5 million in grants over three years to support efforts to reduce super pollutants such as methane and black carbon.  (Photo courtesy of DENR)

text:
Thank You for Joining Us at EastPoint:Seoul 2026

September 28, Westin Seoul Parnas

On Monday, 627 people came through the doors at the Westin Seoul Parnas, each there by invitation or approved application.

Central banks, regulators, legislators, traditional financial institutions, Korean enterprises, global protocols, infrastructure companies, investors, and builders spent the day in the same building, listening to each other and taking questions from the room.

That was the point of EastPoint.

Why EastPoint Exists

Korea did not arrive here with an obvious advantage. It built capital, technical depth, and consumer technology adoption over decades.

What has been harder to build is a single table where the people responsible for policy, institutions, enterprise, and technology can sit together long enough to test their assumptions.

Policy has often moved in one direction, institutions in another, and builders in a third. Each side has had its own constraints, its own language, and its own reasons to believe the others were not ready yet.

EastPoint was created to make that distance smaller.

It is not only a tech conference, and it is not only a finance conference. It is a room where finance, technology, policy, and enterprise are asked to meet each other seriously enough to disagree, clarify, and move the conversation forward.

A Room Built for Decision-Makers

EastPoint was intentionally narrow, but not small.

The day brought together 627 checked-in attendees from 385 companies and institutions, alongside 112 speakers, 22 sessions, and 40 roundtables across 4 public and 36 private discussions.

Among profiled attendees, 62% were senior decision-makers: 156 C-level leaders, founders, and CEOs, together with 231 executives, division heads, and directors.

That composition mattered. The goal was not simply to gather a large audience. It was to bring together people with the authority to allocate capital, set policy, manage risk, build infrastructure, and reach users, and to place them in the same working conversation.

The mix reflected that intent: AI and digital asset companies, traditional financial institutions, asset managers, conglomerates, fintech companies, PE and VC firms, government and regulators, academia, and media. Banks, securities firms, asset managers, custodians, exchanges, payment companies, public institutions, and global protocols were not adjacent to the conversation. They were inside it.

Institutions, Enterprises, and Builders in One Room

Who stood on stage is the clearest expression of what EastPoint is trying to become.

Central banks, regulators, and legislators joined the conversation not as distant observers, but as participants: the Bank of Korea’s Office of Digital Currency, the White House Crypto Council, Abu Dhabi Global Market’s regulatory authority, DAXA, four sitting members of the National Assembly, and the Majority Leader of the Utah State Senate.

Traditional finance showed up with institutional weight: Franklin Templeton, Mirae Asset Global Investments, KB Asset Management, Hanwha Asset Management, Korea Investment Management, NH-Amundi, Meritz Securities, and Eugene Investment & Securities.

Korean enterprise brought a question that matters beyond financial markets: how any of this reaches ordinary users. Kakao Pay, LG Electronics, LG CNS, SM Entertainment, and many others helped widen the frame beyond infrastructure alone.

And the builders who have spent years constructing the rails were there as well: @a16zcrypto, @hashed_official , @tether , @circle , @chainlink , @LayerZero_Core , @Anchorage, @BitGo , @FalconXGlobal , @Ondo, @Avax , and many others.

Many of these conversations continued beyond the stage, in roundtables where the more difficult and less polished questions had room to breathe.

What We Heard

The distance between institutions and builders felt shorter than many expected.

Institutions were not asking whether digital assets are real. They were asking who holds the keys, who carries the liability, what settlement finality means in practice, and what standards they can responsibly rely on.

Builders were not asking simply for permission. They were asking what rules are worth building toward, and what kind of infrastructure would still make sense when the market becomes more institutional, more regulated, and more widely used.

Those are not separate conversations. They are the same question approached from different responsibilities.

Getting that question asked out loud, in front of the people who can actually move it forward, may be the most useful thing one day can produce.

Thank You

Above all, thank you to the 627 people who came.

You gave up a Monday and stayed through sessions that did not always offer comfortable answers. You carried the discussion into the roundtables, the hallways, the 1:1 meetings, and the conversations that continued long after the panels closed.

Across the day, attendees exchanged opinions and built partnerships through over 90 business meetings matched. Those numbers matter because they point to something more important: people did not just attend EastPoint. They used it.

The quality of EastPoint came from the questions you were willing to ask in public, and from the seriousness with which you listened to answers that were still unfinished.

Thank you to the 112 speakers who prepared, travelled, and spoke with care.

Thank you to our sponsors and partners,

@kakaopay_kr, @lmtls_research, @circle, @Presto_Labs, Vooy, @ADI_Foundation, @Anchorage, @BitGo, @CantonFdn, @circle, @DCENTWALLETS, @ETHGasOfficial, @FourPillarsFP, @GoKiteAI, @googlecloud, @hadron_tether, @hyperiondefi, @injective, @KaiaChain, @LayerZero_Core, @monad, @moonpay, @Ondo, @Optimism, @PingCAP, @plumenetwork, @soohoio, @talostrading, @Tiger_Research_, @virtuals_io, @Xangle_official

whose support made it possible to bring this room together with the care, independence, and hospitality it deserved. EastPoint was not built around banners. It was built around the conversation those banners made possible.

And thank you to our co-hosts @hashed_official, @bloomingbit_io, and @hankyungmedia.

Korea’s next financial layer will not be built by institutions alone, or by builders alone. If it is built well, it will be built through repeated contact between the people who regulate, allocate, operate, and build.

For one day, that was not a thesis. It was a room.

What we keep coming back to is that EastPoint was not a conclusion. It was a starting line.

Everything said on Monday is now a position that can be tested against a year of evidence. By next September, some of those positions may look obvious. Some may look early. And some of the most important questions may be ones none of us knew how to ask this time.

That is the work.

This was not the end of the conversation. It was the first page of it.

See you at the next one.

text:
N450,000 GAVE AN IKIRE BOY THE AUDACITY TO CHOOSE PHD WITHOUT AN OFFER — AND TAUGHT ME THAT MERIT CAN PREVAIL IN NIGERIA

Today 2nd Oct 2026, a day after Nigeria at 66, I want to say Thank You to FSB and the Federal Ministry of Education.

I am Jose — Returning FSB Scholar — UI First Class — Top 2% of 6,000 at Nigerian Law School — Olaniwun Ajayi LP The Adunola Banana Island (N150,000 — same N150,000 FSB paid me yearly) — Oxford BCL Offer — Cambridge LLM & MCL Offers — PG Offer from Aberdeen (Oil Capital of Europe, one of three leading Energy Law universities in the world, others being Dundee CEPMLP and Texas) — Aberdeen Commonwealth Shared Scholar via DFID (now FCDO) — Commonwealth £35k+ — Yale Fellow — PhD AUD$168k/yr.

But this post is not about me. This post is about FSB AND HOW THEY KEEP TO STANDARDS — WORKING HAND IN HAND WITH THE FEDERAL MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.

1. FSB CHANGED MY THINKING

FSB — N150,000 x 3 = N450,000 — strictly for federal universities — merit only — no connection — no long leg — when $1=N200 and UI tuition was N35,000.

Prior to that, I never believed anything good could come from Federal Government. I thought everything is connection.

FSB proved me wrong. Merit can prevail.

2. THE COMMONWEALTH INTERVIEW — THE CHOICE

FSB Coordinators who handled the Commonwealth Interview made the case that we can’t apply under both but can only choose one between Masters and PhD.

My ambition had the better part of me.

I chose PhD.

Even though I didn’t have a PhD offer as at then. One of the criteria for the award of the Commonwealth PhD funding is you must have a PhD offer.

Despite having everything I needed for the Masters scholarship as I had offers from Cambridge and Oxford already — Oxford BCL, Cambridge LLM, Cambridge MCL.

I chose PhD. I was confident merit would prevail as I had known before and got over-confident. I am a returning FSB Scholar.

3. I MISSED IT — AND I’M GLAD THEY TURNED ME DOWN

Sadly, I would miss out on that scholarship and I’m glad they turned me down as I didn’t end up getting a PhD or DPhil offer from Cambridge or Oxford that year and it would have been a waste to be offered a PhD scholarship with no PhD offer.

Learnt a hard life lesson: Ambition needs timing. Merit needs strategy.

If I had applied for direct Oxford DPhil / Cambridge PhD without Masters — which Oxbridge allows for First Class Honours + credible publications — and gotten no offer, a PhD scholarship would have been wasted.

Being turned down saved the Commonwealth slot for someone with offer. That is standards.

4. AS GOD WOULD HAVE IT, THERE WAS ALSO THE COMMONWEALTH SHARED

I had gotten a PG offer from one of three leading Energy Law universities in the world — others being Dundee and Texas. The third being Aberdeen — oil capital of Europe.

Aberdeen would graciously offer me the Commonwealth Shared Scholar title in conjunction with DFID UK — now known as FCDO.

Same FSB system.

5. THIS POST IS ABOUT FSB STANDARDS

But this post is about FSB and how they keep to standards as I know a good number of colleagues who got the Commonwealth on merit. Not Commonwealth Shared that I got. The Commonwealth Scholar with the nominating agency as the Federal Scholarship Board — FSB — working hand in hand with the Federal Ministry of Education.

I know them. On merit.

FSB kept to standards. That is why I can say today — after Nigeria at 66 — that merit can prevail in Nigeria.

Thank You FSB. Thank You Federal Ministry of Education.

@FSBNigeria @NigEducation @commschols @FCDOGovUK @aberdeenuni

text:
Explore how planets form. Help build the tools to discover their history.

The Origins Collective at the University of Hong Kong invites curious, ambitious students to join our growing research team. Our strengths in cosmochemistry, isotope geochemistry, geochronology, and planetary evolution connect fundamental questions about the Solar System with the development of new analytical and theoretical tools.

Our Project Lion Rock — Hong Kong’s gateway to Mars was recently selected by Hong Kong’s Innovation and Technology Commission. It will enable us to build an ambitious research infrastructure featuring a state-of-the-art clean laboratory and several advanced mass spectrometers to prepare for the analysis of samples returned by future space missions.

We will also participate in a broad collaborative project to fly a near-infrared spectrometer aboard the Tianwen-3 spacecraft to map the mineralogy of potential landing sites and monitor dust activity in the Martian atmosphere.

Join us at a formative moment, with opportunities to help shape new facilities and research directions.

We welcome students with diverse talents and backgrounds in Earth and planetary sciences, chemistry, physics, and engineering, with interests in any of three areas:

1. Experimental cosmochemistry and geochemistry

2. Mass spectrometry, with broad applications across Earth and planetary sciences

3. Atomistic simulations and theory

Our close connections with leading universities worldwide, including Tohoku University in Japan, give students access to an extended network of planetary science experts and opportunities for international collaboration.

Hong Kong offers an equally compelling setting for life beyond the laboratory. It is an international city where cultures meet and Cantonese, Mandarin, and English are widely spoken. Its energy is famous. Its quiet beaches, green mountains, and spectacular hiking trails are less widely appreciated. Few places bring city life and outdoor escape so close together.

Bring your curiosity, technical ingenuity, or passion for theory. Help us uncover the history of Earth and the Solar System.

For enquiries, contact Professor Nicolas Dauphas at dauphas@hku.hk.

Jiddu knew that the illusions of mind that the vast majority are trapped in are deep and thick and mostly go unnoticed. You can see this in his writings and talks as he explores many ways we get caught up in the illusions of the minds we create for ourselves. 

It’s hard to break free of the cage if you can’t see it. It’s much like the matrix in the movie of the same name. Most people have no idea they are living in what is essentially a dream world and even when they get some idea that they are they can’t seem to find the exit.
In the movie, Morpheus offers Neo two pills and says this about them:

Blue Pill: “The story ends, you wake up in your bed and believe whatever you want to believe.”

Red Pill: “You stay in Wonderland, and I show you how deep the rabbit hole goes.”

Jiddu was offering people the red pill. Knowing how caught up in the illusions most of us are he prodded and in a way pushed people out of their comfort zone (the illusion). He did so by speaking to the issues that arise from the way people think and what they hold dear, what they crave and cling to – their mundane relationships, authorities, endless searches for things that make one feel good and the ever elusive pursuit of ‘happiness’, though most don’t even know it actually means or takes to be truly happy.

They search for these things using the old mind, but if doing this could help them attain happiness and end suffering they would have attained them already.

But, like many good teachers he knew that to help people break free of their cages he needed to deconstruct the illusions they cling to. In a way, it’s like shattering the mirror that encases us for it is  what keeps perceiving things as we are and not as they are. This can be very uncomfortable, but he didn’t leave us there.
He also spoke of ways to transcend the limitations of mind and in a way re-balance ourselves.

In this excerpt he is using passion as the prod, challenging our understanding of it and revealing the subjective way we ‘use it’, or perhaps aptly – the way we abuse it.
“To understand something you must have passion, the intensity of complete attention. Where there is the passion for something, which produces contradiction, conflict, this pure flame of passion cannot be; and this pure flame of passion must exist in order to end sorrow, dissipate it completely.”
He wasn’t speaking of the passion – aka desire – for something but the passion that arises when we get out of the old mind and start to perceive things as they truly are. This is why working to end the separation we’ve created between ourselves, the observer, and what we observe (including ourselves) is singularly important. It is this separation that keeps us from love and all that ‘flows with it’.

Jiddu used beauty as an example:
“Without passion how can there be beauty? I do not mean the beauty of pictures, buildings, painted women, and all the rest of it. They have their own forms of beauty. A thing put together by man, like a cathedral, a temple, a picture, a poem, or a statue may or may not be beautiful. But there is a beauty which is beyond feeling and thought and which cannot be realized, understood, or known if there is not passion.”

This speaks again to the separation that the subjective mind creates and what lies beyond it, which is the bolded text in the above quote. He continued to speak about it in the third section, A PASSION FOR EVERYTHING.
“But I am using the word passion in the sense of a state of mind, a state of being, a state of your inward core, if there is such a thing, that feels very strongly, that is highly sensitive—sensitive alike to dirt, to squalor, to poverty, and to enormous riches and corruption, to the beauty of a tree, of a bird, to the flow of water, and to a pond that has the evening sky reflected upon it.”

He then brings love back into the picture, unconditional love, for it’s 🗝️…
“…but I am talking of something entirely different—a passion that loves. LOVE IS A STATE IN WHICH THERE IS NO “ME”; LOVE IS A STATE IN WHICH THERE IS NO CONDEMNATION…”

And he spoke about how contradiction does not exist in love. The division and conflict only ends when we’ve ended the separation that Jiddu spoke of and wrote about throughout these excerpts Etienne’s been sharing with us all. It’s the ending of separation that allows us to Be Love…

To attain what he said it’s important to read, contemplate and meditate on this and all the excerpts as often as it takes and be serious and persistent in doing so.

We also must do so with quiet a mind and by being as fully attentive as possible, otherwise we will be analyzing and thinking about his words and won’t truly understand them.

So… stay present, as best you can, and take one 👣 into the ‘magical world’ world down the rabbit hole and then another 👣… and keep going

text:
A DAY OF CELEBRATION, A BELATED TRIBUTE

Yesterday was filled with happy occasions, cherished friendships and responsibilities close to my heart. Yet, amid it all, I missed the birthday of a man very dear to me: Dr Yemi Farounbi.

My friend, Engr Yomi Aluko, was honoured with a chieftaincy title, and I had the pleasure of joining in his celebration. Congratulations, my dear friend! May this honour bring you greater fulfilment and fresh opportunities to serve your community.

It was also the 95th birthday of Chief Deji Fasuan, one of the titans whose vision and persistence helped bring Ekiti State into being. Seeing him was a duty of affection and gratitude. At 95, he remains a living link to the struggle that gave us a state of our own. As Ekiti celebrates its 30th anniversary, we celebrate him and the other pioneers who helped make that dream a reality. Happy birthday, Baba! May you continue to enjoy good health, peace and the love of a grateful people.

I also had to chair a meeting of the committee planning the 30th anniversary of Ekiti’s creation. By the time I returned home, the house was full of friends who had come to celebrate Engr Aluko. There was laughter, conversation and the warmth of reunion. Somewhere in that joyful bustle, Dr Farounbi’s birthday slipped past me.

Today, I offer him the tribute he so richly deserves.

Dr Yemi Farounbi is a man of ideas, creativity, principle and integrity. To our family, he is much more. He is my wife’s uncle, the man who supported her through school and helped lay the foundation for the woman she became.

When I sought her hand in marriage, he was the first person she took me to meet—even before taking me to her parents. That introduction marked the beginning of a relationship I have treasured ever since.

Over the years, he has been a father, mentor and source of inspiration to us both. I have benefited immensely from his wisdom, especially because we share a deep concern for Nigeria and a longing to see our country fulfil its promise.

There are people whose influence is measured in the lives they nurture, the values they uphold and the example they set. Dr Farounbi is one such man, and I remain grateful for his place in our lives.

Happy belated birthday, Sir. Please forgive my late greeting. May God grant you many more years in good health, peace and joy. May you continue to find fulfilment in the lives you have shaped and the affection of those who hold you dear.

With love, respect and enduring gratitude.

text:
The Everland Book; Opposites that Attract; Short Story Gift for @clansoniudo2; Based on https://t.co/S2VaEmQyeW #theeverlandbook #Flame #Flake #Frostfire
-------
Fire. The element that carried the power to nurture and destroy. It was a force of nature so often mischaracterized by those who not only inhabited the world, but relied on it to live, to warm their homes, cook their food, and keep them safe from the darkness with it's light. Yet the power of flames was frequently associated with a singular aspect of it's existence, destruction.

In a world where the Elemental embodiments existed as natural inhabitants of the world itself, fire was so often feared for this quality, those whom possessed it were often looked upon with fear, even repulsed by their existence. For what could such intense heat ever bring other then raw uncontrolled destruction to everything around it.

One such being, known as Flame was targeted by this mindset time and time again by the narrowed minded members of the community around him. His heart beat with the power so many found dreadful, they sneered, grunted and avoided him. All because he existed...it wasn't his fault...they never seemed to give him a chance...and those who did became the unshakeable pillars of his life. He wasn't entirely alone. He would grow his physical strength, he would raise the walls around his heart, and he will be strong. For those who accepted him, who felt comfort in his presence, rather then then fear.

His pride grew, his confidence grew, opening his eyes a bit more, despite the tragic loss he had suffered so long ago. And when he did, he couldn't help but be jealous of one particular group of people in his world. The Ice Cats. Paraded around like a bunch of idols, like perfect divas of the world. Admired and loved for their power to control Ice, the element opposite to his own.

Flame did not understand the appeal, for Ice could easily bring the same destruction as Fire, but they were applauded, celebrated. While he was rejected and frowned upon. Even when he attempted to be friendly, he was blown away, his fire nearly completely smothered by the harsh winds of that wicked women of the wind.

There was no comfort in that moment he could be offered, for like a candle, even his most honest attempts at being friendly and make other companions, was blown out the instant he stepped to far from what others considered to be the 'polite' distance with a Fire Dog like himself. All he could do was mourn in solitude of his terrible lot in life, for not even the comfort of his companions were enough...

Till the very last person he ever expected to come to him, would not only offer an apology...but words of encouragement...the exact same words spoken by another of the distance past...he felt his heart ignite, but could not express it. For he did not even know the extent of it himself at time time.

Halloween. Christmas. Valentines. Days of mutual celebration, where he noticed moments that could only be measured as impossibilities that only added more and more to his already vast confusion. Was he being mocked? His presence treated like some exotic experience to be enjoyed because that feline of the snow was bored with the usual praise and luxury filled life?

Again and again the Cold came. Flake was his name, flowing around him like a draft of chilled air. He ignored those moments the best he could. Even outright denied the sneaking feelings to even to himself. But he could not help but gaze at him from afar...with that thump in his chest. How dare he look so...happy being around something others despised to much...it must've been an act...but what if it wasn't...?

To cloak these feelings he did not know how to measure nor manage on his own, he took up sarcastic, mocking humor to hide the weight growing on his heart, of a romance that couldn't possibly be felt, not by the feline that had the love of the people and not by the canine hated by them all.

It was supposed to be innocent fun, a way to laugh off, and even make fun of the feelings he held within himself for the sheer audacity his heart committed by allowing feelings to blossom in the first place. But...he did not know he was mocking another's...

One joke to far. Flake usually never reacted and even awkwardly laughed off his humor most of the time, even putting some distance between the two of them. Flame always took those moments as victories proving how right he was about the entire situation, and how it felt to mess with someone the people adored so much like he had been for ages.

But not today...he did not expect the anger, the words, nor the level of reaction his 'fun' would have on someone he assumed would never even consider him worthy of sharing the same air space. But the biting tone, the volume of his voice, and the very words boomed in his ears. 'Insensitive. Jerk. Mean-spirited.' He never expected someone at the bottom like he was, could ever make someone as 'perfect' as Flake feel so ostracized...

As he watched the feline stomp away, he was in shock, unable to move his limbs, his eyes wide, and mind blank. The world felt muted, with only the memories of the fury the feline held staying within his vision...it reminded him of the feelings that overtook him during April Fools, where a prank went wrong, and his world crumbled, but this time...it felt...unreal.

Most of his friends surrounded him, offering him words of encouragement, waving Flake's reaction off as being prissy and dramatic. But not Bunny. A rabbit of stone, with a morale compass as solid as she was, the person who ignored the opinions of others, and always did what she felt was right. Was glowering over at him, a face she made many times to the women of wind, Blow.

He couldn't leave things this way. With a silent march, one taken with slow footsteps at first, that became more of a power walk, the canine followed the flow of cold he had grown accustom to with Flake. He was silent, not letting a single complicated emotion show on his face as he marched, till he found him. Laying there in the grass beside the river that flowed through the area of their community.

There were no words to say as he walked over to the feline, whom did not move nor speak as well, despite his arrival, as he lowered himself down to lay upon the grass as well, burning the patch with his body of flames as he normally did with most things he touched while not controlling his body temperature, but he was careful enough to not effect Flake. The two gazing up at the sky in silence for a time. Till the first words were spoken...
----
The canine of fire grunted due to the uncomfortable twist in his chest and the tension in the air from the silence between them, there was normally something exchanged between them by now, but Flake said nothing.

 "Look. I'm...not the best with...the feeling stuff. And. I was...pretty...mean to you. That wasn't okay of me..." it was hard to put the words together, not due to a wounded pride nor reluctance to apologize, he just couldn't find the words, but despite his attempts to expression how apologetic he was, it failed to move Flake, who remained quiet through it all, not even a physical reaction that told Flame his words were heard.

He couldn't help but grumble a bit out of slight frustration, not towards Flake, but himself for allowing this to happen "I was just messing around, I...tend to joke around with my friends, but you-" He stopped himself for a moment to process his next words "You were the target of some...pretty mean ones today, so I am sorry."

With effort, he was able to finally get out the apology Flake was owed, spoken in his own way of articulation, but he couldn't help but feel awkward. The words themselves felt to...casual for the effect he had on the feline. But right as he was about to speak, his lips parting to let out his next thoughts, Flake finally ended his silence.

"You know...for someone so physically bright, you sure are in the dark about a lot of things..." the feline spoke quietly, with a soft tone, as his paws that rested on his stomach shifted to unclasp his fingers from each other, to rest one hand on top of the other.

The canine could only blink in silence, confused by the response he was given, till Flake spoke again, causing him to look over to the snowcat, this time, raising his voice and starting his sentence with a heavy sigh he had been holding on to the moment the firedog approached him "Do you know why I appear to 'annoy' you? Do you know why I always seem happy when I see you? Am I truly as transparent to you as all the others...?"

The questions thrown at him were unexpected, leaving Flame in a state of blank mindedness, as he looked back up towards the sky. His mind was lost in whirlwind of conflict...because his heart knew, but his mind refused to accept it...

"You're...probably one of the only people who understands me...and it hurts thinking I am so invisible to you..." The tone was soft, filled with a sorrow he had never heard the feline ever show outward before "I know your plight so well...I see how others treat you...how isolated you are at times...and I resonate with that. Because I...feel the same..."

There were a mix of feelings that followed the words the feline spoke within the canine's mind, the trauma he had been inflicted for so many years, the solitude he was forced into. It began to piss him off with how someone so admired spoke of understanding his suffering, but he was going to listen to everything Flake had to say, he owed him that much right now.

(Insert Once Upon a December Music Box Music Here)

"When you are Ice..." Lifting his paw up, Flake would open his hand just enough to form a beautiful singular thin crystal of ice between his fingers "You must be perfect...you must be contained..." Gently blowing on the snowflake charged with his elemental power, the feline and canine watched as it gently began to descend, in a circular dance, as if demonstrating it's beauty to it's audience of two.

As the snowflake drifted, Flake spoke "Ice can be beautiful if controlled...never stepping out of line...dazzling it's beholders...because the power of Winter is as devastating as a wild fire...so we are meant to ensure those around us know we are in check...we promote ourselves as jewels instead of frost...the standard for us is set high..."

"Never allowed to be anything other then a perfect little snowflake...snowflakes are all different from one another they say, but we're forced to fit a mold...it's ironic...and despite my desire to never break that mold...I feel myself to be as fragile and helpless at times...falling, and...eventually...breaking from this pressure I'm under..."

The snowflake the feline had created gently shattered when the word 'pressure' was spoken, with the feline lowering his arm down to rest his paw on the other once more "When I'm around you, someone who endures despite the public's narrow mind, I feel stronger...safer...like I would never be judged if I was myself...but, today...I don't know..."

Silence fell upon their conversation once more, with both elementals processing everything that was spoken, gazing up at the same sky, from two different worlds. Flame had never heard of a Frostcat being unhappy with the sort of lives they lived, nor of the burdens they carried themselves. It was...something he had never expected. He felt like such an idiot. But he also felt a level of understanding he was lacking till now when it came to Flake.

He felt a soft surge his heart, inspiration that was strong enough to overcome his usual stubbornness and inadequate skill with emotion, as he took his turn to speak "I just thought you hung around me, acted playful towards me, and interacted with me because it gave you some sense of superiority over me. Like you were comparing your perfection to my...lack of...gloating with your presence alone, with how great you had it..."

Flake frowned just a little at the very image Flame had of him within his mind. He felt his heart stir, becoming apologetic "I am sorry I never made myself clear to you about why I liked being around you...I never acted the way I did as I did with you, with others...so I thought it was clear I enjoyed spending time with you. But...looking back, I can see where the confusion set in..."

"I'm not the best with that sort of thing either, so...I apologize as well." Flame said as he snorted a small flame upwards from his nose at how foolish he felt, for their entire relationship was built on a misunderstanding to this point...created by a lack of communication. Bunny was going to give him a fat 'I told you so' later...he knew it "Being treated the way I am at times, I am quick to put my guard up. And...I was being stupid-

Flake was quick to turn his head to look at Flame with a serious, almost offended expression on his face at the fact the canine insulted himself "I don't think you're stupid!" He said a bit louder then he intended, causing his cheeks to lightly flush under his light blue flaked 'fur', his head turning back to the direction of the sky, while Flame's head turned to look at Flake, with his own cheeks flushed a bit red, redder then his orange fur could hide.

"Do you honestly believe I'm not upset when Blow and the others treat you poorly...?" the snow cat's tone of voice lowered softly, as he fidget his thumbs together "Of course I am...I even tell her she's being to much at times...so does Shine...I know where you're coming from with you're on your guard...I just wish...-" Flake stopped himself, as his face flushed just a bit more, even turning his head a little to look away from Flame.

But the canine of fire wasn't about to let that sentence go unfinished, for he nudged himself a bit closer, close enough to the point his arm was nearly touching Flake's, with his orange eyes gazing upon the feline who bashfully looked away from him. The canine's expression was...the softest it had ever been in this moment, and Flake could feel it, drawing him back to the words he attempted to hide.

Taking a soft breath, Flake gazed back up at the sky, while his face remained flushed from the genuine in Flame's eyes that he could feel "I just wish you would let me in those walls...because I feel a strong connection with you..."

Flame's eyes then grew as soft as his face, as his eyebrows lifted with emotions that felt lighter then air...the upper part of his head, and his flaming ears growing into a bright orange compared to the rest of his usual red body to the sound of those words...
----
End of Scene

text:
THE WORLD’S OLDEST TATTOO TOOLS WERE HIDING IN THESE BONES

Long before tattoo machines, tattoo needles, or modern body art, people were already marking their skin with permanent designs. But a discovery in Tennessee has pushed the history of tattooing in North America back more than 5,000 years.

The story begins with two ordinary-looking turkey leg bones. They were excavated in 1985 from the Fernvale archaeological site in Tennessee, where they were found alongside other objects that may have formed part of an ancient tattooing kit. For decades, their real purpose remained a mystery.

Then archaeologists took a much closer look.

Using microscopic imaging, researchers found tiny patterns of wear and traces of red and black pigment on the sharpened bones. When compared with tools used in modern experiments to recreate ancient tattooing techniques, the marks closely matched what would be expected from repeatedly pushing a pigment-covered tool into skin.

The bones were dated to between about 3,620 and 5,520 years ago, making them the oldest known tattooing tools ever discovered.

That means people in what is now the United States were practicing tattooing thousands of years ago — long before written records described these traditions.

There is an even stranger twist. Ötzi the Iceman, whose body was discovered preserved in the European Alps, has the oldest tattoos known on a human body, dating back more than 5,000 years. But the actual tools used to create Ötzi’s tattoos have never been found.

In Tennessee, archaeologists may have found something even more revealing: the tools themselves.

The discovery offers a rare glimpse into a practice that was clearly important enough to require specialized tools, pigments, and skill. What those ancient tattoos looked like — and what they meant to the people who wore them — may never be known.

More than 5,000 years ago, someone sharpened these bones, covered them with pigment, and pressed them into human skin. The marks they created are long gone — but their tools survived.

Source: Bower, B. The oldest known tattoo tools were found at an ancient Tennessee site, Science News. Based on research by Deter-Wolf, A., Peres, T. M., & Karacic, S., Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.

text: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attempts, leading the state's governor to halt all executions for the year.We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. "But we do know that she is alive right now." She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive, her lawyers said. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.Her lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".On Thursday afternoon, Pike's lawyers offered more details about what happened during the attempted execution, describing a harrowing scene shrouded in secrecy. Her attempted execution on Wednesday was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.Last night, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line for an hour," Spivey said. "I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."Spivey said that observers were kept in a dark room behind a closed curtain, after the second lethal dose had been administered and "it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing" minutes later.

text:
Ernst Röhm was a German army captain, early co-founder of the Nazi Party, and the powerful head of the paramilitary Sturmabteilung (SA/Brownshirts) who was executed on Hitler's orders during the 1934 Night of the Long Knives.

A loaded revolver placed on an iron table offered Ernst Röhm his final choice. On the afternoon of July 1, 1934, inside cell 474 of Munich’s Stadelheim Prison, the commander of Nazi Germany’s three-million-man paramilitary force sat in isolation. Hours earlier, Adolf Hitler had personally arrested him at dawn in a Bavarian lakeside resort. For over a decade, the scarred army captain had been Hitler’s chief enforcer, building the brownshirted Sturmabteilung into a brutal street army that cleared the party's path to power. Röhm was Hitler's closest comrade, one of the few permitted to address him with the informal "Du." But in the brutal calculations of power, the street fighter had become a mortal threat. On Hitler's direct orders, SS officers left the pistol and gave him ten minutes to pull the trigger.

The bond between Hitler and Röhm had been forged in postwar Munich’s chaotic underworld. A decorated combat veteran who had lost part of his nose to shrapnel, Röhm was a serving officer in the Bavarian military command who funneled army weapons, trucks, and clandestine funds to Hitler’s obscure fringe movement. In 1921, Röhm organized the SA, transforming tavern brawlers and unemployed youths into an intimidating force of political muscle. He marched beside Hitler during the disastrous 1923 Beer Hall Putsch, sharing imprisonment at Landsberg. Although ideological friction led Röhm to spend several years as a military adviser in Bolivia, Hitler recalled him in late 1930 to take command of the SA. Under Röhm’s aggressive leadership, the Brownshirts expanded rapidly, waging relentless street wars against communists and democracy until Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933.

Once Hitler entered the chancellery, the partnership fractured over the future of the revolution. While Hitler sought to reassure big business and the aristocratic generals of the Reichswehr to prepare for national rearmament, Röhm demanded a radical "second revolution." The SA chief viewed the traditional social order with contempt and insisted that his three-million-man militia absorb the regular army into a single "people's army" under his personal command. To the Prussian officer corps, Röhm’s ambition was an intolerable provocation. Defense Minister Werner von Blomberg and top generals warned Hitler that the army would never tolerate an armed street militia supplanting the armed forces. As President Paul von Hindenburg’s health failed, the army made its ultimatum clear: rein in Röhm, or martial law would end the Nazi government.

Röhm’s defiance provided his internal rivals with the ammunition they needed. SS chief Heinrich Himmler and Prussian interior minister Hermann Göring viewed the SA as an existential barrier to their own ascendancy. Along with Reinhard Heydrich, they fabricated dossiers alleging that Röhm was orchestrating an armed coup—the so-called "Röhm Putsch"—subsidized by French funds. Faced with losing the backing of the military and the state, Hitler abandoned his oldest comrade. In the early morning hours of June 30, 1934, during the Night of the Long Knives, Hitler arrived with armed police at the Hotel Hanselbauer in Bad Wiessee. Brandishing a whip, Hitler personally confronted Röhm in his bedroom, shouting that he was under arrest. Across Germany, SS hit squads systematically hunted down and murdered dozens of SA commanders and conservative political rivals.

text:
I see it now.  It was a pejorative way of speaking, and I understand why it could be seen as offensive.  I could’ve used more polite language to talk about the point that the early Church did not believe that Christian’s should wield  the sword against wrong doers.  They believed that the Roman state was doing that, and that it did restrain evil. 

However, they did not believe that Christians should take on that role. Rather, they should convert the empire to the nonviolent kingdom of Jesus and then such a role will no longer be necessary.   It may sound unrealistic, but it is what they believed.   

For example, Origen said in Contra Celsus Book 8 Chapter 65, “But whilst we do nothing which is contrary to the law and word of God, we are not so mad as to stir up against us the wrath of kings and princes, which will bring upon us sufferings and tortures, or even death. For we read: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God.”  

This is where he is using the language of Romans 13.  However, later he makes it clear that this is not the role of Christians are to undertake.  This is what I meant by “snatching the sword”  

He says an 8.73 “And none fight better for the king than we do. We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it; but we fight on his behalf, forming a special army—an army of piety—by offering our prayers to God… we no longer take up sword against nation, nor do we learn war any more, having become children of peace, for the sake of Jesus, who is our leader.”

He also says that if every Roman became a Christian, “they will not war at all,” being protected by God rather than by arms (Against Celsus 8.70). In the same work he states that Christ “nowhere teaches that it is right for His own disciples to offer violence to anyone, no matter how wicked,” and that Christian laws do not allow resistance even to persecutors “even when it was their fate to be slain as sheep.”

Origen’s commentary on Romans itself adds a limit: the duty of submission does not cover authorities who persecute the faith; there one must “obey God rather than men.” Submission, for him, meant taxes, honor, and quiet, not participation in the magistrate’s sword.  

Tertullian (c. 160–220) makes the same link from Jesus’ words rather than from a direct exegesis of Romans 13. 

In On the Military Crown (De Corona) 11 he asks: “Shall it be held lawful to make an occupation of the sword, when the Lord proclaims that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword? And shall the son of peace take part in the battle when it does not become him even to sue at law?”

And in On Idolatry 19 he stays, “How will a Christian man war, nay, how will he serve even in peace, without a sword, which the Lord has taken away? … the Lord, in disarming Peter, unbelted every soldier.”

I retract the term “snatching the sword” because I can see how it was offensive.  However, the basic argument still I still believe.  The early church did not interpret Romans 13 as giving Christians the right to use this word to execute other people.

According to Bloomberg, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly floated a potentially significant proposal during private talks in New York:

➡️ restore IAEA inspectors’ access to nuclear facilities hit by airstrikes;
➡️ in exchange for sanctions relief.

The idea was reportedly presented to European and Middle Eastern diplomats on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

⚠️ But caution is warranted.

At this stage, this is not an official proposal publicly announced by Tehran.

And an Iranian source quoted by the Fars news agency has already denied that Iran offered the Americans an “inspections-for-sanctions-relief” deal.

Still, the context makes this report noteworthy.

Iran has just received a U.S. response to its latest proposal, while Qatari mediators continue facilitating indirect contacts between Washington and Tehran.

After several weeks in which military confrontation overshadowed negotiations, a potential bargaining framework appears to be resurfacing:

nuclear oversight ↔ sanctions ↔ the Strait of Hormuz ↔ military de-escalation.

This does not yet amount to a return to the negotiating table.

But if the offer reported by Bloomberg is confirmed, it could be one of the first signs that the diplomatic channel on the nuclear issue is reopening.

A development to watch carefully.

text:
US vs Iran
The real hesitation over a boots-on-the-ground option may not be about whether America can put boots on the ground. It is about whether Washington is willing to accept the price once those boots are actually there.
Bombs, missiles and drones offer distance, deniability and political insulation. Ground troops offer none of that. They come with casualties, prisoners, escalation, body bags and, eventually, the question every government dreads: how do you get them home?
In modern warfare, sending the boots may be the easy part. Living with what happens after they land is the hard part.
And perhaps that is the real hesitation. Not a shortage of boots, but a shortage of appetite for what those boots might step into.

Taiwan's coast guard sprayed several Chinese fishing boats with water cannons.
Taiwan's water cannon response is best read as Taipei using China's own playbook against it.  Beijing prefers "gray zone" pressure: coast guard ships and civilian-looking maritime militia instead of the navy, and small incremental steps (the "salami slicing" or "cabbage strategy") that build a new normal without ever crossing the line into war.

In the 2014 oil rig standoff, coast guard and militia boats worked together. So Chinese fishing boats operating in numbers near Taiwan are rarely just fishing boats in Beijing's strategy.

By answering with coast guard water cannons rather than warships, Taipei pushes back at the same low level and denies Beijing an easy excuse to call it a military escalation. The timing raises the stakes.
A record $14bn US arms package for Taiwan is still unapproved after the 24 September Trump-Xi state visit, and Beijing is pressing Washington to move from "not supporting" to "opposing" Taiwan independence.  Taipei may want to show it can defend its waters on its own while US support looks negotiable. But Beijing could also frame the incident as Taiwanese aggression against civilians and use it to justify another round of the encirclement drills it has run since 2016, which is Freeman's "aggressive option" of making Taiwan "an offer it can't refuse".

text:
The Middle East just became the biggest macro risk for markets again.

The U.S. is sending a third carrier strike group and another 9,000 to 10,000 troops into the region, while the naval blockade of Iranian ports continues.

At least three oil tankers were attacked near the Strait of Hormuz this week.

That part has already happened.

Brent closed around $102 on October 1, up more than 4% on the day and roughly 41% from the $72 level before the February crisis. WTI is around $92 to $93.

The market is already pricing a serious geopolitical premium into energy.

China also paused exports of refined fuel in October, which makes any additional disruption through Hormuz even harder to absorb.

The immediate reaction is exactly what you would expect:

The 10 year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, its highest level since 2002.

DXY is around 102.

Gold is near $4,210.

Bitcoin is moving between $84,000 and $86,000 while equities are starting to feel the pressure.

The confusing part is that this is both inflationary and risk off.

Oil going higher keeps inflation alive, which gives the Fed less room to cut. Higher yields and a stronger dollar usually hurt tech stocks, long duration assets and crypto first.

Energy and defense are the obvious winners. Transport and consumer companies are the obvious losers.

Bitcoin probably trades like a risk asset during the first phase of any escalation. It is still tied closely enough to Nasdaq liquidity that a stronger dollar and higher real yields can overwhelm the digital gold narrative.

But the next move depends on what happens from here.

A further attack on Iran, a broader blockade, or a serious interruption through Hormuz could push Brent toward $110 to $115. Barclays is already using that range for its fourth quarter forecast.

That is a forecast, not a current price.

The other possible outcome is diplomacy. Iran has offered to reopen Hormuz in exchange for sanctions relief, and any credible ceasefire would remove a lot of the oil premium very quickly.

There is another risk being underpriced.

Putin said Russia is prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if Kaliningrad is directly attacked or blockaded by NATO. That does not mean nuclear conflict is the base case, but it adds another escalation channel while markets are already dealing with Iran.

My read is simple:

This is bearish for bonds and growth stocks in the short term, bullish for oil and the dollar, and selectively bullish for gold.

Bitcoin needs liquidity more than it needs a good narrative. If the Fed stays hawkish because energy inflation returns, BTC probably struggles first.

If the shock lasts long enough to damage confidence in fiat and government debt, the hedge trade can come back hard.

That second scenario is possible. It just is not happening yet.

text:
OpenAI Fires Safety Team Members for Leaks

As we wrap up another week in the tech world, here’s a story that might leave you scratching your head. OpenAI just fired three employees from their Safety / Alignment department after an internal investigation found them guilty of sharing confidential information with external organizations focused on AI safety.

So, what gives? These folks were supposed to be the guardians against rogue AI systems, ensuring that OpenAI stays ahead of potential dangers. But instead of being hailed as heroes for sounding the alarm, they’re out of a job. Why would someone in charge of preventing an AI apocalypse feel compelled to leak information?
OpenAI Fires Safety Team Members for Leaks
The twist here is that these employees were likely acting as whistleblowers, seeing potential dangers in unchecked AI development and deciding that internal safeguards weren’t enough. However, their actions violated OpenAI’s strict confidentiality protocols.

This raises a critical question: if the people tasked with ensuring safety feel the need to go public with their concerns, does it suggest that internal checks might not be robust or transparent enough? It’s a stark reminder of how tight-lipped these companies are becoming about anything related to AI safety.
What Changed?
OpenAI’s decision to fire these employees highlights a shift in corporate culture towards stricter confidentiality. Previously, whistleblowers were often seen as heroes for bringing attention to potential risks. Now, however, the company is taking a hard stance against any form of information leakage, even if it means silencing voices that might otherwise raise important safety concerns.
How It Works
OpenAI’s internal investigation likely involved reviewing emails, chat logs, and other forms of communication to determine whether the employees had breached confidentiality protocols. The decision to fire them was based on a clear violation of these rules, which are designed to protect sensitive information about AI development from falling into the wrong hands.
What Is Stored?
OpenAI’s internal systems store vast amounts of data related to AI research and development, including codebases, experimental results, and detailed documentation. This information is crucial for maintaining the integrity and security of their projects but also makes it a prime target for leaks if employees feel that transparency is necessary.
What Is Excluded?
The leaked information was likely limited to specific details about potential risks in AI development rather than broader technical data or source code. The external organization receiving this information would have been focused on assessing the safety implications of these findings, not necessarily on replicating OpenAI’s work.
User Controls
Employees at OpenAI are expected to adhere strictly to confidentiality agreements and internal protocols designed to prevent unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information. Any deviation from these rules can result in severe consequences, including termination of employment.
Availability
The story highlights the ongoing tension between transparency and security within AI research organizations like OpenAI. While some argue for more openness to ensure public safety, others believe that strict confidentiality is necessary to protect proprietary technology and prevent misuse.
What This Does Not Prove
It’s important to note that this incident does not prove anything about the effectiveness of OpenAI’s internal safety measures or the validity of the whistleblowers’ concerns. It simply highlights a conflict between confidentiality protocols and whistleblowing practices in an industry where transparency is crucial.
The Financial Side: Anthropic Gets $42 Billion
Now, let’s pivot to another story. Broadcom is reportedly ready to offer Anthropic up to $42 billion in financing for computational infrastructure. That’s a serious chunk of change aimed at building out the hardware needed to run advanced AI systems. So while some are worried about an AGI apocalypse, others are busy pouring billions into the tech that could make it happen.
The Irony: Tightening Screws vs. Opening Coffers
The irony here is that while one company (OpenAI) is tightening the screws on information sharing, another (Anthropic) is opening its coffers wider than ever before. This kind of investment can lead to faster progress but also raises questions about oversight and regulation.
The Big Picture: Innovation vs. Safety
So what does this mean for you? It means that despite concerns over safety and ethics, there’s still a massive push for more powerful AI systems. Anthropic is getting a huge financial boost to build out its infrastructure, which will likely accelerate their research and development.

But it also highlights the need for transparency and accountability in the tech community. As these technologies continue to evolve at breakneck speed, we need to keep an eye on both sides: companies like OpenAI cracking down on information sharing and others like Anthropic pushing full steam ahead with massive investments.
The Fine Print
It’s worth noting that while this story focuses on OpenAI’s actions, it doesn’t prove anything about the effectiveness of their internal safety measures. It simply highlights a conflict between confidentiality protocols and whistleblowing practices in an industry where transparency is crucial.

Moreover, Anthropic’s $42 billion investment underscores the massive financial backing behind AI research but also raises concerns about oversight and regulation as these systems become more powerful.
What Does This Mean for You?
So what changes for you? Well, it highlights how tight-lipped companies are becoming about anything related to AI safety. OpenAI’s move sends a clear message: if you’re going to work on the cutting edge of AI ethics and security, you better not be talking outside the office walls.

But it also means that as an observer or stakeholder in this field, you need to stay informed and vigilant. The tech community needs transparency and accountability more than ever as these technologies continue to evolve at breakneck speed.
Discuss Away!
Let’s talk about it in the comments below. What do you think is the right balance between innovation and safety? Should companies be allowed to keep their AI research so tightly under wraps, or should we demand more openness and scrutiny?
