text:
Podcast Summary | Candace: LEAKED! Erika’s Texts, TPUSA Contracts, And The J6 Patsy’s Connection To Tyler Robinson. | Ep 396

Overview
The core thread running through this episode is a claim that Turning Point USA rapidly became a money-and-donor operation in the days after Charlie Kirk’s death, with Erica Kirk stepping into CEO and chairman roles within 48 hours and immediately focusing on wealthy supporters rather than the manhunt for the killer. Around that, Candace Owens layers in newly surfaced contracts, a student loan refinancing company called YRefi, a detailed timeline of Epstein-related meetings and donor pressure, and a separate argument that the January 6 pipe bomber case looks like another federal setup. The most consequential claim is that the same pattern appears across all of it: institutions protect money and narrative first, and the public gets a story that does not hold up under scrutiny.

Key Themes
- Erica Kirk’s swift elevation at TPUSA undercuts the grieving-widow narrative and points to donor and revenue priorities taking precedence over the search for Charlie’s killer.
- The YRefi relationship reframes the fall campus tour as a paid speaking pipeline, not a mission-driven event, and raises questions about what Charlie may have been trying to fix financially.
- A July 2025 one-page addendum adding $1.25 million specifically for the Charlie Kirk fall tour is presented as evidence the sponsorship was unusual and possibly retrofitted.
- Charlie’s shifting Israel stance and his lobbying against U.S. involvement in the Iran-Israel war coincide with donor backlash, Epstein pressure, and a White House confrontation.
- The Epstein situation-room meetings repeatedly fall on or near the release of Candace’s own Epstein episodes, which she frames as unnerving rather than coincidental.
- The January 6 pipe bomber case is presented as a coerced confession built on fear rather than evidence, with Brian Cole Jr. denied bond and pleading not guilty.
- The same two Scripps journalists obtaining obscure footage of both Tyler Robinson and Brian Cole Jr. is treated as a signal of coordination rather than routine reporting.

Detailed Summary
The episode opens with the claim that Erica Kirk assumed both CEO and chairman roles at TPUSA within 48 hours of Charlie’s death. Vanity Fair reportedly confirmed the timeline. Board member Doug DeGroot attributed the speed to pressure from journalists, not concern about the unlocated killer. Candace disputes that account, citing a PR source who says the rush was about securing control.

Erica allegedly celebrated merch sales at Charlie’s memorial and announced “Turning Point 2.0” on Zoom calls within the first two weeks. A Telegram group titled “Dominate 2.0” was reportedly used before the Mar-a-Lago event. In it, Erica asked for a full list of wealthy donors described as “big hitters” so she could “make notes.” Taylor Scornovako responded with a list sorted by major gift officers, noting “brand new six-figure donors.”

TPUSA encased Charlie’s bloodied microphone as a donor appeal at Mar-a-Lago and Amfest. The Mar-a-Lago event allegedly raised $40 million. Candace links Charlie’s heavy tour schedule to financial pressure after Zionist donors pulled millions over his shifting Israel stance.

The YRefi thread is the most contract-heavy portion. YRefi is a student loan refinancing company run by CEO Lane Shonberger. A February 5, 2025 contract ran through February 2026 and stated YRefi would pay TPUSA $2.25 million, though the listed payments total closer to $2.47 million. That contract voided all previous agreements and included Winter Gala sponsorship, America Fest donor dinners, a spring investor retreat, a young women’s leadership summit, a church event, Student Action Summit, Believer Summit, America Fest, and more. Benefits included platinum tables, Four Seasons rooms, speaking minutes, email blasts, VIP lounges, hyperl logo placement, kiosk ads, and naming the TPUSA feed theater the YRefi Theater.

YRefi requested Riley Gaines for several events, plus social media posts, IG stories, and three video endorsements shot at TPUSA headquarters and events. A proposed influencer list included Alex Clark, Riley Gaines, Morgan McMichael, Benny Johnson, Jack Pobic, Anthony Watson, Isabelle Brown, Lauren Chen, Chrissy Clark, and Savannah Hernandez. Candace says only Riley Gaines can be confirmed as participating. Additional benefits included Dean’s List banner mentions, Turning Point Ball participation with four hotel rooms, six seated inauguration tickets, and 25 Turning Point Ball tickets.

A July 25, 2025 one-page addendum added $1.25 million specifically for the Charlie Kirk fall campus tour. It covered 12 events and included a branded wall, presenting sponsorship title, premier branding for evening campus sessions, 5 minutes of mainstage speaking time, a mainstage video, and an email to all attendees. Lane Shonberger spoke for five minutes at UVU before the event. Candace notes there was no video opportunity at UVU despite the addendum mentioning one. She cannot confirm whether the money was actually paid, though employees past and present describe YRefi as “shady” with many contracts but alleged non-payment.

Mainstream coverage from the Daily Mail and UK International Business Times alleged YRefi paid TPUSA for speaking slots to pitch to college kids. The Daily Mail reported YRefi faced $750,000 in state sanctions in a settlement over deceptive marketing and investment materials aimed at private funders. Shonberger told reporters the company changed its investment marketing materials and resolved about $2.1 million in regulatory issues in Massachusetts in 2025. Allan Kh, founder of Student Loan Justice, is quoted criticizing the arrangement. TPUSA refused to comment.

Shonberger, his daughter, and Dylan Ericson were reportedly at UVU on the day of Charlie’s assassination and flew in together. Ericson is TPUSA’s sponsorship lead, allegedly also paid by YRefi, and runs an influencer management company that flew pro-Israel influencers to the Hamptons. Candace says she cannot confirm YRefi hand-selected UVU, only that it is hearsay. She ties the contracts to prior claims that money was missing at TPUSA, citing Charlie’s establishment of a “Doge” seven days before his death as reason to believe money was missing. She questions why the fall tour sponsorship was not in the original contract and suggests the late addendum may support a tip that Charlie intervened to make up missing money.

A large timeline follows. February 2025: YRefi initial agreement. February 11: TPUSA reopens a shuttered chapter at University of Nebraska Lincoln. February 12: Frank Turk speaks there. February 24: Charlie contacts Candace saying Emanuel Macron asked the White House for her to stop discussing Brexit. February 25: Sergio Gore calls Candace asking her to stop as a favor to Trump. February 26: Trump calls Candace and asks the same.

June 2025: Boston Consulting Group abandons the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation. Johnny Moore takes over as chairman of the Gaza Humanitarian Aid Project on June 3. June 13: the Iran-Israel 12-day war begins. June 17: UVU hosts a fake mass-casualty drill with crisis actors. June 18–19: Charlie argues at the White House for limited action. June 19: Erica deletes 126 Instagram posts. June 22: Operation Midnight Hammer. June 22: Bradley Hansel confirmed as Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

July: Netanyahu visits Washington July 7–9. July 9: Candace’s college video is archived for the first time. July 10: TPUSA asks UVU club president Caleb Chilikut to book Charlie for a courtyard event. July 11–13: Charlie speaks at Student Action Summit; Tucker Carlson tells him to go “max” on Epstein; donors including Bob Showman pull millions. July 11: Frank Turk deletes his website. July 12: Trump angrily calls Charlie and calls his event an “Epstein grievance fest.” July 14: Charlie announces he will stop covering Epstein. July 14: Erica flies private to Long Beach and speaks at James Catie’s Calvary Chapel, delivering a pro-Israel call to arms.

Candace premieres her Epstein series “Dead Men Tell No Tales” on July 9. The first episode, “The Midas Touch,” covers Epstein’s money, blackmail, DOJ, Bill Barr, Dalton School, and a fake genius persona. A situation room meeting on Epstein files reportedly occurs the same day, without Trump, with JD Vance, Susie Wilds, David Warrington, Todd Blanch, Steven Chung, Caroline Levit, Taylor Budawick, James Blair, Stanley Woodwick, Cash Patel, and Pam Bondi by phone. JD Vance argued for full files release.

July 18: a formal request is submitted for TPUSA’s UVU chapter event. July 20: an Egyptian plane flies Cairo–Paris–Omaha–Lincoln. Charlie vacations in Maine for a couple weeks with family. July 22: Candace drops episode 2, “House of Maxwell.” July 23: another Epstein situation room; House Oversight votes to subpoena the president on Epstein files. July 25: YRefi sponsors the Charlie Kirk fall tour. July 27: the Egyptian plane departs Wilmington and returns to Cairo. August 3: Charlie and Erica land in Bedford, New York for the Hamptons retreat. August 4–6: Netanyahu reportedly calls and offers to take Turning Point “to the next level,” and invites Charlie to Israel, which he declines. August 6: Charlie appears on Megan Kelly and alludes to Hamptons events. August 13: Candace drops “Mega Maga and the MSAD.” Another Epstein meeting runs about two hours.

A previously missing July 9 situation room meeting is added to the timeline, coinciding with BBNet/Yahoo in DC, the archived college video, and the first Epstein situation room over backlash to an FBI memo stating there was no Epstein list. The host plans an interactive public timeline with links within about a week.

The host argues Candace’s changed stance on Israel reads as inauthentic, and says you do not allow your husband’s enemies into his organization. The host disputes Andrew Wilson’s leaked texts, suggesting Charlie had two Telegram accounts: one shared and one personal. Turning Point people reportedly confirmed the two-account arrangement. The host says their side will not pay people, use dirty operators, or join group chats.

On the January 6 pipe bomber, Brian Cole Jr. is described as an autistic man arrested in December 2025 at his home about 20 miles outside Washington, DC. He lives with his mother and family and worked for a family bail bond company. During interrogation, Cole asked for a break, was left alone shivering in a blanket, and repeated “I didn’t.” He told agents he had a giant pain in his stomach. He wrote that everything was blank and too much to process. Agents cued a surveillance video and asked him to identify the man. Cole denied recognizing the person. Agents then told him lying to federal agents is a crime. After that threat, Cole answered yes when asked if the individual was him. His legal team says the confession was coerced. He has pleaded not guilty and was denied bond in January.

Tucker Carlson interviewed Cole’s parents. Scripps News correspondent Lori Jane Gleha reported on obtained footage of Cole from a 2024 Virginia crash involving a blue Nissan Sentra rear-ending a truck. Scripps also obtained bodycam footage of Tyler Robinson from a 2022 accident. Erica Kirk attended daycare in 1991 at the Scripps building at 312 Walnut Street, Cincinnati. The same two journalists obtaining obscure footage of both men is presented as suspicious. Tyler Robinson was found 33 hours after the assassination. TPUSA employees are reportedly disgusted by the UVU independent review and feel they were lied to.

The host credits Vanity Fair, the UVU Independent Review, and Lake Forest Group with vindicating earlier claims. A commenter noted Erica’s Telegram contact name matched the contact name in texts Andrew Wilson leaked of Charlie. The host says Charlie’s real account was the one speaking to donors, including the message about banning the pro-Israel cause. The host questions why messages would go to Andrew Wilson rather than Andrew Kovette, Tucker Carlson, Megyn Kelly, or media friends. The “Black Robe Mafia” will be exposed, and discovery “sucks for liars.” Book club is set for tomorrow at 4:00 p.m. Eastern. The host is in the final weeks of pregnancy and expects to be done by end of October.

text:
Several Tennessee private schools are choosing independent football schedules and giving up playoff eligibility. A lot of the discussion has turned into accusations about Baylor, money and recruiting.

I went to Baylor, played sports there, and now have a child there. So I’ll speak about Baylor.

If you’re saying Baylor pays kids to play football, what specifically are you saying they’ve done? That’s a big accusation, and repeating it doesn’t make it evidence.

TSSAA allows students to earn NIL money. Its rules prohibit schools and coaches from arranging those deals. Financial aid has rules, too. Families have to demonstrate financial need. A football player receiving aid doesn’t automatically mean he’s being paid to play.

I can’t speak to every player’s private arrangements. Neither can most of the people commenting. If someone has evidence of a violation, let’s hear it.

I also support giving families a chance to transfer. Sometimes a school isn’t the right fit. Sometimes circumstances change. And sometimes a kid sees what another school offers and wants to go there. Schools should be asking what would make families want to choose them, too.

Sports had nothing to do with choosing Baylor for my child. I know what that school offers, and it has only gotten more incredible since I was there. People talk so much about football that they overlook the academics, arts, research, opportunities and everything else available to those kids. They still have to keep up in the classroom. The teachers don’t care what sport they play.

People also talk about how much money goes into Baylor. Do they ever ask why people want to give it?

Baylor has built an alumni community that stays involved. There are events alumni and current families actually want to attend. You can see the improvements and where that support is going. That doesn’t happen by accident.

Shouldn’t every school want great facilities, teachers and coaches? Some of the schools in this discussion have had dominant programs themselves. I don’t remember their success being treated as a problem then.

When I was an athlete at Baylor, people complained about how good we were. They didn’t see the four hour practices, six days a week, or the training we did on our own from the day school ended for summer until it started back. They saw the results without seeing what went into them. That expectation of effort went well beyond sports.

There are hardworking kids and good teachers at other schools. But reducing Baylor’s success to money and recruiting dismisses a lot of people’s work.

If rules are being broken, address it. But schools also need to ask themselves what they’re building and why families would want to be part of it. Kids hear the adults around them. Constantly telling them another school only wins because it has money doesn’t do them any favors.

The Once-for-All Sacrifice

Shadow vs. Reality: The old Mosaic law's animal sacrifices were only a temporary shadow.

Incomplete Cleansing: Bulls and goats could never truly take away human sins.

Permanent Perfection: Jesus offered His body once for all time, perfecting believers forever.

Ceased Offerings: Where absolute forgiveness exists, no further sacrifice for sin remains or is needed.

Welcome to the New Testament!

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Armchair Anonymous: Dinner Party

Overview
Dinner parties fail not from one catastrophe but from stacked small failures: a misplaced ingredient, a cramped kitchen, weather, an anxious pet, and an injury. The episode's throughline is that hosting is a timed system, not a vibe, and that amateurs often underestimate the logistics until everything compounds at once. Three stories carry the hour: a Cousinsgiving where vegetable oil mistaken for broth coats a turkey and a kitchen floor; a lakeside dinner interrupted by a hostess who shoots crows mid-meal and sits back down; and a formal dinner where a guest projectile vomits across a sofa and a silk rug, followed by a child's pool-cue injury that required surgery. The common thread is that the gap between a "manageable" gathering and total chaos is usually a few independent failures, not one dramatic event.

Key Themes
- A dinner can spiral through compounding small failures rather than any single disaster, and the recovery matters more than the mishap.
- The grill functions as the universal fallback when the oven is compromised, proving improvisation can save an ambitious meal.
- Hosting demands a timed cooking system with dishes entering and exiting on schedule, which first-timers rarely appreciate.
- Extreme host reactions, like shooting crows mid-dinner, reveal how thin the line is between hospitality and eccentricity.
- Graciousness under pressure, such as offering a guest clean clothes to be laundered later, converts humiliation into a story worth retelling.
- Childhood injuries around pool tables and man caves recur as a predictable feature of suburban entertaining.
- Shared disaster stories bond people more than flawless evenings ever could, and the retelling often outlasts the embarrassment.
- Bodies fail at the worst possible moments when dehydration, restrictive diets, and alcohol collide with a heavy carb meal.

Detailed Summary
The first story comes from Jillian, born and raised in New Jersey, living in the northern part of the state near where New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania meet, close to High Point Monument. She hosted a Cousinsgiving in December 2022 for two cousins, a cousin's wife, her sister, herself, and her husband. Jillian admits she cannot cook, so her husband handles the kitchen while she manages cleanup. He went shopping, bought the turkey and side ingredients, then went out with friends planning to set up the turkey later.

Jillian took Tylenol PM and went to bed early, anxious about hosting. The next morning she slipped on the kitchen floor, which was covered in vegetable oil. Her husband had seen the words vegetable and gallon on a container, assumed it was vegetable broth, and bought oil instead. He used it in preparing the turkey, and the mixture spilled or erupted when spices were added or heat was applied, leaving spots on his face. Jillian suspects he may have been tipsy after returning from being out. Since a replacement turkey was not an option, they proceeded with the oil-coated bird.

The kitchen was tiny, so cramped that the fridge and oven could not be opened simultaneously. The turkey pan was too large for the oven anyway. Jillian recalled from childhood that a turkey could be cooked on a grill because their oven once caught fire during a holiday. Her husband went for propane in pouring rain and ended up cooking the turkey outside in the downpour.

Guests arrived early while nothing was ready. Jillian had invited her cousin, his wife, and their dog. The dog was nervous and barked and nipped. When Jillian approached with her palm up instead of offering the top of her hand, the dog bit her hand and it bled heavily. With no paper towels in the house, she grabbed fancy Thanksgiving napkins that barely absorbed anything. She mixed sides one-handed with her non-dominant left hand while bleeding, on a floor that was still slippery. Another cousin arrived, surveyed the scene, and asked what was happening.

With the door open for ventilation, the dog bolted outside. Jillian lived on a busy street corner and feared the dog would run into traffic. She and her husband chased it through the rain. The cousin's wife called, and the dog ran back to her. The turkey came off the grill beautiful, with a crispy crust, and Jillian now recommends using a grill as an oven when in a pinch.

The hosts note that the oil incident happened late at night. Broth and spices were supposed to boil before the turkey was added, but the mixture never boiled and became superheated oil instead. Agitation caused a geyser-like explosion. No fire occurred, but oil covered the window and surfaces, and they used an entire Costco package of paper towels to clean it. The hosts stress the need for a timed cooking system when making a full Thanksgiving meal, with dishes going in and out at set times. The hosts say they have not hosted Thanksgiving again since that year, preferring to go out.

A second story comes from a caller reflecting on a dinner around 2001, the summer after her first year of college, at her aunt's new cottage in Muskoka between Port Carling and Bracebridge. Her family has deep Muskoka ties: her great-great-grandparents had an island there, and her mother and aunt grew up going every summer. The dinner was at a friend's island, reachable by boat, with an outdoor setup for fifteen to twenty people.

Mid-dinner, the hostess, called Betty, left the table and returned with a shotgun. She fired one shot to flush out crows, then three more, killing several birds. Betty went back inside, returned to dinner, remarked that the crows were a nuisance, and said she would clean it up later. No one at the table said a word. The caller's aunt laughed it off, calling Betty a little quirky. Betty was married, and her husband was present and very quiet. The caller was nineteen, and drinking was legal in Canada at that age. Betty had earlier told the caller she was going to be super tacky and leave the wine bottle on the table, which the caller and hosts note they have never heard considered tacky.

A third story comes from a speaker who waited four years for the prompt to tell a dinner party story set in 2022 in Qualicum Beach on Vancouver Island, described as a pristine, wholesome, quaint coastal town with one of the oldest average ages in Canada and no chain stores or restaurants. The speaker felt socially obliged to accept a formal dinner invitation from her father's best friend, Nathan, and his wife, Susan, partly to avoid hearing about it from her dad.

The day was stressful: the speaker and her then-husband, Simon, unexpectedly closed on a house and scrambled to get a deposit to a realtor on a Saturday. Simon, a health-conscious former fitness-focused big guy who had been off carbs, planned to eat carbs at this dinner. Nathan was a gin connoisseur, so the speaker brought a bottle of local gin. Nathan made a one-pan creamy pasta bake and was proud of it.

Mid-dinner, Simon became visibly unwell, gray and swaying. He moved to the sofa and then violently projectile vomited across himself, the coffee table, the sofa, and the silk rug. The speaker's first instinct was to apologize profusely, describing it as the most sick she has ever seen. Simon had loaded his plate fully twice, including after a long bathroom trip.

Susan brought a dustpan and two cake slicers to scrape vomit off the carpet. Nathan used a bowl to push vomit off the coffee table. Nathan offered Simon workout gear and suggested leaving his clothes to be washed later with a switcheroo. Simon was later seen naked facing a window while his clothes sat on the floor, with curtains open and lights on. The group piled into a minivan and drove about forty minutes before emerging. Simon had considered making himself sick, then came back and got more food. The next-day explanation was dehydration plus little food or drink, followed by a couple of drinks and a large carb-heavy meal.

A separate guest, Sarah, describes being ten years old in December 2005 in Geneva, Illinois, during her parents' dinner party. Geneva is the last stop on the train from Chicago before cornfields. Her sister Emily was eight. The dinner party took place in a neighborhood square with a central park and many families with kids around their ages. The basement was finished with a bathroom, kitchenette, playroom, wood-paneled walls, blue patterned carpet, a television, a leather couch, and a pool table that came with the house and was rarely used. Her parents stopped hiring a babysitter for this dinner party because Sarah was ten.

Neighbors Matthew and William, ages eight and ten, were invited over during the upstairs dinner, and the parents ordered pizza for the kids. The speaker and her sister lacked toys for boys, and the boys wanted to play pool. She used a kid-sized pool cue that reached about her belly button. She proposed a bet: if she jumped over the cue, they would stop playing pool and she could pick the next game. She tried to hold the cue upright herself while jumping, landed on it, and it went through her sweatpants. Blood pooled, she lay on the ground for about thirty seconds, then told her sister to get their mom.

Her parents realized the injury was beyond their control and took her to the emergency room, nearly empty about two weeks before Christmas. The doctor who could operate on children had gone home, so they waited for him to arrive. She watched Disney Channel while waiting. Her mother asked the doctor in the hallway whether she would still be able to have children, and he said yes. The doctor described the injury as an episiotomy. She received stitches and was given a stuffed teddy bear, a little reindeer, and candy.

Sarah was the only kid in the emergency room and received a lot of attention while her mom was stressed. She underwent about an hour of surgery for roughly a dozen stitches, which later dissolved. Peeing and any position other than lying down were painful afterward. The boys did not spread the story at school, likely because their mom and Sarah's mom were good friends and the boys' mom was a stern Southern lady. Sarah always tells the story and her friends all know it. Her parents waited about a year before hosting another dinner party after the incident.

She later had nightmares about falling into a pit of pool cues and saw a pelvic floor therapist for related fear and trauma. Sarah is now working on a doctorate in education; her husband works as an IT recruiter. They met on Hinge, and he praises her as smart and says he knew immediately. He is originally from Northern California and has lived in Massachusetts long enough to be somewhat used to the cold.

The episode closes with casual banter. The hosts reflect on old yearbook-style phrases like stay cute and variants such as too cute to be forgotten and too sweet to be forgotten. They note they do not have a theme song for the new show, mention asking random questions and using cherries for suggestions, and plan an on-the-fly rhyming segment referred to as on the fly rhyme dish. The hosts call Sarah one of the cutest human beings they have met and ask her husband if he feels he got a unicorn.

text:
Happy birthday to former Owasso, University of Oklahoma and NFL defensive back Aaron Colvin, born on this day in 1991 in Old Hickory, Tennessee.

Colvin attended Owasso High School and was the Class 6A-4 defensive player of the year and earned All-State honors from both the Tulsa World and The Oklahoman in 2009 after making 72 tackles, breaking up ten passes and intercepting two others, one of which was returned 70 yards for a touchdown in a win over Ponca City.

He signed with OU over offers from OSU, Missouri an Tulsa and appeared in all of OU's games as a freshman.

In 2011, he led the Sooners with 84 tackles and a year later, he finished with four interceptions which tied for second in the Big 12 Conference and earned him first-team All-Big 12 honors.

He earned first team all-conference again in 2013 after making 55 tackles, a sack, an interception and recovered a fumble.

In 2014, Colvin was selected by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the fourth round of the NFL Draft. He played in six games as a rookie including one start and recovered a fumble that he returned 41 yards for a touchdown in a 25-24 win over the New York Giants. 

In 2015, he started 15 games at cornerback, recording 73 tackles, six for losses, while breaking up seven passes and making four sacks.

He played four seasons in Jacksonville, two with the Houston Texans and one with Washington.

In all, Colvin recorded 211 tackles, had five sacks and recovered four fumbles in his NFL career.

Following his playing career, Colvin became an entrepreneur and community mentor as the co-founder of Sozo Farms, a 150-acre healing and wellness sanctuary located in Terrell, Texas. He also serves as a board member for Camp Exposure, which is dedicated to mentoring and guiding young athletes.

text:
ALNYLAM $ALNY'S OWN FORECAST NEEDS $1.13B A QUARTER. JUNE BROUGHT $1.03B:

Alnylam Pharmaceuticals ALNY at $231.18, -$15.56 / -6.31% on Thursday.

The name that does not get the headline usually carries the open question, and an open question teaches more than a settled one. This morning the sharpest one belongs to Alnylam, second on the Hypergrowth Len5. Its drug sales are up 74% in a year. Its stock is 53% under its $495.55 peak of October 20, 2025. One number in the next report decides which of those two facts the price should believe.

The Cambridge, Massachusetts company makes RNAi drugs, medicines that switch off the gene behind a disease. Its biggest seller, Amvuttra, treats ATTR amyloidosis, where a misfolded protein clogs the heart and nerves. Amvuttra and an older drug make up what Alnylam calls its TTR franchise.

The Hypergrowth Len5 hunts very fast sales growth at a business that already makes money. Alnylam has both halves. June quarter, reported July 30:

- Product revenue, money from its drugs: $1.172B, up 74% from a year earlier.
- Profit under standard accounting: $164.5M, or $1.21 a share, against a loss of $0.55 a year earlier.
- TTR franchise revenue: $1.030B, up from $910M in March.

The same day, Alnylam cut its full-year TTR forecast to $4.2B-$4.5B, from $4.4B-$4.7B. Amvuttra's $1.01B missed analysts' estimates by about 4%, and management said demand from patients switching over from older treatments had normalized. The shares fell 28.3% that day.

Here is what the cut forecast actually asks for. The first half brought $1.94B of TTR sales. The low end of the range needs $2.26B more, an average of $1.13B a quarter. That is about 10% above June. The step from March to June was 13%. So the bottom of Alnylam's own range needs a slower climb than the one it just delivered. The top of the range is the hard part: $1.28B a quarter, 24% above June.

Thursday's drop came with no company news. The broad biotech fund fell about a third as far:

iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) at $205.96, -$4.57 / -2.17% on Thursday.

Alnylam's close was its lowest since August 20. The strongest fact against the case: a forecast cut once can be cut again, and the September quarter is the first full one since the cut.

Outside calendars list Thursday, October 29, before the open; Alnylam has not confirmed the date. If September's TTR sales land near June's $1.03B, December would need about $1.23B just to reach the low end.

What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5: TTR sales slipping below June's $1.03B, or a second cut to the range. A September quarter at or above $1.13B would show July was a reset, not a slide.

The verdict: the bar is written down and within reach of Alnylam's recent pace, and the price is betting it misses.

MOMENTUM LEN5:

CBIZ (CBZ) at $54.71, +$0.02 / +0.04% on Thursday.

The Independence, Ohio firm does accounting, tax, and benefits work for midsize companies. The Momentum Len5 hunts a climb that is still going. CBIZ is second, and its climb was real before anyone bid:

- March 24 low, during the session: $24.29.
- July 28 close: $46.70.
- Grant Thornton Advisors' cash offer, agreed July 28: $55.00 a share.

The hurdles are falling. A 31-day window to shop for a higher bid closed August 27, and the September 18 proxy still carries $55. The federal antitrust waiting period expired September 10. Shareholders vote October 27, and a majority of all shares must say yes.

What would knock it off the Momentum Len5: the vote failing, or the deal closing, which ends trading in the shares. If the deal breaks, the $46.70 pre-offer close is the reference point.

The verdict: $0.29 is all that is left of this climb.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:

Visa (V) at $359.85, +$0.52 / +0.14% on Thursday.

Visa runs the network that moves card payments between banks. The Quality-Value Len5 hunts a durable business priced under a cautious reading of its earnings. Visa is second: the network is as durable as they come, and the gap under its value is thin. June quarter, reported July 28, with currency swings removed:

- Payments volume: +10%. Spending across borders: +13%.
- Net revenue: $11.6B, +13%.
- Operating expenses, the cost of running it, without one-time items: +17%.

Costs grew faster than revenue. Visa paid an average $330.71 for the 14.5M shares it bought back that quarter, about 8% under Thursday's close.

What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: costs outrunning revenue again for the year that ended September 30, or the price climbing back to August 26's $385.57 peak. Outside calendars list October 27; Visa has not set the date.

The verdict: the toll road still grows at double digits, and its costs are why the discount should be wider.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:

Graco (GGG) at $77.76, +$0.92 / +1.20% on Thursday.

The Minneapolis company makes pumps and sprayers that move paint, coatings, and glue. This Len5 hunts a price under a cautious value, or a dated event that changes the math. Graco is second, with both: shares 18.7% under February's $95.69 high, and a deal inside the next report.

- June quarter adjusted profit per share: $0.91, +17%. Sales: +3%, mostly from businesses it bought.
- Its own shares bought back that quarter: $315M.
- August 31: Valco Melton, which applies glue on factory lines, bought for $447M in cash. 2025 revenue: about $145M.

Graco priced the deal at about 14 times last year's adjusted EBITDA, a measure of cash profit before interest and taxes. Orders at the businesses it already owned grew at a mid-single-digit pace in June. Sales from those businesses did not.

What would knock it off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: those orders failing to become sales on October 21, after the close, the date Graco has set.

The verdict: the price is well under February's, and October 21 is the first look at what $447M bought.

GROWTH LEN5:

NMI Holdings (NMIH) at $38.08, +$0.76 / +2.04% on Thursday.

The Emeryville, California company insures lenders when a buyer puts down less than 20%. The Growth Len5 hunts years of rising profit at a price that has not paid for them. NMI Holdings is second, and Wednesday handed it a new test. The whole mortgage-insurance group sold off that day, and NMI lost 8.4%. The Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly survey, out that morning:

- 30-year fixed mortgage rate: 7.3%, the highest since November 2023.
- Home-purchase loan applications: 14% below a year earlier.

Fewer home loans mean fewer new policies. The offset: owners holding older, cheaper mortgages do not refinance at 7.3%, so existing policies stay in force longer. Persistency, the share still in force after a year, was 81.4% in June. The catch: on September 15, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte had Fannie Mae let servicers tell homeowners when they can drop the insurance.

- June-quarter profit per share: $1.38, against $1.21.
- Insurance in force: $227.1B, +6%.
- Adjusted book value, the owners' stake per share: $36.88. Thursday's price is about 3% above it.

What would knock it off the Growth Len5: profit per share sliding under $1.38 as new policies shrink, or persistency falling as cancellations climb. Outside calendars list November 3; NMI has not set the date.

The verdict: Wednesday priced fewer new policies, but the $227.1B already on the books earns the profit.

INCOME LEN5:

Global Ship Lease (GSL) at $45.44, +$1.30 / +2.95% on Thursday.

The Athens company owns 71 containerships and rents them to shipping lines for years at a time. The Income Len5 hunts cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying. Global Ship Lease is second, and its cover is easy to measure:

- June-quarter profit for common shareholders: $89.3M, or $2.48 a share, down from $2.61.
- A full year of the $0.625 quarterly dividend: about $90M, roughly one quarter's profit.
- Charters already signed: $3.2B of revenue, over an average 3.3 years.

The bigger claim on the cash is 15 new ships ordered for $1.33B, delivering from late 2028 into early 2030. At June 30 the company held $388.6M of cash against $676.4M of debt.

What would knock it off the Income Len5: a cut to the $0.625, or the shipbuilding bill pulling away the cash that now funds it. Outside calendars list November 9.

The verdict: one quarter of profit pays a year of dividends, and the risk sits in 2028, not in this payout.

Five of these six have a dated test before Thanksgiving. Alnylam's is the cleanest: one quarter of heart-drug sales measured against $1.13B, and a stock already priced as if its own forecast is out of reach.

Not investment advice.

text:
Liberty Mutual is an American insurance company.  

They sell car insurance... just like hundreds of others.

So how do they beat the competition?  

If they market themselves like everyone else... it becomes a coin toss:  

"Who did the customer see first?"  

That’s a terrible position to be in.  

So instead, the creative strategist came along..  

..and looked for an untouched angle in the market.  

"What can we highlight that makes people look at us differently?"  

And they found it.  

They didn't just drop their prices to look cheap.  

They positioned their new offer into a self-identity play.  

They basically told the market:  

We ONLY insure safe drivers. 

Because safe drivers get in fewer accidents, they cost us less money... so we give them cheaper coverage.

So now...  

..the customer isn't just seeing a price cut.  

They're thinking:  

"Yes, I’m a safe driver. And I do qualify for that lower price... so why would I pay more somewhere else?"  

The price was cheaper... but because Liberty Mutual tied it to safe driving...

..it didn’t feel like discount budget insurance.  

It felt like a reward for being a safe driver.  

When your market is saturated, handing your audience a brand-new perspective helps them..

..to stop comparing your product to others.

This Day in History - British Spy John André Executed After Militiamen Foil Arnold’s Treason

On October 2, 1780, British Major John André was hanged as a spy at Tappan, New York, after a military board concluded that he had entered American lines under a false name and carried intelligence concealed in his clothing.

Nine days earlier, New York militiamen John Paulding, David Williams, and Isaac Van Wart had stopped André near Tarrytown. They discovered papers revealing Benedict Arnold’s plan to surrender West Point to the British. André offered rewards for his release, but the three citizen-soldiers refused and delivered him to American authorities. Arnold escaped; André did not.

The episode demonstrates how ordinary armed citizens could alter the course of a war. The militiamen were not famous generals or professional intelligence officers. They were local men performing public duty, and their vigilance protected the Hudson River fortress that linked New England with the other states. Liberty sometimes survives because citizens recognize that self-government carries responsibilities as well as rights, and act when the moment demands courage.

text:
Most people don’t yet grasp what is happening in France. Markets are pricing French sovereign debt as junk, rating agencies will eventually have to follow. This will have two major impacts:

1. Most French banks are already rated at or just below the sovereign, so a move toward junk would likely drag domestically focused lenders with it. Credit to households and firms would slow sharply, hurting the economy and widening the fiscal deficit even further, a vicious cycle.

2. For the ECB, the constraint is legal as well as financial. A fall below investment grade would force sales by ratings-bound investors while making any backstop harder to justify under current rules.

The next euro crisis will begin in France. The first, which began in Greece, will feel like a walk in the park compared with what comes next.

text:
Black biped in a Unitree jacket turns on open asphalt while a circle of coats reaches for the arm and laughs.

Crowd is the frame, not the machine. Man in an olive jacket keeps a hand on the shoulder, woman in a navy suit claps once and steps back, older man in black watches with both hands in his pockets. Nobody is operating a pendant. They are standing inside the reach.

Legs are the part that does not look dressed. Reverse knees, exposed actuators, flat feet on the yellow line, torso wrapped in a dark coat so the head and the hips read as two different objects. Jacket hides the chest. Joints below the waist stay bare.

Back of the coat carries the Unitree mark once it turns. Helmet stays fixed. Arms swing as one bar, not as fingers, so the greeting is a whole limb moving past the people who offered a hand.

Weight plates and a blue strap sit on the asphalt behind the feet and never get used in this clip. 

Whatever lift was planned already happened, or never started. What is left is the turn.

Shift happens around the fifth second. One foot slides, hips rotate, coat swings with the torso, and the man who was touching the arm has to pull his hand clear. Balance holds. No person steps in to catch it.

Laugh from the woman in the red layer is the tell. Hand goes to her mouth, shoulders drop, and the rest of the circle smiles at the same beat. Officials outside a glass lobby are not clapping for a spec sheet. They are reacting to a body that moved inside their space.

Building behind them is all glass and white columns. Daylight, no stage, no rope. Robot is on the same pavement as the shoes around it, which is a harder test than a booth tile with a second unit standing still for contrast.

What the nine seconds actually prove is narrow. Coat on, crowd close, one turn, feet stay under the hips. 

Plates on the ground stay plates. Reach from the olive jacket gets answered by a moving limb, not by a voice calling the move.

Reasonable Japanese terms 

The Japanese very much wanted to end the war as expeditiously as possible. After consultations among the Foreign Ministry, the Army, and the Navy, the government and military authorities agreed to accept any offer of impartial mediation conducted by a third party, if the terms thereof were within the scope of the Funatsu Initiative. On October 27, Foreign Minister Hirota notified the UK, the US, France, Germany, and Italy of Japan’s willingness to accept amicable third-party mediation of negotiations with China. 

The decision was made that Germany would mediate the peace talks. On November 2, the day before the Brussels conference began, the Japanese officially conveyed their seven peace conditions to Herbert von Dirksen, the German ambassador to Japan. 

Dirksen thought that the seven conditions were so reasonable that, when he sent a report to his government, he commented that Nanjing could accept the terms without losing face, and that it would be prudent to put pressure on the Chinese to accept them.²  

Upon receipt of Dirksen’s report, the German government adjudged Japan’s peace terms appropriate and communicated them to Chiang Kai-shek through Oskar Trautmann, the German ambassador to China, on November 5. However, Chiang, having placed all his hopes in the Brussels conference, rejected the peace proposal. 

² Miyake Masaki, “Trautmann kōsaku no seikaku to shiryō: Nicchū sensō to Doitsu gaikō” (The character of the Trautmann mediation and relevant historical resources: the 2nd Sino-Japanese War and German Diplomacy), Kokusai seiji (International Relations), no. 47, 1972.

text:
$AMZN trades near US$ 253 on Oct 2 (~+2% vs Thursday close US$ 248.23) after the Financial Times reported Amazon is seeking to move about US$ 8 billion of Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips into a special purpose vehicle and lease them back.

Facts from FT / Reuters coverage dated 02/10/2026:
1. Talks with investors in recent weeks. Chips bought or leased by Amazon sit in more than a dozen U.S. data centers across five states, including Nevada and Virginia.
2. The SPV would raise outside debt. Amazon would offer an equity stake of up to 10% and, per the report, would not keep an ownership stake in the vehicle.
3. Context on the spend: Amazon expects about US$ 220 billion of capex this year, mostly AWS chips and AI data centers. It raised plans for about US$ 50 billion of bonds earlier in 2026 and sold US$ 25 billion in July with softer demand for long dated paper.
4. Status: discussions ongoing and subject to change. Amazon declined to comment. Nvidia had not immediately commented to Reuters.

Reading this:
1. This is balance sheet engineering for AI infra, not a cut in capacity. Same chips, different owner of the asset.
2. Offloading silicon to debt financed SPVs preserves credit metrics while hyperscalers keep burning cash on GPUs.
3. Investors pricing IG paper off Amazon's double A rating is the real product. Insurance and pension money enters the AI capex chain.
4. Watch residual value and lease terms. When Grace Blackwell ages into Vera Rubin, who owns the depreciation risk matters more than the headline US$ 8B.

Insight: the scarce question in AI is shifting from "will they spend" to "how do they fund US$ 200B+ years without cracking the balance sheet." Sale and leaseback of GPUs is that next chapter.

Fatos da cobertura FT / Reuters de 02/10/2026:
1. Conversas com investidores nas últimas semanas. Os chips comprados ou arrendados pela Amazon estão em mais de uma dúzia de data centers nos EUA em cinco estados, inclusive Nevada e Virgínia.
2. O SPV captaria dívida externa. A Amazon ofereceria participação acionária de até 10% e, segundo o report, não manteria stake no veículo.
3. Contexto de gasto: a Amazon espera cerca de US$ 220 bilhões de capex neste ano, em grande parte chips e data centers de IA da AWS. Elevou planos para cerca de US$ 50 bilhões em bonds no começo de 2026 e vendeu US$ 25 bilhões em julho com demanda mais fraca no papel longo.
4. Status: discussões em curso e sujeitas a mudança. A Amazon não comentou. A Nvidia não havia comentado de imediato à Reuters.

Leitura:
1. É engenharia de balanço para infra de IA, não corte de capacidade. Mesmos chips, dono do ativo diferente.
2. Tirar silício para SPVs financiados com dívida preserva métricas de crédito enquanto hyperscalers seguem queimando caixa em GPUs.
3. O produto real é papel IG precificado na nota double A da Amazon. Dinheiro de seguros e fundos de pensão entra na cadeia de capex de IA.
4. Olhe valor residual e termos de lease. Quando Grace Blackwell envelhecer para Vera Rubin, quem carrega o risco de depreciação importa mais que a manchete de US$ 8 bi.

Insight: a pergunta escassa na IA migra de "vão gastar" para "como financiar anos de US$ 200 bi+ sem rachar o balanço". Sale and leaseback de GPUs é o próximo capítulo.

text:
Acts 7:48 is not a defense of an LDS temple. It is Stephen telling Israel the building never contained God. Solomon already said that at the dedication (1 Kings 8:27). The New Testament then tells you what happened to the temple itself.
The biblical temple had one job. Sacrifice. Blood on the altar. A high priest entering the Holy of Holies once a year, and not without blood (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). That is what the house was for. An LDS temple does none of it. No altar. No sacrifice. No high priest with blood. What happens inside is endowment, garment, sealing, and baptism for the dead. None of that is the temple work God commanded in the Law, and none of it is commanded anywhere in the New Testament. Using the word “temple” does not make the use biblical.
And that temple was finished when Christ finished His work.
The veil tore the moment He died (Matthew 27:51). He said the temple He would raise was His own body (John 2:19–21). He told the woman the hour had come when worship would not be tied to Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). Hebrews says the earthly sanctuary was a copy and a shadow, now obsolete, and that Christ entered heaven itself, not a holy place made with hands (Hebrews 8:5, 13; 9:11–12, 24; 10:1–14). Jesus foretold the stones coming down (Matthew 24:1–2). They did, in AD 70. God was not relocating His presence to another building. He put it in His people.
You are the temple. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:19). The church is “a holy temple in the Lord… a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21–22). And the last word in Scripture is not a measured building. John sees the city and says, “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (Revelation 21:22).
The apostles praying in the temple courts while it still stood does not rebuild what Christ ended. A transition is not a restoration. The sacrifice is offered. The veil is open. The house came down. God dwells in the Christian, not in a recommend-only building doing work the Bible never gave the temple to do.

@RepJasmine had "government relations and lobbying" on a campaign-funded merch site. That is not a clapback. That is a receipt.

Zeteo reported today that Rep. Jasmine Crockett's Clapback Collection site, paid for by Jasmine For Us, carried a "Political Consultant, Book Now" button. Click it and the services listed included campaign management, communications and PR, government relations and lobbying, digital and social media, and political risk management. Contact email on that page: jasminefor100@gmail.com.

The lobbying offer appeared after she lost the Texas Senate primary in March. Zeteo says it was up by May. After the outlet asked for comment, the consulting and lobbying offering was removed.

Her spokesperson told Zeteo the site "is and has always been focused on selling campaign merchandise," that Crockett "did not build it," and that she "never directed anyone to add the button." Fine. Then explain why a sitting member of Congress had "government relations and lobbying" sitting on a campaign-paid storefront until a reporter called.

Ethics rules exist because Congress is not a side hustle. You do not get to lecture America about power, then soft-launch lobbying on the same domain selling your "Bleach Blonde" tees.

This is the same Congresswoman who stays in the drama lane on X while the hard questions about her own shop get the silent treatment. Zeteo asked. The button vanished. The public still gets to read what was offered.

Detroiters know the difference between a brand and a conflict. If it was a staff mistake, put that on the record with names and dates. If it was intentional, own it. Either way, stop hiding behind merch copy.

Facts over vibes. Campaign cash is not a consulting agency.

❤️🙏 Some songs do more than touch your heart—they remind you who has been carrying you through life. This song touched my heart and soul to the core💜

Last night in Grand Prairie, Texas, I had the privilege of experiencing Anne Wilson performing her powerful song “My Jesus” live. 🎶✝️

There is something special about hearing a song like this in person. The music, the lyrics, and the voices coming together create a moment that reaches beyond entertainment. It becomes a reminder of the personal relationship we can have with Jesus Christ.

Life doesn’t always go according to our plans. We all face struggles, disappointments, heartache, and seasons when we wonder how we’re going to make it through. But our faith reminds us that we don’t have to carry those burdens alone. Jesus meets us in our brokenness, offers hope when we feel lost, and reminds us that His love isn’t reserved for people who have everything figured out.

That’s what makes “My Jesus” so meaningful to me. It’s a reminder that Jesus isn’t just a name we sing about on Sunday. He is the One we can turn to in our everyday lives—in our prayers, in our tears, in our gratitude, and in the quiet moments when we need Him most.

I’m thankful I could capture a little piece of tonight’s experience and share it with you all. ❤️

Who else has a song that brings you closer to God every time you hear it? I’d love to hear what song has strengthened your faith. 🙏

May we never forget the hope we have in Jesus!

On this day—October 2, 1947

David Ben-Gurion stood in Jerusalem and asked the Arabs to take a state of their own and meet the Jews as sovereign equals.

Not after the war. Seven months before it. The UN had not yet voted. No Arab army had crossed a border. The British were still the government.

Ben-Gurion admitted the Arabs had refused to even sit at the same table as the Jews. But he made the offer anyway:

“We will do everything in our power to maintain peace, and establish a cooperation gainful to both. It is now, here and now, from Jerusalem itself, that a call must go out to the Arab nations to join forces with Jewry and the destined Jewish State and work shoulder to shoulder for our common good, for the peace and progress of sovereign equals.”

Six weeks later, the UN recommended two states. The Arab Higher Committee said no. In May 1948, five Arab armies invaded to kill in the crib the state whose chairman had just asked them to be partners.

The people who left during that war are now described as the victims of a plan drawn up in the Jewish Agency. The plan on the table that October was the opposite: have your own country, and those who stay in ours will become citizens and together we will build our countries as equals.

The Arabs heard him, and then chose war.

text:
The Hypocrisy of Ed Miliband and the UK Labour Government’s Israel Policy-- A long read if interested in a thorough rebuttal of his speech.

The Hypocrisy of Ed Miliband and the UK Labour Government’s Israel Policy
A line-by-line deconstruction of the “You Were Right” speech
On 28 September, in Liverpool, the Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom stood in front of a hall of people who have spent two years marching under “from the river to the sea” and told them they were right. The speech deserves an answer, line by line.
“As we think about our role in the world, we will never be silent about injustice and suffering.”
Never silent. Let us test that. In June 2025 this government endorsed Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara — a territory under military occupation since 1975, settled by the occupying power, whose native population has sat in refugee camps in Algeria for fifty years. Britain does not ban goods from occupied Western Sahara. It grants them preferential access under its trade agreement with Morocco. Turkey has occupied northern Cyprus since 1974, moved in settlers and partitioned an EU member state; Britain is a guarantor power there and sells Turkey weapons. Then there is Tibet, Xinjiang, the prisons of Iran, and Sudan, where mass killing has proceeded for three years in near-total silence from this podium. Silence is not the word for British foreign policy. Selectivity is. Of every occupation on the planet, exactly one draws an import ban, a supply-chain interdiction and a bespoke sanctions regime, and it is the Jewish one.
“The only route to peace is two states, a secure Israel and a secure Palestine, with freedom, dignity, and self-determination for both peoples.”
Like the two states of Gaza and Israel. In 2005 Israel removed every soldier, every settlement and every grave from Gaza. That is what a withdrawal looks like when a country actually means it. Within two years Hamas held the territory; within eighteen it produced the 7th of October. The formula is recited in London as though it has never been attempted. It was attempted, unilaterally, at enormous domestic cost, and the answer came back first in rockets and then in a massacre. A serious foreign secretary would spend his conference speech asking what happened between the withdrawal and the massacre. Mr Miliband simply repeats the formula in a firmer voice and calls it a reset.
“Hamas's murderous attack on October the 7th united the vast majority of the world in rightful condemnation.”
Not really, and only for about a fortnight. The dead had not all been identified before the marches began, and they were not marches against Hamas. The condemnation was real and it was brief, and its expiry date is the single most revealing fact of the last three years. Note who Mr Miliband has chosen to address in this speech: not the people whose condemnation held, but the people whose condemnation lapsed first.
“We stand, I say, against antisemitism wherever we find it and in whatever form.”
The Equality and Human Rights Commission found that his party broke the Equality Act — unlawful harassment and discrimination against Jews. That is a finding in law, not a matter of opinion, and it was made about his own party, five years after he led it. Since October 2023 antisemitic incidents in Britain have run at record levels: Jewish schoolchildren advised to cover their uniforms on public transport, synagogues under guard, students hounded off campuses. And it is to the movement that supplied a good deal of that atmosphere that the Foreign Secretary says: you were right. Wherever we find it — except here, except now, except in this room.
“This party will always recognise the threats Israel faces and stand emphatically against those who seek its destruction.”
This is the same government that suspended arms export licences to Israel and has now widened the policy to refuse anything judged to contribute to the occupation, indefinitely. You cannot stand emphatically against a country's destruction while rationing what it is permitted to defend itself with against the people attempting that destruction. Nor can you stand against them while telling their loudest supporters in Britain, from the stage of your own conference, that their judgement was sound.
“But this cannot justify the suffering the Netanyahu government has inflicted in Gaza and the West Bank. This suffering is a stain on the conscience of the world.”
Read the construction carefully, because the argument is in the grammar. The suffering was “inflicted by the Netanyahu government” — not caused by a war, and certainly not by the side that began it, refused every ceasefire that required it to give up the hostages and its weapons, and then fought from beneath hospitals, schools and apartment blocks. Hamas could have ended the war on any day of it, and chose instead to go on fighting at the expense of its own civilian population. But for Mr Miliband, everything is Israel's fault, and the sentence is built so that nothing else can be said.
And as for the stain on the conscience of the world. Britain did not kill German civilians incidentally. It set out to. The Area Bombing Directive of 14 February 1942 instructed Bomber Command “to focus attacks on the morale of the enemy civil population and in particular the industrial workers.” The following day the Chief of the Air Staff removed any remaining ambiguity: “the aiming points will be the built up areas, and not, for instance, the dockyards or aircraft factories.” Civilians were not collateral damage in the British campaign. They were the target, by written order, signed and filed.
The bill came to something on the order of four hundred thousand German civilians. Forty thousand in Hamburg in a single week. Dresden. The cities of the Ruhr. No telephone calls to the occupants, no leaflet naming the building, no evacuation map by grid square. And the Allies killed at least sixty-eight thousand French civilians, more than fifty thousand of them in Normandy alone, in the course of liberating France — more Frenchmen killed by British and American bombs than Britons killed by German ones in the whole of the Blitz.
Was the liberation of Europe a stain on the conscience of the world? Or was it a war against an enemy that had to be beaten and that fought from among its own people? Britain does not apply to its own history the standard it has just written into law for somebody else's present. If it did, no British government since Churchill's would survive the audit.
“To the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere, who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you. You were right.”
Right about what? This is the sentence that ought to follow Mr Miliband for the rest of his career, because he does not say. Right that Israel is committing genocide? Right that it should never have been founded? Right to chant for a Palestine from the river to the sea? That slogan is not a demand for a state alongside Israel. It names the whole of the land, from the Jordan to the Mediterranean, and what stands on most of that land today is Israel. It is a demand for the destruction of the Jewish state, and it leaves no room for the seven million Jews living between those two points. Everybody chanting it understands this perfectly well, and so does the Foreign Secretary. The movement he is congratulating has nothing whatever to say about a regime that throws gay men from rooftops, denies women equal standing in law, conscripts children and executes its critics in the street. It went quiet about the hostages within a week. Its outrage has always had a very specific shape, and the Foreign Secretary has just validated it without once specifying what he is validating.
Here is what a serious government would say instead: that Palestinians are adults and political actors, responsible for what they do. That their leadership tried to annihilate the Jews of Palestine before there was a State of Israel to object to. That they refused partition in 1947 and invaded; refused negotiation at Khartoum in 1967; refused Barak and Clinton in 2000 and answered with the bombing of the buses and the cafés; refused Olmert in 2008 without so much as a reply. A century of no, and not one British minister has ever suggested that the people saying it might bear some responsibility for where it has left them.
“We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank.”
Words have meanings, and this one has a meaning. Settler violence is real, it is criminal, and Israel should prosecute far more of it than it does — that is a fair criticism and Israelis make it loudly in their own press and their own courts. It is not ethnic cleansing. The Palestinian population of the West Bank has grown from roughly six hundred thousand in 1967 to more than three million today. Populations being cleansed do not multiply fivefold. The Foreign Secretary reached for the gravest charge in the vocabulary of atrocity and attached it to a phenomenon whose defining feature — the removal of a people — has demonstrably not occurred.
Ethnic cleansing did occur in this conflict. It occurred in 1948, in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem, emptied of every last Jew by the Jordanian army. It occurred across the Arab world, where some 850,000 Jews were stripped, expelled or driven out of communities two and a half thousand years old, from Baghdad to Tripoli to Sana'a. Britain has never once called that out. There is no import ban attached to it, no sanctions regime, no reset.
And note what is now offered as the remedy. The settlement Britain has recognised and intends to enforce would make eastern Jerusalem the capital of a Palestinian state. Consider what that means. Eastern Jerusalem is Arab today for precisely one reason: in 1948 the Jordanian army expelled every Jew living there, dynamited their synagogues and barred their return for nineteen years. Jews had been the largest community in Jerusalem since the nineteenth century. The proposal on the table is to take the one piece of ground in this entire conflict that was successfully and completely cleansed of its Jews, and award it in perpetuity to the side that did the cleansing.
Britain's stated objection to Israeli settlements is that territory may not be acquired by force. Run that principle across eastern Jerusalem and it comes out the other way: Jordan took it by force in a war of aggression, held it illegally for nineteen years, and lost it in a war it chose to join. The principle is only ever made to run in one direction. This is not the correction of an injustice. It is the ratification of one — a rule that ethnic cleansing confers good title, provided the people cleansed were Jews.
“We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza.”
Whose evidence? The casualty figures that drive every one of these findings come from a health ministry run by Hamas, do not distinguish combatants from civilians, and are then recirculated by institutions with their own record — including an aid agency several of whose employees are alleged to have taken part in the attacks of 7 October, and many more to have cheered them on. Serious allegations deserve serious investigation, and Israel's own courts have a longer record of prosecuting Israeli soldiers than most of Israel's critics have of prosecuting anyone at all. What Mr Miliband has is a conclusion in search of a citation.
Set against that, consider the people who study this for a living. John Spencer, chair of urban warfare studies at the Modern War Institute at West Point, has said that Israel implemented more measures to prevent civilian casualties than any military in history, and warned that it has set a standard that will be hard, and perhaps impossible, for any Western army to repeat. Colonel Richard Kemp — a British officer, former commander of British forces in Afghanistan — has said the same of successive Gaza campaigns. These are not publicists. They are the professionals whose job is to know what urban warfare costs.
Nor are they alone, and this is the part Mr Miliband should find hardest to dismiss. The High Level Military Group — eleven former chiefs of staff, generals and senior defence officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Australia and Colombia, chaired by General Klaus Naumann, former Chief of Staff of the Bundeswehr and Chairman of NATO's Military Committee — went to Israel, examined the conduct of the Gaza campaign, and reported that Israel “not only met a reasonable international standard of observance of the laws of armed conflict, but in many cases significantly exceeded that standard.” They added that none of them was aware of any army that had taken such extensive measures to protect an enemy civilian population, and that Israel's adherence to the laws of war had cost Israeli soldiers and Israeli civilians their lives. They delivered that assessment to the United Nations Human Rights Council's own Commission of Inquiry, which proceeded as though it had never been written.
In August 2024 the same body returned to the subject, submitting to the International Criminal Court that the Prosecutor's allegation of a deliberate policy of starvation was “unsupported by all available evidence,” that Gaza is the most complex and challenging battlefield of modern times, and — this is the sentence for the Foreign Secretary — that the standard being applied to Israel is an unbearable and unrealistic one that no democratic army conducting similar operations could meet. That includes the British Army. Mr Miliband is legislating against Israel on a basis that would convict his own soldiers, and NATO's most senior retired officers have told him so in writing.
Since October 7th the judgement has been tested again, by people who went and looked. General Sir John McColl — former Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe, which is to say one of the most senior officers Britain has produced in a generation — led a team of military experts from six NATO countries into Israel and observed operations in Rafah. His conclusion, published in The Times: “I came away from the trip satisfied that the IDF's operations and rules of engagement were rigorous compared to the British Army and our Western allies.” He recorded operations aborted because of the danger to civilians, and tunnels running beneath schools, hospitals and mosques. Britain's own former deputy commander of NATO forces in Europe has compared the Israeli army's rules of engagement to Britain's, and found Israel's the stricter of the two.
A parallel American assessment reached the same place. A task force of seven retired US flag officers — among them General David Rodriguez, former commander of AFRICOM, Admiral Michael Rogers, former head of US Cyber Command, and General Charles Wald, former deputy commander of EUCOM — concluded that the IDF had prosecuted the campaign “with operational and tactical excellence and in overall compliance with the Law of Armed Conflict,” and that the United States military would benefit from studying how Israel fought in so complex an environment. That same group criticised Israel sharply on other grounds, which is rather the point: these are not advocates. They are professionals who found fault where they found it, and did not find it here.
And consider what the measures actually are, because no army has ever done anything like them. Leaflets naming the buildings to be struck. Telephone calls and Arabic-language text messages to the occupants of specific apartments. Evacuation maps published by numbered grid block. Roof-knocking. Daily humanitarian pauses and corridors held open while the enemy used them to move. Every one of those warnings also warns Hamas, which is the point most often missed: Israel has repeatedly traded away operational surprise, and with it the lives of its own soldiers, to reduce the deaths of the civilians of a population that elected its enemy. Britain did not telephone Hamburg. The United States did not publish grid maps of Fallujah. No one has ever fought this way, and the reward for it has been a British import ban.
“We call out Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine.”
Occupation of what, taken from whom? Between 1948 and 1967 Judea and Samaria were held by Jordan and Gaza by Egypt — seized in a war of aggression and recognised by almost no one on earth. Jordan expelled every Jew from the Jewish Quarter, destroyed or desecrated some fifty-eight synagogues, used the headstones of the Mount of Olives for paving and latrines, and barred Jews from the Western Wall for nineteen years in open breach of the armistice it had signed. Britain, which had governed the place until the day before, said almost nothing. Jordan then stripped its Palestinians of citizenship in 1988 and walked away from them. There was no Palestinian state there to occupy, for the simple reason that the Arab leadership had refused one in 1947.
“We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction, and British services for illegal settlements.”
Then ban the others. Britain has never in its history banned imports from an occupied territory — not from Western Sahara, whose produce it actively privileges; not from northern Cyprus, held by Turkey for fifty-two years with settlers moved in, while Britain maintains a free trade agreement with Ankara and sells it weapons. Britain does not ban goods from Xinjiang, where a million people have been put through camps and forced labour is systematic. Yet Britain goes on importing tens of billions of pounds a year from China.
“When it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government says: we will not let you succeed.”
Britain recognised a Palestinian state in 2025 — with no agreed border, no demilitarisation, no functioning government, no recognition of Israel required in return, and with hostages still held in tunnels. Whatever else that achieved, it established a principle and taught a lesson. The lesson is that you may refuse every offer put to you for a hundred years, launch the largest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, hold the bodies of the murdered as bargaining chips, and be handed statehood anyway, having conceded nothing at all.
That is not a two-state policy. It is a policy that rewards rejectionism. If anyone is destroying the two-state solution it is Britain and the European governments that have decided appeasing a movement founded on the destruction of the Jewish homeland is the way to resolve a dispute about whether that homeland may exist. Mr Miliband says he will not let anyone destroy the two-state solution, but his government's policies encourage the maximalist goals of a movement that refuses to accept the legitimacy and the rights of the Jewish state. That is not a condition that leads to a peaceful resolution of anything.
The Defining Principle
So we are left with a government that bans settlement wine and not Xinjiang cotton. But look harder at the inconsistency, because it is sharper than it first appears. Northern Cyprus has been under Turkish occupation since 1974 — the territory of a sovereign state, seized by force from a government that still exists and still claims it, with settlers imported to change the demography. Western Sahara has been under Moroccan occupation since 1975, and Britain does not merely tolerate that one: it endorses Morocco's plan for the territory and grants its produce preferential access to the British market. Two unambiguous occupations, one of them against a member of the European Union, and from Britain not a ban, not a sanction, not a word.
Then there is the occupation Britain has chosen to act upon, which is the only one nobody can define. Occupied from whom? There has never been a Palestinian state in Judea and Samaria. The territory was held illegally by Jordan for nineteen years, before that by Britain itself, and before that by the Ottomans. There is no dispossessed sovereign waiting to have it restored. The Foreign Office is sanctioning an occupation whose victim it cannot name, while ignoring two whose victims it could name in a sentence.
And underneath the inconsistency sits something worse than inconsistency. To call the Jewish presence in Judea and Samaria an occupation is to declare that Jews are foreigners on the one piece of ground on earth that is named after them. Britain is not neutral on that question any longer; it has taken a side. It has decided that Hebron and Shiloh are places where Jews do not belong, and that the Palestinian state it proposes to midwife must be emptied of them before it can be born. A government that would treat the demand to clear any other territory of any other people as a scandal has adopted it here as policy. So the stated principle — we will never be silent about injustice — plainly is not the operative one. Something else is selecting the targets, and it is not hard to find.
The Labour Party has discovered that Gaza is a direct threat to Labour's hold on power. In July 2024 five pro-Gaza independents took seats from Labour, there were double-digit swings against the party across constituencies with large Muslim populations, and the present Health Secretary held his own seat by a few hundred votes against an independent running on a single issue. In May 2026 Labour lost close to fifteen hundred council seats, with its Muslim vote fragmenting to the Greens, to independents and to the new party on its left. In July Sir Keir Starmer was gone. In September the Foreign Secretary stood up at conference and announced a reset.
Read those four dates in order and the foreign policy explains itself. This is not a moral position arrived at through reflection on injustice. It is a price list. Sanctioning China would cost Britain tens of billions and its supply chains. Sanctioning Turkey would cost it a NATO partner and a trade deal. Confronting Morocco would cost it influence in North Africa. Sanctioning Israel costs Britain a rounding error in trade and buys back a bloc of marginal seats and, with them, a grip on power. Of every injustice on the Foreign Secretary's list, the Jewish state is simply the cheapest item on the shelf.
Mr Miliband said: we hear you. He does, and that is precisely the objection. He heard a constituency, not an argument.
The Test His Own Party Wrote
There is an objection that will be raised against everything written here, which is that Ed Miliband is Jewish and the grandson of refugees, and is therefore beyond this particular reproach. He is not. Being Jewish confers no immunity from applying a double standard, and no special insight into one either. Jews hold every political opinion available to human beings, including those that assure the world its suspicions about the Jewish state were correct all along. A policy is judged by the policy, not by the ancestry of the minister announcing it.
And there is a test. It has a definition, and his own party adopted it. In September 2018 the Labour Party formally accepted the IHRA working definition of antisemitism together with all of its illustrative examples, one of which is applying double standards to Israel “by requiring of it a behavior not expected or demanded of any other democratic nation.” Now read back over what this government has done. It has never in its history banned imports from an occupied territory, and has now banned them from one. It privileges the produce of occupied Western Sahara and interdicts the produce of Judea and Samaria. It rations arms to a democracy fighting for its survival while trading freely with Turkey and China. It holds the Israeli army to a standard that NATO's own former commanders have said in writing no Western army could meet. That is not antisemitism by implication or inference. It is the example, almost word for word, as the Labour Party itself wrote it down and signed it.
Mr Miliband is not calling for Jews to be harmed, and nothing here suggests that he wants it. But policy does not run on intentions. He has told a movement that marches under a slogan with no room in it for the seven million Jews living between the river and the sea that its judgement was sound, and he has lent it the authority of the Foreign Office to say so. Whatever he believes privately, the people who do want Jews harmed left Mr Miliband's speech stronger, better funded and more confident than they arrived. They, unlike him, know exactly what they mean.
The Foreign Secretary told that hall he was guided by survivor's responsibility. His family survived because somewhere a state's door was open and a war was fought to the end against an enemy that hid behind civilians. He might reflect on which side of that inheritance he was speaking for on Monday.
