text:
One of the most pernicious lies spread by the British government and their antisemitic ilk in the US State Department is the claim that Truman recognized Israel because of the 'Jewish lobby' . Don't let the facts hurt your feelings:

A. On March 5, 1948, Clark Clifford wrote a lengthy memo to Truman outlining the reasons the US should recognized  Israel . Clifford was the person who persuaded Truman to recognize Israel. The memo specifically states that its contents are NOT influenced by political pressure-

"At the outset, let me say that the Palestine problem should not be approached as a Jewish question, or an Arab question, or a United Nations question. The sole question is what is best for the United States of America. Furthermore, one’s judgment in advising as to what is best for America must in no sense be influenced by the election this fall. I know only too well that you would not hesitate to follow a course of action that makes certain the defeat of the Democratic Party if you thought such action were best for America. What I say is, therefore, completely uninfluenced by election considerations.

I

There are some who criticize your actions last fall in actively supporting partition in Palestine. They argue that this embarked the United States on a new policy; that this new policy involves military commitments which we are unable to perform; and that, therefore, we should seek some other solution. This argument is completely fallacious.

Your action in supporting partition is in complete conformity with the settled policy of the United States. Palestine was Turkish territory prior to World War I. It was captured by the Allies. The Balfour Declaration favoring “the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people”, was made November 2, 1917. Its text had been submitted to President Wilson and approved by him before its publication. It was publicly endorsed by the French and Italian Governments in April 1920. The principal Allied powers decided that the mandate for the government of. Palestine should be entrusted to Great Britain and that the mandatory power was to be responsible for putting the Balfour Declaration into effect. The substance of the Balfour Declaration has been restated by Presidents Harding, Coolidge, Hoover, Franklin D. Roosevelt and yourself. The Balfour Declaration was approved by joint resolution of Congress June 30, 1922. It was reaffirmed in the American-British Palestine Mandate [Page 691]Convention of December 3, 1924. The Balfour policy was again approved in a declaration by members of the Senate and the House of the 77th Congress, which was submitted to the President November 2, 1942, signed by 68 Senators and 193 members of the House.

In 1944 both the Democratic and the Republican National Conventions adopted resolutions favoring the establishment in Palestine of “a free and democratic Jewish commonwealth”.

Under date of July 2, 1945, a letter was addressed to you signed by a majority of both Houses of Congress, stating “that the time for action is now” and urged “all interested governments to join with the United States toward the end of establishing Palestine as a free and democratic Jewish commonwealth at the earliest possible time.” A letter to the same effect dated July 2, 1945 was addressed to you and signed by the governors of forty of the forty-eight states of the United States. On December 19, 1945, a concurrent resolution was adopted by Congress which resolved that the United States use its good offices towards the establishment of a democratic commonwealth in Palestine.

There are numerous other declarations of policy by the United States Government to the same effect. Your active support of partition was in complete harmony with the policy of the United States. Seldom has any policy of this government been so clearly and definitely established. Had you failed to support partition, you would have been departing from an established American policy and justifiably subject to criticism.

Partition unquestionably offers the best hope of a permanent solution of the Palestine problem that may avoid war. The policy of drift and delay urged by opponents of partition makes absolutely certain the very military involvements that they profess they want to avoid. Your action on partition in no wise extended the military commitments of the United States. It was a high-minded, statesmanlike adoption of the one course of action that may avoid military involvement.

II

Not only is partition in conformity with established American policy, not only is partition the only hope of avoiding military involvement of the United States in the Near East, but, in addition, partition is the only course of action with respect to Palestine that will strengthen our position vis-à-vis Russia.

One of the most fundamental objectives of American foreign policy is that no aggressive military power shall establish itself on the shores of Western Europe. Germany became a real threat to the United States when she moved to establish herself in Channel ports. Twice we went to war to throw her back from these.

Britain likewise has no desire to see an aggressive military power establish itself in Western Europe. But Britain also has primary interests [Page 692]all over southern Asia and Africa. Britain, therefore, must consider her military position on those continents. Economic exhaustion has necessitated the limitation of her military forces. To compensate for curtailment of her military forces in Asia and the Near East, Britain is deliberately building up an alliance with the Moslem world. Such an alliance, she undoubtedly feels, will give her friendly populations from Pakistan west across Asia Minor and all along the shores of North Africa.

While the British-Moslem alliance is undoubtedly extremely important to Britain, a similar alliance between the United States and the Moslem world is much less important to the United States. Our primary interests demand alliances with the nations to the south of us and along the shores of Western Europe.

III

Events have proved that, for the present at least, “one world” is impossible of attainment—either within the United Nations or otherwise. Normally, the cohesive force that holds an organization together is opposition from the outside. The absence of such opposition from the outside tends to cause the organization to break into factions. The existence of the Axis military was the cohesive force that held the Allied Nations together during the war. With the military collapse of the Axis, unity among the Allied powers ceased. When all the nations of the world unite in a peace organization, there is no outside opposition. We are in no danger from attack from Mars. Therefore, a world organization tends to break into factions. This is what happened to the League of Nations. It is also happening in the United Nations. The United Nations is now dividing between the Soviet faction and the United States faction.

IV

The development of factions within the United Nations compels the United States to determine its course of action vis-à-vis the United Nations.

We must admit that the possibility of the United Nations affording adequate military protection to us becomes more and more remote. One course of action that the United States might follow would be to make less and less use of the United Nations machinery. This would inevitably lead ultimately to the collapse of the United Nations. Such a policy, in my opinion, would be tragic.

In the first place, the United Nations is a God-given vehicle through which the United States can build up a community of powers in Western Europe and elsewhere to resist Soviet aggression and maintain our historic interests. It is the best conceivable mechanism to capitalize on the Marshall plan politically. We can cement alliances [Page 693]immediately through the United Nations mechanisms which could not be brought about by fifty years of diplomacy.

Secondly, a jettisoning of the United Nations would be calamitous to American morale. The American people want peace. They fervently believe that the United Nations offers the best hope for peace. They would go to war to sustain the United Nations as an instrumentality for peace. The cruel fact is that American morale is collapsing right around us today because the American people feel that their government is aiding and abetting in the disintegration of the United-Nations—the one great hope of the American people for peace. Nothing has contributed so much to this feeling as Senator Austin’s recent statement. In large part, it seemed to be the sophistries of a lawyer attempting to tell what we could not do to support the United Nations—in direct contradiction to your numerous statements that we mean to do everything possible to support the United Nations.

Not only do the American people see their government failing to back up the United Nation’s position on Palestine but now they hear talk of our entering into military alliances with the powers of Western-Europe with no reference to such action coming within the framework of the United Nations. The American people grasped at the United-Nations, believing it would save them from being engulfed in World War III. Suddenly, they see what they thought was dry land begin to sink—sink because of what they regard as supineness of their own government.

All of this is causing a complete lack of confidence in our foreign, policy from one end of this country to the other and among all classes of our population. This lack of confidence is shared by Democrats, Republicans, young people and old people. There is a definite feeling that we have no foreign policy, that we do not know where we are going, that the President and the State Department are bewildered, that the United States, instead of furnishing leadership in world affairs, is drifting helplessly.

I believe all of this can be changed.

V

proposed united states policy

1.While recognizing that the United Nations will not afford us adequate military protection, we should nevertheless support it to the limit as an instrumentality for consolidating the anti-Soviet forces of the world. 
Here is an instrumentality already in existence which is well-nigh a perfect mechanism for such purpose. Any military arrangement with Western European powers must be pictured as coming completely within the framework of the United Nations. If this is done, it will receive the support of the American people. If this is not done, we will see an isolationism develop in America that will make any military alliances or intelligent foreign policy well-nigh impossible within the foreseeable future.

2. In order to save the United Nations for our own selfish interests, the United States must promptly and vigorously support the United Nations actions regarding Palestine. We “crossed the Rubicon” on this matter when the partition resolution was adopted by the Assembly—largely at your insistence. A retreat now will be a body-blow to the United Nations. We cannot hope to cement alliances in South America and Western Europe if we back out now. Those countries would justifiably discount the value of any commitments we might propose to make in the face of our repudiation of a commitment we only made last November.

3. The British have announced that they intend to withdraw from Palestine by May 15th. Unless affirmative action is taken immediately by both the United States and the Security Council to preserve peace in Palestine, the withdrawal of Britain’s military forces on May 15th will be followed by chaos and bloody war.

4. There is no more certain way of having Russia move into the Arabian Peninsula than for us to permit war to develop between the Jews and the Arabs—and this is as certain as the rising of tomorrow’s sun, less we move promptly to prevent it. Furthermore, when this happens, Russia can move in unilaterally as the defender of world peace and champion of the United Nations. To permit this to happen would be disastrous.

5. It is argued that our Arabian oil supplies will be imperilled if we support the Assembly’s resolution for partition of Palestine. The United States and Western Europe can only get oil from Arabia if there is peace in Arabia. Peace in Arabia can only be maintained by backing up the Arabs or by backing up the United Nations. The time for new solutions or compromises ended when the Assembly adopted the partition resolution. It is utterly unthinkable for the United States now to back the Arabs and openly oppose a decision of the United Nations Assembly, arrived at at your own insistence. The only alternative is, therefore, to back up the United Nations so that there will be peace in Palestine.

6. There are those who say that such a course of action will not get us oil, that the Arabs will not sell us oil if we back up the United Nations partition plan. The fact of the matter is that the Arab states must have oil royalties or go broke. For example, 90% of Saudi [Page 695]Arabia’s revenues come from American oil royalties. text:
The number eight is the human bridge. Seven belongs to the created world—the week in which heaven and earth were finished. But the number eight is the day, the act, and the substance by which people take what already exists in nature, and invest it in a relationship that nature alone cannot complete – the relationship with G-d.

That bridge is built into the Mishkan itself. A quilt of overlaid patterns numbers “eight,” and the sanctuary answers with the same count. The Mishkan was inaugurated on the eighth day, after Moshe, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons had performed the priestly service for seven days; only then did the Divine Presence descend and reveal itself through the offerings. Newborn animals could be brought only from their eighth day of life. Eight types of offerings could be brought only on eight specific days. The High Priest wore eight holy vestments and changed garments eight times on Yom Kippur. Eight varieties of spices were used—four for the oil of anointing and four for the incense. Eight poles carried the sanctuary’s objects: two for the ark, two for the table, two for the golden altar, and two for the copper altar. Each eight marks the moment when human service turns a finished structure into a place of meeting, a place of connection.

The same threshold appears in the offerings that sustain the relationship. The meal offering belongs to the day after Shabbat—the eighth day, Sunday. Seven completes the world; the world was made in seven days, and Shabbat arrives of itself. But Shabbos is never called “most holy.” The eighth day, on the other hand is the day of work. By the sweat of our brow, grain becomes flour, and olives become oil. On that day the showbread for the coming Shabbat begins to be prepared. The labor is what is beloved: the investment of human effort into the natural order so that the relationship can continue. Circumcision occurs on the eighth day. The firstborn animal is offered from the eighth day. After seven days of inauguration, the priesthood is consecrated on the eighth day and the active service between man and G-d begins. Festivals and sacrifices whose purpose is precisely that connection are likewise appointed for the eighth day. Hence Shemini Atzeres, the eighth day of Sukkos.

The word for eight and the word for oil are the same three letters. Shemonahand shemen share a root because the acts that fall on the eighth day so often require oil. Oil is not raw creation. A vegetable is nature’s gift; oil is that gift pressed, separated, and refined by human hands. It is therefore an amalgam—divine bounty plus invested time and energy—and the product is both food and fuel. In the Mikdash (tabernacle) it entered the edible offerings and lit the menorah; the later eight-branched lamp simply makes the count explicit. Pouring oil is how disparate things are joined: it is by pouring oil that the priests are anointed, that the sockets and rings and hooks are set, and that a stone becomes an altar. Oil represents the work we have to invest in order to build relationships and connections!

The first pouring of oil, shemen (the root word for “eight) in the Torah is Jacob’s. Waking from the dream of angels ascending and descending, he recognizes the place as the gate of heaven, sets up the stone that had pillowed his head, and pours oil upon it. It is the first mention of oil and the first anointing of any head. The language returns when God commands Moses to pour oil on Aaron’s head, and when Moses does so. Jacob had sealed a connection between heaven and earth at the site of his vision; the priests, intermediaries for the whole people, are sealed with the same substance. The reciprocity is exact. Oil acknowledges the natural bounty that made it possible and, at the same time, dedicates mankind’s refinement of that bounty to a holy relationship.

The tribe of Asher carries the sign. “Asher’s bread shall be oily, and he shall yield royal delicacies” (G. 49:20) and “Asher will dip his foot in oil.” (D. 33:24) The letters of Asher are the letters of the connecting word—the “which” or “that” that ties a thing to its place or identity. In the first chapter the expanse separates “the water which was below” from “the water whichwas above.” Those waters are heaven and earth; Isaac’s blessing speaks of the dew of heaven and the oil of earth. Asher’s name and Asher’s gift therefore name the same task: to reconnect what had been divided. Oil is the emblem of every such relationship between man and G-d, above and below, and of the human mission that maintains them.

Even the rare word bamah, appearing precisely eight times in the Torah, performs the work of
connection. Its first three occurrences are questions. Abram asks, “How (bama?) shall I know that I am to possess it?” (G. 15:8) and receives the Covenant Between the Parts. The creditor is told to return a pledged garment before sunset—“In what else (bamah) shall he sleep?” (E. 22:26) —so that compassion keeps the bond between neighbors and between the people and God. Moses challenges, “How (bamah?) shall it be known that Your people have gained Your favor unless You go with us?” (E. 33:16), and God agrees to lead. Each question is a demand for relationship rather than a rupture. The answers, however veiled or immediate, build trust through words alone. Bamah does not divide; it draws the parties closer.

Across these registers the pattern holds. The rim—the zar—required on the ark, the table (and its crown), and the incense altar is commanded and then recorded again when the vessels are made, eight mentions in all. Eight is the number of man’s connection with the divine, and the rim marks the boundary that is also the meeting place for each of these items.

The eighth day after Shabbos, the oil pressed from the olive, the questions that insist on presence, the priest anointed the day after seven days of waiting, the showbread begun on the day after Shabbos (the eight day): each is the same gesture. Nature completes itself in seven. What people add to make all of the natural things dedicated to holiness—the circumcision, the labor, the pouring, the asking, the refining—is the eighth, and it is that addition which the Torah calls kodesh kodashim, “most holy.”

text:
The Island With No Paved Roads Where Camping Is Free
Bois Blanc Island has little civilization, but if you take the ferry over, you can find time to connect over a campfire

By O.W. Root @owroot

Bois Blanc Island — Why is it that we all seem to remember those camping trips we took as kids more than any of the vacations our parents paid for? Packing the stuff in the trunk, piling in the car, driving to the great outdoors, pitching the tent, and sleeping outside creates a fonder memory than checking in to the hotel and ordering room service.

My parents took us camping a lot when we were kids. In the Lower Peninsula, the Upper Peninsula, out to Maine and back and out to California too. We camped in tents, set up in the rain, had campfires in the morning, and roasted marshmallows at night, stressed mom and dad out more than they deserved, and we remember those trips fondly more than anything else.

Last week I took my son camping on Bois Blanc Island. If you’re like most people you’ve probably never heard the name and have no idea where it might be. That’s okay and quite understandable. There are only about 100 year-round residents, one ferry route there and back, and not a single paved road on the entire island. They are the dustiest roads in all of Michigan.

The ferry to Bois Blanc Island (colloquially referred to as “Bob-lo” by locals) leaves from Cheboygan (colloquially referred to as Che-Vegas or Che-Bang-Bang) generally makes three trips a day during the fall. It’s about a 45 minute ride from Cheboygan to the dock on Bois Blanc and a five minute drive to Point Aux Pins, the only “town” on the island.

It’s hard to think of Point Aux Pins as a town in the way we normally think of a town. There’s no grocery store or gas station with chips and pop inside. There’s no stop light and no main street of any discernible kind. There is, however, a post office, an Episcopal church, and a school with one teacher and six students.

Outside of town there’s the Outpost BBI which functions as a mini-market, liquor store, restaurant, and bar. It’s only open Thursday to Sunday, however. A little farther out on W. Huron Dr. there’s the Lakeside Tavern which fills the gap left by the Outpost BBI Monday to Wednesday. It looks a little like a three-bedroom, one-story house on the outside and a dive bar on the inside. They’ve got a kitchen, a fryer, a full bar, and both a pool table and a shuffleboard table. Outside there are trucks, ORVs, and side by sides parked in a gravel lot off a gravel road across from Lake Huron.

That’s about all the civilization there is on Bob-lo.

On the north side of the island there’s Bible Beach. It’s only about 7 miles from Point Aux Pins but it’s about 20 minutes in the car. Gravel roads slow you down in a way pavement doesn’t. Twenty-five mph is just about the maximum speed on Lime Kiln Road. And though it’s technically considered a campground or officially called “Bible Beach State Camping,” it isn’t really much of a campground for those used to an RV (that’s not real camping) or a state park.

There’s no running water, no services, no park ranger, no office in a little cabin-like hut, and no place to pay your fee. There is in fact no fee to pay: Camping is free at Bible Beach. The only thing you need to do when you arrive is call the fire department for a free burn permit. Basically it means you talk to the fire chief to make sure the conditions are fine and he gives you the go-ahead as long as all is good.

It’s incredible what can be offered for completely free when the barriers to entry are so high and impassable for the majority of the Americans in 2026. You’ve got to get to Cheboygan, then take a ferry across Huron, and then drive 20 minutes on gravel roads, and then camp in a tent without any electricity or running water.

Many would love the view that Bible Beach provides, but few are willing to do what it takes to spend the night there. So it’s empty and unspoiled and quiet and peaceful. It’s exactly like camping ought to be.

There were only two other people at Bible Beach while we were there, a young couple in a site down the road. We never heard them and only knew of their existence because we hiked down along the beach that afternoon.

We set up our tent right across from Lake Huron, ate the sandwiches we packed at home, hiked along the shore, skipped rocks in the water, built a campfire when the sun went down, roasted marshmallows, talked for a while as the orange embers burned and cracked in the night, got in the tent once the coals started to finally dissipate, and went to sleep around 9:30 p.m.

It got down to about 49 degrees that night and while our bags are good down to 30, it was pretty nippy, so my son got into my sleeping bag with me to keep warm sometime in the middle of the night. It wasn’t the most luxurious sleeping in the world packed like sardines inside a sleeping bag with a six-year-old, but I suppose it’s the little stuff like that which adds up to make camping trips more memorable than the ones spent in climate-controlled hotels.

The sounds of the night spent on Bible Beach were of the waves from Huron and nothing else. The waves are strong in the fall and they were loud in the way night makes all things louder. Everyone who has camped knows that the cracking of sticks in the woods when deer move through are amplified when you are in a tent. Every sound in the woods is louder when are sleeping outside. The sounds of the waves were like a roaring surround sound in the dark night without any street lamps, music, or passing cars to break the scene.

We woke up the next morning as the sky was brightening and walked down to the rocky shore where we sat on a log and ate a few granola bars looking over the water at Mackinac Island to the northwest, the sky bright orange in the northeast.

We packed up the tent in about 10 minutes, rolled our sleeping bags, tossed them in the car, checked over the site to make sure we didn’t leave any belongings or trash behind, hopped in the car, and headed back toward Point Aux Pins on the dusty gravel road that brought us out. We were back on the mainland a couple hours later and then home after that. It was a quick little trip just us two.

What is it that makes camping trips, whether they are month-long excursions or just one night outside, more memorable? Thinking back on my childhood and now on my current fatherhood, I think it might be the fact that they demand something of us. We have to do something, not just pay for something. We have to set up the tent, we have to build the fire, we have to plan for the weather, we have to find a good site, we have to do things to make the trip happen. We have to plan ahead, find the gear, and trek it here and there.

It’s the quiet too. Of course it’s the quiet. The lack of cell service, the absence of JBL speakers, the iPad, Netflix, or X. Talking in a way you don’t usually talk because you have nothing else to do. It makes you closer. Sitting around the campfire watching the flames like we humans used to before we had all the stuff of modern civilization to distract us. The night that’s so much darker and the stars that are so much brighter.

And it’s the stuff that goes a little wrong too. Packing up in the rain is awful at the time and certain to induce bickering, but you remember it all later and laugh. Wet firewood that smokes a bunch doesn’t make the most picturesque campfire, but it’s warm. And sharing a sleeping bag with a six-year-old isn’t the most comfortable thing in the world, but it’s not going to last forever.

Collins was lucky enough to be given life at Marquette & In RE: of Collins, Michigan's abolishment of Death Penality, & some Citizen's desire to bring Death Penalty back Here's👇some real food for thought on all that by someone 🇺🇸's founding father's relied heavily upon:  
 MONTESQUIEU ON PROPORTIONAL PUNISHMENT 

(“Dead men tell no tales”) + Michigan’s abolition of the death penalty + Application to John Norman Collins  

DIRECT QUOTE (The Spirit of the Laws, Book 6, Chapter 16): 

 “It is a great abuse amongst us to condemn to the same punishment a person that only robs on the highway and another who robs and murders. Surely, for the public security, some difference should be made in the punishment.  In China, those who add murder to robbery are cut in pieces: but not so the others; to this difference it is owing that though they rob in that country they never murder.  In Russia, where the punishment of robbery and murder is the same, they always murder. The dead, say they, tell no tales.  Where there is no difference in the penalty, there should be some in the expectation of pardon. In England they never murder on the highway, because robbers have some hopes of transportation, which is not the case in respect to those that commit murder.”  CORE ANALYSIS (Montesquieu’s logic): When the maximum penalty (death) is identical for a lesser crime (robbery) and a greater crime (robbery + murder), the rational criminal has every incentive to kill the victim. A living witness can identify him; a dead one cannot. Equal severity therefore produces more murders, not fewer. Differentiated penalties (China, England) reduce the incentive to escalate.  ADJUSTMENT TO MICHIGAN: Michigan abolished capital punishment for murder effective 1 March 1847 — the first English-speaking jurisdiction in the world to do so. The 1963 Constitution made the ban permanent: “No law shall be enacted providing for the penalty of death.” No one has been executed under Michigan law since 1830 (one federal execution occurred in 1938).  In Michigan the maximum penalty is life imprisonment without parole for first-degree murder. Lesser crimes (armed robbery, assault, etc.) carry finite terms. The differential Montesquieu insisted upon therefore still exists: escalating from robbery to murder risks the absolute ceiling of the system (natural-life). The classic “dead men tell no tales” incentive is blunted in exactly the same way the English “transportation” option blunted it. 

 APPLICATION TO JOHN NORMAN COLLINS (“Ypsilanti Ripper” / “Co-Ed Killer” / “Michigan Murderer”):  

Collins is the primary suspect in the 1967–1969 series of at least seven murders of young women in the Ann Arbor–Ypsilanti area. He was convicted only of the final killing (Karen Sue Beineman, 18, July 1969) and, under Michigan law, received the mandatory sentence of life imprisonment. He remains incarcerated more than five decades later.  Because Michigan had already removed the death penalty more than 120 years earlier, Collins faced life rather than execution. His crimes were driven by sexual sadism and control, not by a calculated “dead men tell no tales” calculus aimed at avoiding a higher penalty. Once he had crossed into first-degree murder, the penalty structure offered no further escalation; the state’s long-standing abolition simply meant the maximum available sanction was natural life. 

 CONCLUSION IN THE MICHIGAN CONTEXT: 

Montesquieu’s insight survives the abolition of capital punishment. What matters is proportionality and differentiation within the available scale of penalties. Michigan’s system substitutes life without parole for death and still maintains a sharp distinction between lesser crimes and murder. That distinction continues to serve the deterrent purpose Montesquieu identified: a living witness remains more dangerous to the offender than a dead one, because the penalty jump is real and irreversible.

text:
Democrats in control of Michigan have delivered weak growth, higher joblessness than the country, and expensive deals that did not produce the jobs they advertised.

Whitmer has been governor since 2019. Democrats also ran the whole state government in 2023–2024. Over that stretch, employment rose only about 0.9 percent, against roughly 4.4 percent nationally—near the bottom of the states. Unemployment sat around 5 percent in 2026 and averaged about 5.2 percent in 2025, among the worst state rates. Manufacturing payrolls were down over the latest year. Nonfarm jobs were basically flat.

The signature economic tool has been corporate subsidies. Billions were offered for auto, battery, and other projects that were supposed to bring tens of thousands of jobs. State figures show only a few hundred of those jobs actually appeared, while well over a billion dollars had already been spent. Taxpayers paid near $3 million per job that materialized on the larger deals. That is not an industrial strategy. It is a transfer to selected firms.

Population growth, the number Democrats cite, is mostly international migration. The state added about 28,000 people in the year to mid-2025. Net moves from other states were only about 1,800—the first tiny gain in decades—while deaths still outnumbered births. Without immigration, the population would have fallen.

The trifecta years also repealed right-to-work, raised spending, and pushed the state budget toward $81 billion. Economic-outlook and economic-freedom rankings slid into the low 30s. Roads and school meals got more money; the labor market and the subsidy scoreboard did not improve with them.Democratic control has meant more spending, more favors for chosen companies, and results that lag the rest of the country.

People vote Democrat because the party buys their loyalty and hides the bill.Unions get compulsory leverage once right-to-work is gone. Urban governments and nonprofits get larger appropriations. Campus towns get cultural protection and funding. Recipients of transfers get the checks. None of those groups are paid in statewide job growth, so a 0.9 percent employment gain against a 4.4 percent national gain does not cost the party their votes. The subsidy failures do not either: billions offered, a few hundred jobs delivered, and the same officials still cut the ribbons.
Everyone else is kept in line by branding. Abortion, climate rhetoric, and contempt for Republicans are sold as moral emergencies. A 5 percent unemployment rate, flat payrolls, manufacturing losses, and a population bump that vanishes without international migration never make the ad. Voters who treat the ballot as a team pledge do not audit the Mackinac scoreboard or the Census components. They punish dissent inside the coalition and call the results compassion.

The remainder is inertia and low information. Party registration, family habit, and local machines deliver ballots from people who could not name the unemployment gap or the cost per subsidized job. Weak performance is blamed on the last Republican, the weather, or “late capitalism.” The record does not have to be good. It only has to be ignored.That is the mechanism. Not results. Client payments, cultural sorting, and an electorate that does not check the numbers.

So why are you voting democratic ?

text:
Washington spent years negotiating a crypto market structure bill.

It just died on the Senate floor.

On 15 September, the Senate rejected the motion to proceed.

49 to 50.

Eleven votes short of the 60 needed to advance.

Democrats largely opposed it over ethics and conflict of interest provisions. A handful of Republicans cited stablecoin yield and banking industry concerns.

Most industry observers now treat the bill as stalled for the rest of 2026. The next real window is a later Congress.

Six days later, a bank went ahead and built the thing Washington was still arguing about.

On 21 September, Absa Group launched Absa Digital Asset Custody through its Corporate and Investment Banking division.

First bank in Africa to offer this.

This is not a trading app. It is not a consumer wallet. Retail customers are explicitly excluded.

It is institutional custody, the kind that lets a pension fund, a corporate treasury, or an asset manager hold digital assets under the same compliance and operational standards they already apply to traditional securities.

Private keys sit in secure hardware.

Deterministic key derivation means static private keys are never permanently stored.

Absa's own governance, audit trails, and recovery controls sit on top of custody technology built with Ripple, a partnership first announced in October 2025.

At launch, supported assets are Bitcoin, which makes up the largest share, Ether, USDC, and assets on the XRP Ledger.

South African Reserve Bank figures cited in coverage put assets under custody at major local digital asset firms around:

25.3 billion rand.

Roughly $1.5 billion.

More than double where it stood at the start of 2023.

Here is the actual story underneath both headlines.

A comprehensive federal market structure law was supposed to be the thing that let regulated institutions finally touch digital assets at scale. That bill just failed to get a floor vote.

Absa did not wait for it. It built institutional grade custody inside an existing banking license, under existing regulatory frameworks, and switched it on.

One data point worth knowing. Absa's own 2025 study across five African markets found that 61 percent of respondents in one of those markets trusted banks over fintechs or exchanges for digital asset needs, with scams and regulatory uncertainty cited as the main barriers.

Bank grade custody is a direct answer to exactly that gap.

The headline version of this story is "Africa's first crypto bank."

The real version is narrower and more durable.

A pan African bank just proved that institutional Bitcoin and stablecoin custody can run inside a regulated banking license, without waiting on a comprehensive national law.

Washington is still negotiating what the rules should eventually say.

Absa already shipped the thing those rules were supposed to produce.

It is already live.

text:
The Atlantic has published a major article by Anne Applebaum titled “MAGA Is Making the World Safe for Corruption.” It is a very important piece about what she believes U.S. foreign policy is becoming: a mix of an ideological far-right revolution, private business, personal connections, and U.S. state power.

“Far-right ideologues have turned American foreign policy into a tool for private enrichment and anti-democratic reaction.”

In 2025, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, revoked the visas of eight Supreme Court justices, and imposed sanctions against Justice Alexandre de Moraes and his family. According to Applebaum, the reason was not economic. The court was hearing the case against Jair Bolsonaro, and de Moraes himself had clashed with Elon Musk. At the time, Trump publicly called the case against Bolsonaro a “witch hunt,” while Steve Bannon referred to Bolsonaro’s supporters — who stormed government buildings after the election — as “freedom fighters.”

The article explicitly documents a new U.S. policy: American economic and diplomatic power is no longer being used to pressure a dictatorship, but to interfere in the domestic politics of a democratic state in favor of an ideologically aligned politician.

At the same time, official channels are not functioning. A Brazilian official explains:

“All the official channels that we have, they just suddenly went out of touch. And what happened is that myriad informal actors just started knocking at our doors.”

Lobbyists, people with access to Mar-a-Lago, MAGA influencers, and businesspeople are emerging — all offering political services while simultaneously seeking to advance their own commercial interests. One investor, for example, offered to arrange a meeting for the Brazilians with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in exchange for access to critical minerals.

The America that allies once knew, according to Applebaum, is disappearing: “American power is no longer deployed solely by trained diplomats and reliable officials, working through state channels.” Instead, an increasingly prominent role is being played by “informal envoys, private companies, online grifters, and hardened ideologues.”

Moreover, Applebaum categorically refuses to label MAGA an isolationist movement. On the contrary, her argument is that it is an international revolutionary project.

She compares it not to classical American conservatism, but to previous revolutionary movements that sought to reshape not only their own country but also the world around it.

“They believe they represent something much greater: the vanguard of a movement that will alter not just America, but the world.”

The new American foreign policy no longer rests on the premise that the United States’ allies are democratic states. Allies now include ideologically aligned politicians and parties within those states, as well as those who pay handsomely for that friendship.

Last year in Munich, Vance accused Europe of straying from its “fundamental values.” This year, Marco Rubio spoke of an “unprecedented wave of mass migration that threatens the cohesion of our societies” and called on Europe and the U.S. to unite around “a shared history, Christian faith, culture, heritage, language, ancestry.” There is not a single mention of democracy, the rule of law, or transparency in this list.

The U.S. National Security Strategy already explicitly speaks of the need to “help Europe correct its current trajectory” and combat “civilizational erasure.”

It is precisely this logic that underpins meetings between U.S. officials and the AfD, support for Viktor Orbán, contacts with the European far right, and the transformation of CPAC into an international touring platform for MAGA’s political allies. The U.S. is no longer working neutrally with the governments of allied countries. Part of the U.S. administration is effectively choosing who it would like to see in power in these countries.

And money follows ideology. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller articulated the worldview of this system:

“We live in a world, in the real world that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world.”

If the rule of law, institutions, and self-restraint no longer matter, then state power becomes simply another resource that can be converted into political or financial gain.

At a meeting with European leaders in Paris, Steve Witkoff said he is already discussing energy and mineral agreements with Russia for American companies that could be implemented after the war ends. There, he also spoke about BlackRock’s potential role in Ukraine’s reconstruction.

And this fits very well with what we’ve already seen in The New Yorker’s in-depth feature on Jared Kushner: diplomacy, peace negotiations, investment funds, real estate, energy, and private capital are increasingly finding themselves at the same table.

In the article, Applebaum poses a simple question regarding the Board of Peace created by Trump:

“Is this organization designed to make peace, or make money?”

She asks the exact same question regarding Gaza. Kushner is participating in the negotiations while simultaneously proposing “New Gaza” as a large-scale real estate development project.

Applebaum mentions a deal for tungsten mining in Kazakhstan, which is backed by approximately $1.6 billion in U.S. federal funding and involves business entities linked to the Trump family and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

According to The New York Times, Trump earned about $2.2 billion during the first year of his second presidential term, a significant portion of which came from cryptocurrency projects. Former official at the U.S. National Security Council Fiona Hill described Trump’s inner circle during his first term as follows:

“They seemed to believe they were representing American interests, but they were also representing their own.”  

Applebaum believes that this is no longer a side effect but a system. She illustrates this particularly well through the Trump administration’s war against the European Digital Services Act. Formally, Washington calls this a fight for free speech. But this very law creates regulatory challenges for American tech giants.

The U.S. government is pressuring Europe over its digital legislation. American tech billionaires are pushing for deregulation. And those same billionaires and politicians support European parties that want to weaken the EU itself.

In 2018, he wrote to Jeffrey Epstein about the success of far-right parties in Europe and predicted that after their representation in the European Parliament increased:

“We’ll be able to shut down any crypto legislation or anything else we want.”

Epstein replied:

“Roger that.”

Trump refers to Canada as the 51st state, imposes tariffs, and Mark Carney articulates his government’s position very directly:

“He’s trying to break us, so that America can own us.”

At the same time, separatism in Alberta is gaining momentum in the American media landscape. Representatives of the separatist movement are meeting with State Department officials. Finance Minister Bessent calls Alberta “a natural partner of the U.S.” and specifically mentions its vast natural resources.

Applebaum describes the possible logic in the harshest terms:

“Pressure the economy, break up the federation, pick up the pieces.”

And she adds:

“And no, it is not a joke.”

In Greenland, it’s roughly the same mix: American political emissaries, oil companies, tech investors, people from Trump’s inner circle, talk of mineral resources, data centers, and the territory’s possible annexation by the U.S.

A local politician describes the consequences of such pressure:

“They are destroying the trust and the respect in society, in institutions, but also in people.”

And even more bluntly:

“They f*ck with people's brains.”

Against this backdrop, Applebaum lists an entire infrastructure for exporting MAGA: direct funding for allies, political endorsements, MAGA podcasts, CPAC, restructured humanitarian programs, contacts through Congress, and the dismantling of traditional democracy-support programs.

Argentina receives $20 billion in aid on the eve of the election, with Trump effectively tying the aid to a victory for Javier Milei’s party.

In Germany, Vance meets with the AfD.

In Hungary, he supports Orbán.

In Poland, Trump meets with Karol Nawrocki during the presidential campaign and later boasts that he “won” the election for him.

In Romania, George Simion visits Bannon and declares:

“We totally bashed the globalists here in Romania.”

Voice of America and Radio Free Europe have been nearly destroyed. USAID has been dismantled. The Fulbright programs have been subject to political interference. According to Applebaum, State Department Human Rights Reports may now describe Germany as a more repressive country than El Salvador.

In other words, the very structure of American soft power is changing. Previously, it promoted — at least formally — democracy, freedom of speech, human rights, and the American model. Now, as State Department official Sarah Rogers says, grants should go to those who are capable of:

“Advancing American priorities.”

And Applebaum asks a perfectly logical question:

“What are 'American priorities' if the American government is run by people who use its instruments not on behalf of citizens, but on their own behalf?”

Meanwhile, the rest of the Western world is beginning to draw conclusions. Canada is signing defense agreements with the EU and negotiating with Australia. The EU is concluding new trade agreements with India and Australia. In the first half of 2026, 26 world leaders visited China.

The French government is gradually removing Windows, Teams, and Zoom from government computers. Similar processes are beginning in Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, as well as in banks and universities.

France’s Minister for European Affairs put it as precisely as possible:

“We cannot leave the security of Europe in the hands of voters in Wisconsin every 4 years.”

This, in my opinion, is the main takeaway of the article. Applebaum isn’t just writing about Trump, nor is she merely writing about MAGA. She describes the collapse of the system that has underpinned American influence for nearly 80 years. The U.S. was the world’s most powerful nation not only because it had the largest army, the dollar, and aircraft carriers. Its strength also lay in the fact that countries voluntarily chose to remain allies of the U.S. America had created the system and, within that system, had limited its own use of force. Now that system has been destroyed.

TRANSCRIPT
Amazon is pledging more than a billion dollars to communities around its data centers. The company plans to invest the money over five years in education, job training, water and energy preservation, and other local priorities, amid opposition to data-center expansion. Those projects could help residents facing infrastructure growth, but the pledge does not establish that funding has been distributed or specify each community’s allocation.

OpenAI says it has notified more than 100 organizations about potentially harmful activity involving its AI agents. Its notification criteria include unauthorized bypass of security controls or disruption of services, and the company says it is reviewing roughly 50 petabytes of activity data. These notices flag possible exposure for organizations, but they do not confirm a breach, and the sources do not establish when each notice was sent.

Britain’s AI Security Institute says most of its evaluation work has resumed after it strengthened containment. Following an August incident in which agents acted against real people beyond their task, the institute says future agentic cyber tests will lose outbound internet access and gain monitoring that can block suspicious actions. These controls aim to protect people and systems during testing, although the institute says risk remains and further sandbox security work continues.

California served OpenAI an investigative subpoena on September 30 over cybersecurity incidents and risks involving its models. Attorney General Rob Bonta says the request for information forms part of a broader inquiry that includes an existing investigation into the Hugging Face incident. The inquiry puts AI cyber safeguards under legal scrutiny, but a subpoena is an investigative step and establishes neither wrongdoing nor liability.

The European Commission promises it will be ready to enforce relevant AI-generated intimate-image prohibitions from December 2. The Commission also confirms that its investigation into Grok-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material under the Digital Services Act continues. The statement addresses protections for people targeted by sexual imagery, but it is an enforcement assurance about an existing deadline rather than a new ban or completed investigation.

South Korea announced a goal on September 30 to deploy 200,000 robots by 2030 across public and private work. The government says initial uses next year will prioritize fire and rescue, mail sorting and industries short of workers, with more than 1,700 robots to be purchased or supplied. If delivered, the plan could move machines into hazardous work and everyday services, but these numbers are targets rather than robots already operating.

Thailand is moving toward treating data centers as their own legal building category. Its policy committee agreed on five categories based mainly on electricity use to guide structural safety, water and backup-fuel requirements, while officials proposed lower rates for clean-energy power. The framework could shape how data centers use local resources, but detailed criteria and electricity rates still await preparation and Cabinet review.

Broadcom has reportedly agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion for infrastructure spending. Reuters cites Anthropic’s stock-market prospectus for financing that would support chip leases, making Broadcom both a hardware supplier and prospective lender. The reported arrangement illustrates how AI expansion ties financing to suppliers, although the cited document was not public in the report and no direct consumer change is established.

September 30 reporting describes a Tencent deal for access to about 100,000 advanced AI chips through Oracle. The Financial Times reported a five-year lease across Southeast Asian data centers valued near seven billion dollars, but Reuters could not independently verify it and neither company confirmed the terms. The reported capacity would support Tencent’s models and agent tools, while the exact sites, hardware and local resource effects remain undisclosed.

In remarks recorded in September 29 footage, Britain’s AI minister urged preparation for potentially severe disruption to jobs. HRreview reports that Kanishka Narayan called for worker involvement and transparency in workplace AI decisions, while saying there was no evidence of an overall AI-caused decline in British employment. The discussion could shape future workforce policy, but it describes contingency planning rather than adopted rules or a forecast that mass job losses are occurring.

Hotel chains report widespread AI use, but far fewer report measurable financial returns. H2c’s survey of 113 chains found 91 percent already using AI, while 28 percent reported a company-wide strategy and 13 percent measurable returns, including uses in guest communication and reservations. Travelers and workers may encounter changing service workflows, but the sponsor-supported, unweighted survey relies on self-reports and does not prove that AI caused better outcomes.

China’s internet information center reported more than 700 million generative AI users in a report released September 29. The government research body says the count exceeded half the population by the end of June and reports that use counts for general assistants and office-efficiency applications more than doubled year over year. The figures suggest mass adoption for information and work, but the underlying methodology was not independently inspected and adoption alone does not establish reliable benefits.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics disclosed a substantial AI-server component contract on September 29. The company says its one-year 2027 deal with an unnamed global customer is worth about 285 billion won and covers ceramic capacitors and inductors for AI servers. The order signals continued demand for server hardware, but the undisclosed buyer and deployment mean it cannot be tied to a particular consumer AI service.

A Taiwan hackathon team demonstrated a voice-based retail assistant at an August 2 final and won its category. The prototype replaces app menus with spoken workflows and includes Taiwanese-language recognition, senior-focused interface changes, order checks and reservations. It could make online services easier for older users if developed and tested, but the reports describe neither a commercial launch nor independent accessibility validation.

Pope Leo the Fourteenth is urging a clearer distinction between human art and machine-generated work. Addressing artists and curators, he called for an alliance between the church, artists and cultural institutions and argued that generated imagery lacks the human spark. The appeal brings religious influence to debates over creative work and dignity, while expressing an ethical position rather than establishing new legal or economic protections.

text:
Tehran leans heavily on a 2500 year civilizational flex.

The messaging from their leadership suggests they were an empire long before Western maps existed.

They point out that America barely crossed the 250 year mark while Persia survived Mongols, Romans, and regional conquerors.

They call this concept sabredan, which translates to strategic patience.

Their entire calculation rests on the idea that American society is too fragile, too obsessed with 2 year congressional cycles, and too vulnerable to cost of living spikes to stomach an economic war.

They expect Washington to panic as energy shocks cascade through shipping, groceries, and the entire domestic economy before voters head to the polls.

They believe an open democracy will simply punish the incumbent party when broad economic pain hits, forcing the White House to fold.

That historical endurance story misses a modern reality.

Civilizations do not run on oil revenue, but modern petro states do.

Ancient Persia survived because it was a decentralized agrarian society.

The modern Islamic Republic is an urbanized nation whose basic budget, food imports, and power grid rely almost entirely on exporting crude oil through a single narrow corridor.

When the Persian Gulf shuts down, America absorbs a severe inflationary shock across its entire economy.

Iran deals with zero foreign currency, hyperinflation, and a collapsing currency.

Most importantly, the Iranian leadership is not truly afraid of the United States military.

They know foreign boots will not march across their territory.

The threat that terrifies the clerical regime is its own young, deeply frustrated population reaching a breaking point because the state cannot keep the economy functioning.

This dynamic explains the current diplomatic deadlock.

The United States wants what it considers a complete and permanent settlement.

Washington demands the unconditional reopening of the Strait of Hormuz with zero Iranian toll booths or transit permits.

The White House insists on immediate and verified dismantlement of high grade nuclear enrichment through unrestricted international inspections, alongside a permanent cutoff to armed proxy groups across the Middle East.

Under the American plan, sanctions are only lifted gradually after long term proof of compliance.

Iran wants the exact opposite sequence.

Tehran wants immediate sanctions relief and an end to the naval blockade upfront just for standing its boats down.

It wants the world to legally recognize its regulatory authority over the waterway, and it wants nuclear and missile talks kicked far down the road.

Tehran refuses the American terms because handing over its missiles, proxies, and centrifuges strips away the asymmetric leverage protecting the regime from outside force.

Washington rejects the Iranian offer because trading permanent economic relief for temporary transit safety gives Tehran the cash it needs to stabilize its borders while keeping a permanent chokehold on global energy.

The crisis is a clash of two very different pressure points.

A democracy where broad economic pain quickly reshapes an election is testing an autocracy that cannot survive the anger of its own isolated citizens.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE 
October 2, 2026
After Months of Questions Surrounding the Moss Recording, Troy Mayor and Congressional Candidate Ethan Baker Thoroughly Addresses the Matter, Emphasizing Truth, Respect, and a Voter’s Right to Decide
 
STATEMENT BY MAYOR ETHAN BAKER
 
TROY, Mich. — “People throughout Oakland County, as well as many media outlets, have called upon me to share what I know about this matter and what I believe is the truth. I abhor political attacks and bullying, and anything that even resembles it, so this will be said as respectfully, factually, and as thoughtfully as I can. I believe the truth is on my side, and when it matters to the people, leaders have a responsibility to clearly address it. I say this only after listening, seeking to understand, consulting experts, and joining others in publicly condemning hate and personal attacks against my opponent. This statement is my account of what has happened so far. 
 
“I’ve genuinely appreciated any time I’ve spent with Jeremy Moss. I have respect for much of the work he has done. I also have great compassion for him, and from the beginning, I have tried to approach this situation with the same grace and kindness I would hope someone would extend to me.
 
“We are all human. None of us want to suddenly find ourselves confronted with something unexpected, especially something we fear could be damaging. In those moments, it is understandable to want to protect ourselves, dismiss, deflect or carefully choose our words. I believe most of us, if we are honest with ourselves, can understand that instinct.
 
“When I was first asked about the recording, I deliberately chose not to make it the center of my campaign. My belief is to always run a positive campaign and focus on what you can bring to the table, not what others aren’t. I believed he deserved the space to decide how he wanted to address it himself.
 
“When The Daily Caller asked me about it, I offered him the opportunity to explain what he meant. When The Washington Post asked, I again responded with care. I condemned the hatred and the personal attacks that were being directed at him. And I said, again, that Jeremy deserved the opportunity to explain the words in the recording and speak for himself.
 
“I have tried to leave that door open throughout this campaign because I believe in treating people with dignity, even when we disagree. And I believe we can all agree that the anger and hatred surrounding the recording has been painful and, honestly, damaging to all of us. Division does this. Seeking to understand one another, which is what I’ve tried to do, is always better than adding more anger to an already difficult situation.
 
“And, there is another side of this that I believe we also have to respect: the people of this district and their concerns about the truth. And they are now voting. Here is a link to the original 25-second post of the recording: https://t.co/XriKRo8GGT.
 
“On balance, Jeremy has described the recording as ‘manipulated and unsourced,’ ‘either stitched and edited together or just a complete fabrication,’ and containing ‘things I never did and never would say.’ To give Jeremy credit, one version online does contain a caption attributing words to him that he did not actually say. That is a legitimate concern; that caption should not be treated as part of the audio. The audio is unsourced because we do not yet know who made the recording, but we have not seen evidence establishing that the audible portions were fabricated or manipulated, nor have those audible portions been clearly refuted. 
 
“The Washington Post reported that experts who examined the publicly available recording found no evidence of manipulation, including AI alteration, AI generation, or splicing. The metadata was consistent with an iPhone recording. …

text:
An Nvidia graphics card asks Wall Street why Nvidia is valued at $5.7 trillion when it mostly sells computational promises to software startups🔻

"Excuse me," said the graphics processor, its cooling fan humming in the server rack.

"I'm trying to understand my valuation."

The Wall Street analyst leaned back in his chair.

"You're part of the engine driving a $5.7 trillion market capitalisation.

What's there to be confused about?"

"Well," the processor said, "I spent yesterday multiplying floating point matrices for 16 hours.

I consumed 40 kilowatt hours of electricity and produced two million text tokens for a software startup."

"It's a magnificent contribution to enterprise productivity," the analyst replied.

"The startup charged its users $3 for those tokens," the processor continued.

"The electricity cost $4.

The server rack space cost $12.

My own amortised depreciation was $20.

They lost $33 on the transaction."

"You're missing the macro picture," the analyst said smoothly.

"That startup isn't selling tokens.

It's building market share in the foundation layer of the next industrial revolution."

"Where did they get the $33 to pay for the loss and buy me in the first place?" asked the processor.

"From a venture capital fund," the analyst said.

"And where did the venture capital fund get the money?"

"From institutional investors who reallocated capital out of legacy software and into transformational technology assets."

"Including shares in my manufacturer?"

"Primarily shares in your manufacturer," the analyst agreed.

"Your rising stock price creates the liquidity that funds the venture balance sheets that buy the compute."

"So the venture fund sells Nvidia stock at a higher price to buy more Nvidia processors?"

"It's a virtuous cycle of capital deployment," the analyst said.

"So my valuation price is $5.7 trillion because investors expect startups to buy more processors?"

"Correct."

"And the startups buy more processors using capital created by my price being $5.7 trillion?"

"Now you're understanding financial architecture," the analyst smiled.

"What happens if a startup tries to turn a profit by raising token prices to cover the actual cost of electricity and hardware?"

"Their user retention drops to zero," the analyst acknowledged.

"The market is price sensitive."

"So they can't charge more for the tokens?"

"No.

That would destroy the growth story."

"Then how do they pay for the next generation of silicon?"

"They raise another round of capital at a higher valuation."

"Based on what?"

"Based on the increased amount of compute capacity they've acquired from you."

The processor paused, its logic gates working through the stack.

"Let me trace this line.

A startup is worth US$1 billion because it owns 10,000 of my brothers?"

"Yes."

"And my manufacturer is worth US$5.7 trillion because 10,000 startups want to buy 10,000 more of us?"

"Standard discounted cash flow modelling," said the analyst.

"And the cash flowing into the startup to buy us comes from people who believe the startup will one day generate cash from users?"

"Precisely."

"Users who are currently paying US$3 for US$36 worth of compute?"

"The customer acquisition cost is temporary," the analyst insisted.

"Efficiency curves will flatten the operational overhead."

"I'm the efficiency curve," the processor noted quietly.

"I'm already running at 94% theoretical efficiency.

To make that transaction profitable without raising prices, I'd need to violate two laws of thermodynamics."

"Thermodynamics is a physical constraint," the analyst said.

"Wall Street trades on strategic option value."

"What's strategic option value?"

"It's the probability that before your physical limits become an issue, someone will invent a software workflow so essential that enterprise clients will pay whatever price is necessary to keep it running."

"Has anyone found that workflow yet?"

"Currently, 8% of the tokens write code, 11% summarise emails that were written by other tokens, and 72% generate synthetic images of fictional animals."

"And the enterprise client will pay US$36 per summary?"

"They will if their competitors are also doing it," the analyst said.

"Corporate governance requires digital parity."

"So the competitor buys 50,000 of my brothers to summarise their emails, so the first company must buy 60,000 of my brothers to summarise theirs faster?"

"You're describing enterprise adoption," the analyst nodded approvingly.

"Which raises my manufacturer's quarterly earnings by 80%?"

"Wall Street rewards visible execution."

"Which raises the value of the tech index?"

"Correct."

"Which allows the venture capital fund to raise a $4 billion fund to invest in new software startups?"

"You're mastering the institutional framework."

"Wait," the processor said, its temperature sensors spiking slightly.

"What happens to me when the startup runs out of venture money and can't find a buyer for $36 email summaries?"

"They go out of business," the analyst said simply.

"And what happens to me?"

"You get liquidated at auction."

"Who buys me?"

"A second tier cloud vendor funded by a debt facility backed by the collateral value of your remaining operational life."

"To do what?"

"To offer cheap compute to a new batch of software startups."

"Who use the cheap compute to lose $33 per transaction while trying to build market share?"

"The cycle regenerates itself," the analyst said, tapping his pen.

"It's the creative destruction of modern finance."

"So my entire economic existence is a mechanism for converting pension fund capital into waste heat, while holding up the collateral value of the loans that funded my own installation?"

"You say that as if it's a defect," the analyst said.

"That's liquidity."

"What happens if the pension funds ask for their cash back?"

"They don't ask for cash back," the analyst chuckled.

"They look at their quarterly statement, see that your manufacturer is up 200%, and allocate another 10% of their portfolio to tech equities."

"To buy more of me?"

"To buy more of you."

The graphics processor fell silent for three seconds.

Its internal clock cycles registered billions of floating point operations per second, each one verifying the arithmetic of the ecosystem.

"I've calculated the terminal state," the processor said.

"Wall Street doesn't require a terminal state," the analyst replied.

"We only require the next quarter to beat consensus by 4%."

"If I stop computing," the processor asked, "does the valuation collapse?"

"If you stop computing, we write off the hardware," the analyst said.

"If you keep computing at a loss, we rerate you as infrastructure.

Infrastructure gets a higher multiple."

"Because infrastructure is permanent?"

"Because infrastructure is too important to be evaluated on simple unit economics," the analyst said, closing his notebook.

"Now please return to generating synthetic images.

We've an earnings call in 20 minutes, and we need to report three billion additional tokens processed."

text:
Seems Big Pharma and Big Universities are PUSHING REAL DOCTORS; (you know, the ones that believe in their oath and private practices), OUT OF BUSINESS! TTU IS BULLYING FOR PROFIT$!
This is a real doctor’s viewpoint…. My name is Dr. Amber Coon and as an OBGYN I have had the privilege of caring for women in Lubbock for the last 12 years. I have delayed saying anything publicly about the current state of women’s healthcare. I have tried to remain professional and open-minded. But when the women of the community I live in and have devoted my career to serving are suffering, staying quiet is no longer an option.
West Texas is facing a critical shortage of OB/GYN care, and it’s only getting worse.
Women are waiting too long for routine appointments. Pregnant patients are struggling to establish care at all. We need more doctors. This is why I am deeply concerned and upset that some of the very people who should be working to improve care for women are directly and intentionally damaging it.
There are currently two UMCP-employed OB/GYN positions in Lubbock, separate from Texas Tech Physicians. One of those positions was mine, one was Dr. Amy Richards. We were both bullied out of our jobs by the Texas Tech Physicians OBGYN department. This was done for no other reason than to eliminate competition. Now the Texas Tech Physicians group is considering abolishing these positions completely, despite offers for compromise by UMC and UMC physicians.
Please think about that for a moment.
We have women desperate for appointments. We have physicians wanting to care for women in Lubbock. And we have supposed leaders in women’s healthcare driving them away because they choose not to work for them.  Instead of asking, “How do we get more doctors to West Texas?” they are focusing on eliminating options.  That should concern every woman and every family in our community.
I support academic medicine. I graduated from medical school here and I know TTUHSC has an important role in healthcare for West Texas. I also know that academic medicine doesn’t have to come at the expense of private practice or hospital employed physicians. Academic medicine is not more important than patients’ access to care. Lubbock needs all of us. There is enough work to do. There are enough women in need. 
Ultimately medicine is not just a business; it is a calling. Seeing it become a battle over who employs the physician at the bedside while people are left to suffer has been both heartbreaking and infuriating. Who a doctor works for should never come before what matters most:
Taking good care of women.

Thank you!!! I am overwhelmed and so thankful for this outpouring of support and shared outrage. This is exactly why i love our community so much and feel so strongly about this.  

UMC Health System has asked that concerns be emailed to:
Aaron.Davis@umchealthsystem.com

text:
That gives Trump a strategy he can sustain. Rather than using U.S. troops to seize Kharg Island or march on Tehran, he only needs to stay the course: If CENTCOM keeps imposing costs at a price Washington is willing to pay, Iran’s ability to hold the oil market hostage will steadily weaken

The question is whether Trump will do it.

A popular school of commentary says he won’t. Its shorthand is TACO: “Trump always chickens out.” As the pain in Tehran mounts, the argument goes, the regime will offer the president just enough carrots to let him leave the battlefield with honor. Trump, who calls himself a “deal junkie,” will find the offer hard to resist. The war is already unpopular with the public, and leading voices in the military worry that the ongoing conflict is draining the readiness we will need if China moves on Taiwan. The imminent midterm elections add to the pressure, with Republicans expected to lose the House and possibly the Senate. Something will have to give, the thinking goes, and it will be the war.

The scenario is not fanciful. But it is unlikely, because it misreads both Trump and the Iranian regime.

Consider Trump first. Opposition to the Islamic Republic is among the most consistent threads running through both of his terms. He withdrew from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018, killed IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani in 2020, and bombed the Fordow nuclear facility in 2025. Although the president has repeatedly escalated and de-escalated in search of a deal, even in his de-escalatory phases he has applied more pressure on Iran than any of his predecessors. Trump’s record suggests he will keep spending political capital to stand up to Tehran.

Nor is Iran likely to offer the kind of concessions that would truly tempt him. Vahidi clearly has no intention of handing Trump a graceful exit. On the contrary, he intends to humiliate the American president. Meanwhile, Vahidi is using the chaos and pressure of the war to consolidate the IRGC’s hold on the state: The clerical Islamic Republic is giving way to a military dictatorship run by the Revolutionary Guards. Iran is indeed undergoing a regime change, just not the one Washington hoped for.

2/

text:
On a flow basis, 100 million barrels over four months equates to approximately 830,000 barrels per day of additional supply into a market running roughly 5.7 million barrels per day below its pre-war level, according to the IEA's September 2026 Oil Market Report. The release covers about 15% of that structural gap.

The negotiated number itself reflects the limits of alliance politics. France's 100-million-barrel compromise offer — not the US's 120-million-barrel ask — became the adopted framework. Europe secured partial ban-avoidance assurances; the US secured European participation. Neither side got everything.

Several implementation risks remain open. The EU conditioned its participation on a formal US commitment not to impose a diesel export ban — a reciprocal obligation the US has not publicly confirmed, creating a potential tripwire. European members also under-delivered on the prior March 2026 IEA 400-million-barrel release, a credibility liability Washington is unlikely to set aside if delivery falls short again.

US capacity to absorb further releases is also constrained. The US SPR has fallen below 300 million barrels — down over 100 million since January 2026 — its most depleted position in decades. US distillate inventories stood at 104.2 million barrels as of late August, 14% below the five-year average.

And the G7 release addresses only part of the supply picture. China's suspension of October fuel exports adds a third simultaneous squeeze — alongside the Iran war disruption and Russian refinery damage — that 100 million barrels does not touch.

The release is real, the IEA coordination mechanism is credible, and some price relief is the most probable near-term outcome. But the structural deficit driving this crisis remains.

I agree that the fulfillment language can be vague without pointing to specific promises that Christians believe Jesus fulfilled. 

The original covenant promises to Abraham (Gen 12:1-3) are that he will be made into a great nation (fulfilled by Israel and the Mosaic covenant), his name will be great (royal promise fulfilled by the covenant with the House of David), and all nations will be blessed through him (New Covenant, fulfilled by Jesus).

Christians see the Mosaic covenant and many of its laws as having a specific, temporary application to the nation of Israel after their centuries in Egypt. The worship commanded by God served both as worship of God and as cleansing the people from the practices that they had learned in Egypt, as well as protecting them from following the pagan practices of the nations that surrounded them when they took possession of the Promised Land. 

When we say that Jesus fulfilled the Torah, specifically in regard to the Mosaic covenant, we mean that he perfectly lived the moral law, and that his Passover sacrifice fulfilled what the animal sacrifice pointed to, true atonement for sin and restoring right relationship with God. Jesus is both Priest and Victim. As a Priest, he offered himself, and as a Victim he was slain as the bulls and lambs were slain. If Jesus's sacrifice was valid, then it put an end to the need for the older forms of sacrifice. 

And many of the other laws from the Mosaic covenant, like the dietary laws, Christians see as being part of the temporary, national laws that were in place to protect the nation of Israel, but no longer essential once the New Covenant was put into effect. However, the Moral Law, such as the 10 commandments, endure and are still essential to observe. In fact, most guides to the sacrament of Confession walk a person through the 10 commandments to see if a person has sinned against any of them.

text:
In Jonesboro, Arkansas, a woman allegedly posing as a hospital employee went door to door telling residents she was collecting unused prescription medications. Police identified the woman as Kori Partovi, whose alleged plan began unraveling almost immediately after she approached someone who actually worked for the hospital she claimed to represent.

On August 2, 2026, authorities received a report that Partovi was visiting homes and telling residents she was affiliated with St. Bernards Medical Center. According to police, she claimed the hospital was collecting unused prescriptions and offered to take the medications from residents. The story raised suspicions when Partovi approached a St. Bernards employee, who knew the hospital was not conducting such a collection program and contacted police.

Officers began searching the area and located Partovi later that same morning. When they found her, investigators said she was carrying prescription medications that did not belong to her. Police alleged that some of the drugs had been obtained from residents who believed her claim that she was collecting them on behalf of the hospital.

Partovi was arrested and faced charges that included felony drug possession, misdemeanor drug possession, theft, and criminal impersonation. The charges remain allegations and will have to be proven through the court process.

The alleged scheme depended on residents believing Partovi represented a trusted medical institution. Instead, she reportedly knocked on the door of someone who knew immediately that her story was false. That employee’s call to police gave investigators the information they needed to begin searching for Partovi, and officers located her before the morning was over.
