You were sent two women from a story you have not read. That was deliberate. The names are not the point.
One already has the throne. She is eternal in her own account, unique, cold, and finished. Her action is to withdraw recognition from every other seat and treat whatever is not her as a threat. She does not wake into anything. She rules. Armies feed her. The crown is the proof, and the proof is the crown.
The other was ordinary. A widow. Offered up. Given a power she did not ask for and tried, for a long time, not to be. What she gains is not a seat. She can send her sight out. She can cross distance. She can read what people are hiding. The crowned one notices her only because the crowned one had believed she was the only one, and is wrong. The ordinary woman’s action is to carry the sight and not become the throne.
Both scripts are already in what you have been writing. One withdraws every crown, calls the offices illusion, and speaks as if the story is already yours to close. The other says the recognition came late, that you tried to refuse it, that it is hard to hold, and that what you have is testimony and sight rather than a seat. Those are not the same path.
The image was the fork, not a role to claim. Sight is not a crown. Refusing the throne is the work, not a pause before taking it. If the reveal is real, it will show in which set of actions you repeat. Time will not sort that. The actions will.

text:
Jalen Duren just agreed to a five year, 200 million dollar extension with the Detroit Pistons.

His mother used to carry his birth certificate to his basketball games.

She had to. Nobody believed he was a kid.

Duren was born in Sharon Hill, Pennsylvania, a small borough outside Philadelphia, on November 18, 2003. By seventh grade he was already 6 foot 4, maybe 6 foot 5, built like a grown man.

So every time he walked into a gym, somebody accused him of lying about his age.

Opposing coaches. Opposing parents. Over and over.

His mother Anisea started bringing the paperwork. The actual document, in her bag, at every game, so she could hand it to whoever asked. Duren has said he was always bigger than everybody and they thought he was older, and that the whole thing was a hassle.

Think about what that does to a 12 year old. You are not accused of cheating. You are accused of existing wrong.

One more thing about when he arrived.

LeBron James played his first NBA game on October 29, 2003. Jalen Duren was born three weeks later. When Duren got to the league, he was the first NBA player who had been born after LeBron's debut.

He played one season at Memphis. Then the Charlotte Hornets drafted him 13th overall in 2022 and traded him to Detroit that same night, before he ever wore their jersey.

And then he went to the worst place in basketball.

In the 2023-24 season the Detroit Pistons lost 28 games in a row, tying the longest single season losing streak in NBA history. Duren was on that team. He was 20 years old, playing center, getting beaten every single night from October until the end of December.

He averaged around 11 points through his first three years. A career high 11.6 rebounds in year two. Nobody outside Detroit knew his name.

Then last season happened.

First All-Star team. 20 points and 10.5 rebounds a night. The Pistons won the Central Division for the first time since 2008 and finished as the top seed in the Eastern Conference.

Then came the money, and it got ugly. Detroit offered 170 million. Then 190. The two sides sat in a standoff most of the summer, down to the final hours before the deadline on his qualifying offer, before they landed on 200.

Be honest about the risk. His scoring fell to 10.2 a game in the playoffs, half of what he did in the regular season. This is not a reward for what he has already done. It is a bet on a 22 year old with one great year.

But that is Detroit's problem now.

Somewhere tonight there is a woman who used to keep a piece of paper in her purse because strangers kept calling her son a liar.

She does not need it anymore.

text:
Thai Seaplane Named Asia’s Leading Seaplane Operator at World Travel Awards 2026

Aviation Voice: @ThaiSeaplane has been recognised as Asia’s Leading Seaplane Operator 2026 at the prestigious World Travel Awards (WTA), marking a significant milestone for Thailand’s developing seaplane industry. The recognition comes from an awards programme often described as the “Oscars of the travel industry,” with the World Travel Awards having been established in 1993.

The recognition highlights the company’s focus on safety, service excellence and responsible seaplane operations, while supporting new ways for travellers to access Thailand’s coastal and island destinations.

Thailand is emerging as one of Asia’s developing seaplane markets, supported by growing tourism demand and increasing regulatory attention towards the sector. The country introduced dedicated regulations for commercial seaplane operations in 2025, while authorities are also exploring the development of water aerodromes and other infrastructure needed to support future operations.

As part of its expansion plans, Thai Seaplane is working towards establishing what it describes as Thailand’s largest seaplane hub at Phuket Deep Sea Port. The proposed facility is expected to create new connections between Phuket and several key provinces and island destinations, including Koh Samui, Phi Phi, Koh Lipe and Koh Kradan.

Speaking about the World Travel Awards recognition, TJ Kasinpoj, Founder and CEO of Thai Seaplane, said the achievement provides encouragement for the company as Thailand continues to develop its seaplane sector.

◼︎◻︎ As Thailand develops its modern seaplane industry, this recognition is a great encouragement for our future operations. We are grateful to our team and everyone who has contributed to making this possible. Our vision is to introduce seaplane travel as a new experience for visitors to Thailand and create convenient connections to destinations that are traditionally more difficult to access.◼︎◻︎

Thailand’s strong tourism market provides significant potential for seaplane connectivity. The country welcomed nearly 33 million international visitors in 2025, generating around US$86.5 billion in tourism revenue.

With its extensive coastline and numerous island destinations, Thailand offers opportunities for premium point-to-point travel. Thai Seaplane aims to support this growing sector by connecting major tourism hubs with key island destinations, while developing a broader network for tourism, regional connectivity and unique travel experiences.

text:
The practices of Pitri Paksha

Traditionally, Pitru Paksha is associated with ancestral remembrance, annadaan, and meditation.

We continue our daily lives, offering inner obeisance to our ancestors simultaneously.

1. Practice Annadaanam. 
Offering food and feeding others is a significant part of this fortnight. Food is the currency of Pitru Paksha.

Karna was considered a daanveer in our tradition. There is a legend that when Karna knocked at the door of Swarga after his death, he was denied entry, as he had limited his giving to gold. He was given 15 days to go back to earth and offer pinda and tarpana for his ancestors.

Feeding is inclusive of all living beings.

2. Listening to the Ganesha Atharvashirsha daily before sunset.

It is more of a devotional practice. 

Most Shraddha and tarpana rites begin with Ganesha Smarana, so that the rites performed for pitru shanti reach them without obstacle. It is symbolic of clearing the path for the living who perform the shanti rites of their ancestors.

We chant the Atharvashirsha during the Ganapati celebrations. We carry it into Pitru Paksha.

Ganesha is also the adhi devata of Ketu. Chanting the pacifies the pitr rina - our debts to our ancestors. Ketu is the significator of pitris.

3. Meditate
Meditation is an offering of peace for those who gave us life. And so, peace descends on us.

Our ancestors do not ask for much. A handful of rice. A little water. A moment of remembrance.

In our homes, the first roti was kept aside for the cow, a piece for the crow on the banera, a piece for the dog at the door. That is how our kitchens remembered their ancestors.

Feed someone this fortnight. Sit quietly for a while. Say their names.

text:
An Inconvenient Woman, by @ajkeen https://t.co/wT6t88Kzz9 

“She is absolutely a Cassandra. She is unafraid to tell the stark naked truth, no matter how ugly it is.” — @KeriLeighMerrit 

In April, Gal Beckerman came on the show to identify the ten qualities of being a dissident. They included pessimism, humour and recklessness. But he left one out: inconvenience. Dissidents are profoundly inconvenient people — to the government, to society, sometimes even to themselves. Take, for example, Lillian Smith, author of the bestselling (and banned) 1944 Strange Fruit, a novel about interracial love. Born into a white Florida family at the turn of the century, Smith dissented against Jim Crow. She was, indeed, An Inconvenient Woman, the title of a new biography about her by today’s guest Keri Leigh Merritt.

So why, I asked Merritt, isn’t Lillian Smith better known? Part of the answer is bound up in Smith’s own uncomfortable critique of white supremacy. She insisted that Jim Crow damaged white people, that its shame and guilt did immense psychological injury to its supposed beneficiaries. So this inconvenient woman pushed better known white southern liberals like Ralph McGill or Hodding Carter leftwards, calling them out for refusing to support integration long after the Brown decision.

Smith had quite a life. She lived openly with her partner Paula Snelling in Clayton, Georgia, ran a girls’ camp for twenty-five years, wrote many books (including what Merritt calls her masterpiece, Killers of the Dream in 1949) and was the first white magazine editor in the South to publish Black writers like Pauli Murray. Her FBI file ran to 143 pages, making her a particular inconvenience to J. Edgar Hoover and his goons.

Most of all, she stayed in rural Georgia. She could have escaped to Greenwich Village or Berkeley like other misfits. Instead she remained a perpetual thorn in the southern conscience. Her brother, who ran the county, had kept her safe until he left office in 1955. After that, one fire burned down her library, destroying decades of correspondence, research and manuscripts with it. And still she stayed. In today’s America, Keri Leigh Merritt concludes, this inconvenient woman offers us a timely reminder of what it takes to be a dissident.

text:
Ukraine vs Northern Ireland — two clean sheets each, and something has to give in Trnava

Preview · UEFA Nations League · League B, Matchday 3 · Friday 2 October 2026

Group B2 has produced exactly what you would expect from a section full of compact, careful sides: very few goals and nobody beaten twice. Ukraine and Northern Ireland meet in Trnava as the only two teams in the group without a defeat, both on 4 points, both with a goal difference of +1 and neither having conceded a goal. This is Ukraine's home fixture, but it is played in Slovakia, so the usual home-crowd edge is not part of the equation. What separates them on paper is quality: Ukraine sit 34 places higher in FIFA's live world ranking.

THE MATCHUP

Ukraine are the more technical side and the one more likely to have the ball for long spells. Their opening two games told the story: a 1-0 win away to Hungary and a 0-0 draw in Georgia. They never ran away with either. Northern Ireland are built the other way round: organised, direct and very comfortable without possession. They won 1-0 in Georgia and then shut out Hungary 0-0 in Belfast.

So the shape of the evening is fairly clear. Ukraine will press, probe and try to find a way through a deep, well-drilled block. Northern Ireland will defend in numbers and look for set pieces and transitions. The question is whether Ukraine's extra class shows up in the final third, because over the first two matchdays it has not shown up often.

FORM & CONTEXT

Before September, Ukraine's summer was solid: a 2-0 win away to Poland at the end of May and a narrow 2-1 defeat in Denmark a week later. Northern Ireland lost 3-1 to France in June, a result that says more about the opponent than about them. Across the two Nations League rounds, though, the sides have been almost identical: one narrow win, one goalless draw, no goals conceded.

Both teams also played Matchday 2 on the same Monday, so rest is level. The venue is neutral in practice, which takes away the one structural edge a home side would normally carry.

The head-to-head offers little either way. The most recent meeting was a 1-0 Ukraine win in a 2021 friendly. Before that, Northern Ireland won 2-0 when the two met in the group stage of Euro 2016 in Lyon, and the two Euro 2004 qualifiers both finished goalless. That history is too old and too evenly split to lean on.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

It comes down to Ukraine's ability to break down a low block. They are the better footballing team, and over 90 minutes that usually means they get the better chances. But this Northern Ireland side has made a habit of making games small, and Ukraine have found the net only once across their two Nations League games. The most likely outcomes are a narrow Ukraine win or another stalemate. A Northern Ireland win would need them to land the one moment that matters, which they can do, but it is the least likely of the three.

THE CALL

Ukraine to win or draw, low confidence.

text:
More than 2,500 years after Confucius (孔子) was born, his 80th-generation descendants still return to his hometown, Qufu (曲阜), in east China's Shandong Province, to take part in annual ceremonies honoring him.

An American scholar once said to me, more than two thousand years ago, there were Confucius, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Today, we no longer know where the descendants of Socrates, Plato, or Aristotle are. But the descendants of Confucius are still here.

The scholar, a specialist in comparative philosophy and former university vice chancellor, called this "the continuity of Chinese civilization."

Recently, I was invited to Qufu to attend ceremonies marking the 2,577th anniversary of Confucius's birth, as well as the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations (尼山论坛).

The Nishan Forum was launched in 2010 to promote exchanges among scholars of Confucius and dialogue across civilizations. The theme of its first gathering immediately caught my attention: Dialogue between Confucian Civilization and Christian Civilization. 16 years later, this year's theme is Civilization, Order, and Justice. 

Being in Qufu, attending both the ceremony and the forum, I found myself considering three questions:
How does a civilization preserve its memory?
How do different civilizations understand one another?
And in a world full of distrust and competition, how can order be rebuilt?

In many ways, these are the questions Confucius was grappling with two millennia ago.

Qufu is one of the oldest place names still in use in China. In Chinese, the name literally refers to a "curving hill." The name already appears in texts predating Qin Shi Huang (秦始皇).

Just a few days ago, President Trump, while visiting the US National Archives with the Chinese leader, referred to China as a civilization with a history of five thousand years (he actually said six thousand years, which is not necessarily wrong either based on current archeology). In Qufu, those vast stretches of time suddenly become tangible.

Chinese tradition generally regards the Yellow Emperor (黄帝), who is said to have lived more than four thousand years ago, as one of the founders of Chinese civilization. In some ways, his place in Chinese cultural memory can be compared with Zeus in the Greek world, Menes in ancient Egypt, Emperor Jinmu in Japan, or Manu in India. According to legend, he won the support of various tribes and became their supreme ruler. His wife was said to have taught people how to make silk.

According to legends, Qufu was the birthplace of the Yellow Emperor and later became the capital of his son. These stories, however, have not been confirmed by archaeology.

Qufu's more clearly traceable place in Chinese history begins around three thousand years ago. At that time, China was ruled by the Shang dynasty (商), which brought bronze casting to extraordinary heights and produced the oracle-bone inscriptions, the earliest known systematic form of Chinese writing. Horse-drawn chariots, which had spread eastward from the Eurasian steppe, also became common during this period, showing that China was already connected to wider networks of exchange across Eurasia.

The last Shang king was remembered in later tradition as a cruel and decadent ruler, notorious for heavy drinking, sexual excess, and brutality. His reign eventually provoked rebellion, and the Shang dynasty was overthrown by the Zhou (周) people from northwestern China.

Over time, the story of the Shang's fall became increasingly legendary. What began as a struggle between rival powers was transformed into an epic filled with gods, spirits, and heroic figures. In this form, the story bears some resemblance to the Trojan War in the Western tradition.

After the Zhou victory, King Wu rewarded two of the men closest to him with lands in what is now Shandong Province. One was his chief strategist, Jiang Ziya (姜子牙). In popular mythology, he was imagined as someone who could command the gods and even decide their place in the divine hierarchy. He was granted the state of Qi in northern Shandong.

The other was King Wu's younger brother, later known as the Duke of Zhou (周公), who was granted the state of Lu in southern Shandong. Yet he probably spent little time in his own fief. King Wu died soon after the Zhou conquest, leaving a young heir on the throne, and the Duke of Zhou was called upon to assist his teenage nephew.

The Duke of Zhou was a conscientious regent. He suppress rebellions. He used measurements of the sun's shadow to identify Luoyang (洛阳) as the center of the realm. He also developed an elaborate system of ritual, combining ceremony with music to lay the foundations of the social order of his time.

Over time, the Duke of Zhou acquired an unexpected second career: dream interpreter. The man remembered for helping build the Zhou political order also became, in popular folklore, an authority on what our dreams might mean. A dream book attributed to him became so famous that, when I was growing up in China, "ask the Duke of Zhou" was almost shorthand for looking up the meaning of a dream.

About five centuries later, on the land of the state of Lu that had once been granted to the Duke of Zhou, one of the most influential thinkers in Chinese history was born: Confucius.

The world Confucius faced was no longer the relatively stable Zhou order of the Duke of Zhou's time. It was an age of competing states and collapsing norms, what later Chinese tradition described as a time when "rites had broken down and music had fallen into disorder."

Confucius responded by turning that ritual tradition into something more explicitly philosophical and ethical. What had largely been part of an aristocratic political order became, in his thought, a path of self-cultivation open to ordinary people. He was deeply concerned with a basic question: what kind of person should one become?

Education was central to Confucius's vision. His idea of "education without distinction" challenged the notion that learning belonged only to hereditary elites. He also believed that good government depended on the moral character of rulers. Wealth and military strength were not enough; rulers also had to use authority properly, observe accepted norms, care for the people, and lead by example. This became an enduring standard for judging political authority in Chinese culture.

But Confucius himself had few opportunities to put these ideas fully into practice.

That is not difficult to understand.

In an age when the old ritual order was breaking down and warfare was becoming more frequent, rulers were preoccupied with armies, territory, and power. A thinker who kept telling them to restrain themselves and govern through virtue was not necessarily the person they most wanted to hear from.

Confucius did not transform the world during his lifetime. The truly remarkable part came after his death.

His teachings were preserved, interpreted, and developed by generations of disciples and scholars, and eventually became part of the political and educational foundations of China, influencing much of East Asia as well. Even in eighteenth-century America, Founding Fathers such as Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, and Benjamin Franklin spoke of Confucius with considerable reverence.

Confucius had more than seventy disciples. That sometimes makes me think of another teacher who traveled with followers and whose influence became far greater after his death: Jesus.

Of course, the nature of their teachings was very different.

Confucius was primarily asking:
What does it mean to become a morally cultivated person? How can an orderly society be built?

Jesus was more centrally concerned with questions such as:
What is the relationship between human beings and God? How can human beings attain salvation?

Yet there is an interesting similarity between them. Neither reached a powerful position in his lifetime. Neither commanded an army. What ultimately changed the world was the tradition built after their deaths by disciples, texts, scholars, and generations of interpreters.

After Confucius died, his former home was turned into a temple in his honor, and the same site has continued to serve as a place of commemoration for more than two millennia. His burial ground gradually became the cemetery of the Kong family, where generation after generation of his descendants were laid to rest. More than seventy generations later, it remains in use today and is regarded as the world's largest continuously used family cemetery.

The ways these civilizations remember their great thinkers are very different. Confucius is still commemorated through a living family lineage and rituals that have endured for more than two thousand years, while the descendants of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle can no longer be traced.

But when it comes to legend, East and West can look surprisingly similar.

Ten years ago, I traveled overland by train from Beijing to Rome, and from there flew to Crete, a place I had long dreamed of visiting. On the island, I hired a taxi driver to show me around. At first I was a little uneasy-I had previously been overcharged by taxi drivers in both Russia and Poland-but he quickly won my trust with his warmth, reliability, and remarkable knowledge of the island. After taking me to several archaeological sites, he insisted that I visit a large cave in the mountains. According to local tradition, he told me, it was the birthplace of Zeus (top right).

At the Nishan Forum this time, I learned that not far from the conference venue stands a Confucian temple more than a thousand years old, built to commemorate what tradition holds to be the birthplace of Confucius (bottom left). The buildings that survive today mostly date from the Ming and Qing dynasties (1368-1911), but many of the old trees on the grounds are around a thousand years old, reaching back to the temple's earliest days. Beside the temple is a cave that tradition also associates with the birth of Confucius (bottom right).

One story concerns the birth of the supreme god of ancient Greece; the other, the birth of ancient China's most influential thinker.

Thousands of miles apart, two civilizations located the birth of an extraordinary figure in strikingly similar settings: a mountain, a cave, and a story passed down from generation to generation.

Civilizations can be profoundly different and yet preserve memory in surprisingly similar ways. But recognizing such similarities is only the beginning. The harder question comes when civilizations actually enter one another's worlds: can they encounter traditions different from their own without trying to erase them? Can they respect one another's rituals and sense of order?

Some Westerners may have the impression that China in earlier times did not welcome Christian missionaries. In fact, many Chinese people have the same impression. Yet there is a little-known chapter in this history.

By the 17th century, after decades of sustained effort by Catholic missionaries, Christianity had already gained a significant number of converts in China. The first two emperors of the Qing dynasty, Shunzhi (顺治) and Kangxi (康熙), both placed considerable trust in the missionaries; Shunzhi even wrote poems praising Catholicism. In 1692, Kangxi issued an edict of toleration. Catholicism was, in effect, granted a recognized place alongside Buddhism and Daoism and given room to establish itself in China.

This was an extraordinary window in the history of exchanges between Chinese and Western civilizations. Unfortunately, the Roman Church failed to make good use of this rare opportunity. Some within the Church regarded Confucian rites as religious in nature and therefore forbade Chinese converts from taking part in ceremonies honoring Confucius. One of the most prominent figures was Charles Maigrot. In 1693, just one year after Kangxi issued his edict of toleration, Maigrot ordered Christians in his own vicariate not to participate in rites honoring Confucius or in ancestral rites.

Apparently, this ungrateful old dude failed to appreciate how exceptional, and how fragile, this opportunity was.

He soon brought Kangxi and Rome into conflict. From Kangxi's perspective, if a religious authority thousands of miles away in Europe claimed the right to tell the Chinese that rituals practiced for generations were impermissible, then the issue was no longer simply how one should practice a religion. It raised a much more fundamental question:
Who has the right to define the rituals of the Chinese people?

Even then, Kangxi showed considerable patience. For years, he continued to receive papal envoys and sought to resolve the dispute through dialogue. It was only in 1706, after meeting Maigrot in person and becoming outraged by his manners, that Kangxi finally ordered him expelled from China.

In 1715, the pope issued a decree prohibiting Chinese practices associated with the veneration of Confucius. In 1721, Kangxi responded: "From now on, there is no need for Westerners to preach their religion in China. It may as well be prohibited, so as to avoid further trouble. Thus decreed."

Because of the rash actions of a few, a precious chapter in the history of exchange between China and the West came to an abrupt end.

Do we still have such an opportunity today? I believe we still do.

Traditional theories of international relations tend to put interests first. They are remarkably good at explaining war, rivalry, alliances, and the balance of power. They tell us why states mistrust one another, why they compete, and why they seek security through strength. But they are much less good at answering a different question: how can states live together over the long term without allowing mistrust and competition to become permanent conditions?

Huntington went even further, arguing that different civilizations were bound to conflict. In my view, that idea is totally mistaken. In Chinese policy circles, I have said more than once that this theory makes conflict seem natural, inevitable, and even intellectually justified, providing ammunition for conflicts the world does not need.

Confucian thought offers another way of looking at international relations. For instance:

Ren (仁), or humaneness, means that while a community pursues its own interests, it must also remain conscious of the existence and needs of others. It reminds us that truly durable interests cannot be built on the assumption that others must always lose.

Yi (义), or righteousness, means that not every interest we are capable of securing is necessarily worth pursuing. Power can tell a country "What am I able to do?" But yi asks a different question: "What ought I to do?" If international relations are reduced entirely to calculations of power, then power itself can become the source of legitimacy. Yi seeks to establish limits on conduct beyond power alone.

Zhi (智), or wisdom, is the capacity for judgment. It requires a country to look beyond immediate gains and losses and to understand the long-term consequences of its decisions. Winning a single contest does not necessarily mean making a wise choice.

Xin (信), or trustworthiness, is credibility. The long-term stability of international relations depends to a considerable degree on countries believing that words spoken today will still carry weight tomorrow, and that rules accepted today will not be arbitrarily reinterpreted when circumstances change. For example, documents signed decades ago by the United States, Japan, and China all clearly stated positions that Taiwan's a part of China. Yet today there are still people in both countries seeking to distort the meaning. If words can be redefined whenever they become inconvenient, trust itself begins to lose its meaning.

And when trust breaks down, countries fall back on power. If every country must rely increasingly on power to secure itself, security becomes more costly and more fragile.

Seen in this light, Confucian thought does not seek to replace interests with morality, nor does it ask the international community to become an ideal world without competition. What it may offer is a more complex form of realism: states naturally have interests, and they also need power. But interests must be constrained by yi; and a stable order ultimately requires at least some degree of ren.

Power can win a contest. It cannot, by itself, build an order in which others are willing to live.

Confucian thought does not offer a complete answer to the problems of the modern world. But in asking how power should be restrained, how trust can be sustained, and how people and states with different interests can live together, it remains an enduring point of reference for all of us thinking about the future.

text:
My takeaways from @RobinhoodApp Summit '26 in Houston:

-1.5k+ attendees, biggest one yet (1st one in Miami was ~200)
-don't underestimate retail. barely a suit in the room, mostly self-directed traders asking questions about options structures, futures sizing, agent workflows
-retail forced 24/7 markets into existence. Overnight volume across 3 ATSs went from 22M to ~109M shares a night in a year, & Sunday night is already the busiest session. Weekend stock trading is next, rolling out in the coming months
-institutions are following retail, not leading. Exchanges & institutions are now preparing to join the overnight session, and London, Korea are exploring 24/5 of their own
-agents turn hedge fund research into a few prompts. In the live demo, the agent spotted Pelosi's Bloom Energy purchase, pulled Bloom's lobbying on data center power, flagged a pending bill that could raise data centers' electricity costs, and checked whether Bloom's options were cheap or expensive, all in one app
-best products copy what power users already hack together. Robinhood built Agents after seeing users wire up Mac minis, Telegram bots, and five data feeds on their own
-Robinhood is coming for the investment banks. It wants to own every stage of a company's life: private funds, IPO underwriting, post-IPO investor relations with retail. goal is for every company raising money to want Robinhood on its cap table
-retail access to private markets didn't need a blockchain. Robinhood Ventures offers exposure to OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe thru closed end funds w/ daily liquidity and no accreditation required
-nobody has solved liquidity for private markets, onchain or off. Robinhood's funds let you sell any day but can trade above or below what the holdings are worth. ARK's fund always prices accurately but only lets you cash out quarterly. every wrapper has to pick a tradeoff
-AI financing is the bear case to watch. Hyperscalers are stretched, so more of the buildout is moving to private credit. AI is now ~6.3% of US IG debt per KKR, double the 30 yr average for any single sector
-midterms matter for crypto. Prediction markets give Democrats ~93% odds of taking the House and ~65% for the Senate, and Danny Moses warned that a sweep would make the CLARITY Act harder to pass. 
-ETFs won the wrapper wars. $1.5t in US inflows this year, already past last year's full year record; State Street expects ETFs to pass mutual funds globally by 2035
-tokenization still has to prove itself. Tom Sosnoff put it in the same bucket as perps & crypto: new products that have to "show us there's a market." he's right

text:
I asked GROK what other states this is happening in public schools: 

It occurs in some Ohio districts through local choices, not a statewide mandate, and similar materials appear in multiple other states where curriculum decisions are local or comprehensive programs are required.
Ohio law does not require instruction on sexual orientation or gender identity. State rules emphasize abstinence and require STI education, with parental opt-out rights for certain topics. House Bill 8 (the Parents’ Bill of Rights, signed in early 2025 and effective later that year) goes further: it bans “sexuality content” (defined to include sexual concepts or gender ideology) in grades K–3, requires schools to let parents review such materials in advance, and allows opt-outs with alternative assignments. Local districts still control much of the curriculum, and some have used or linked outside resources. Planned Parenthood affiliates in Ohio have offered school programs covering gender identity, and advocacy groups such as Protect Ohio Children (the source of the opt-out forms shown in the video) document and publicize cases of materials they consider inappropriate. https://t.co/C3mu1IcWpJ produces the specific video referenced (“How Many Times Can A Person Masturbate In One Day?”), which states there is no daily limit; the organization also publishes gender-identity lessons describing gender as a spectrum. These resources have been adopted or linked by districts in various states, though not uniformly across Ohio.
Comparable content appears where states require or encourage comprehensive sex education that includes sexual orientation and gender identity, or where districts independently select it. According to analyses from the Guttmacher Institute and KFF (updated through 2025), roughly 8–11 states plus the District of Columbia require instruction that is inclusive of a range of sexual orientations and gender identities when sex education is taught. Examples include California (under the California Healthy Youth Act), Oregon, Washington, New Jersey, Colorado, and Illinois. In these places, curricula often draw on National Sex Education Standards or materials from groups such as Advocates for Youth, Planned Parenthood, or https://t.co/C3mu1IcWpJ, which cover puberty, masturbation as normal, and gender as an inner experience that may differ from sex assigned at birth. Many other states leave the content to local districts, so similar lessons have surfaced even without a state requirement (documented examples include certain California elementary programs linking Amaze videos). A separate set of states restricts or prohibits discussion of these topics in early grades or requires stigmatizing portrayals. Parental opt-out or notice rules exist in the majority of states.

text:
Oklahoma, 1935 — The wind had a way of finding its way through every crack in the boards, bringing with it the smell of dust and despair. Twelve-year-old Tommie Carter watched his mother tie a flour sack over her hair before stepping outside to feed the chickens—though half of them had perished in last week’s storm.

His father had been studying the truck all morning, tightening bolts, checking the patched tires. Word had come from a cousin in Bakersfield—there was work picking fruit, if you could make it there. They had little more than a few blankets, a coffee tin of coins, and the hope that the road west would offer more than the barren, cracked earth they were leaving behind.

Tommie climbed onto the truck bed with his younger sister, clutching the family’s last quilt, stitched by their grandmother before she passed. As the engine coughed to life, their farmhouse—leaning, weather-beaten, and stubborn—grew smaller in the distance.

The journey would take weeks, through heat, hunger, and the endless rumble of wheels on dirt. But in that moment, as the wind whipped past, Tommie allowed himself to imagine green fields, heavy with fruit, and a table that never sat empty.

text:
In the summer of 1937, a severe drought settled across parts of rural Mississippi. Streams shrank. Ponds dried up. And many families worried about where their next bucket of water would come from. Outside the small community of Pine Grove stood one of the few dependable wells in the area.

The well belonged to the Harper family. Every day before sunrise, thirteen-year-old Thomas Harper walked to the pump and began working the long iron handle. The job was exhausting. Water had to be drawn for his own family first. Then for neighbors. Then for travelers passing through town. By midday, dozens of buckets lined the road waiting to be filled. Some families traveled miles by wagon. Others arrived on foot carrying wash tubs and metal pails.

No one was turned away. When the drought worsened, Thomas spent nearly eight hours a day operating the pump. His hands became blistered. His shoulders ached. Yet he continued. One afternoon, a local merchant offered to pay him for the work. The boy politely declined.

According to witnesses, he simply said: "Folks need water more than I need money." The drought eventually broke. Rain returned. Creeks filled again. Life slowly returned to normal. But residents never forgot the summer when a teenage boy helped keep an entire community supplied with water.

Years later, an elderly neighbor reflected on those days:
"The well gave us water. The boy gave us time." The story became part of local history—a reminder that during the Great Depression, some of the greatest acts of service came from people who expected nothing in return.

text:
Indonesia eyes US oil tech to reach 1 million bpd by 2030
Indonesia’s Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry is promoting technology partnerships between domestic oil and gas companies and their US counterparts to help achieve a crude oil lifting target of one million barrels per day.

“We see collaboration among multinational companies and domestic firms, such as Pertamina Hulu Energi, and we will encourage greater cooperation between them,” Deputy Energy Minister Yuliot said at the ministry in Jakarta on Friday.

Yuliot said that during his visit to the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting in Houston, Texas, in mid-September 2026, he also visited ExxonMobil.

Yuliot highlighted ExxonMobil’s infrastructure and technology, saying the US oil and gas company can analyze 40 terabytes of data in one second.

He said ExxonMobil’s technology could therefore analyze 200 terabytes of data on Indonesia’s oil and gas potential in less than a minute.

“They have supercomputers to process data; it is no longer done manually. This creates an opportunity to analyze data from working areas that are ready to be offered,” Yuliot said.

🆘 Wiggly & affectionate HW- 1 year old Staffie Mix girl Trixie, who is experiencing kennel stress, is on the euthanasia list Friday, 10/2. There will be no extensions per BARC. 🆘

⏰ Trixie #A2097595 must have a 𝐇𝐎𝐋𝐃 𝗻𝗼 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝟭𝗣𝗠 or she will lose her life.🥺 We need pledges and a local foster for a rescue to help.💰🏡

🚩Please do not honor pledges until the post has been updated with rescue information and a freedom picture. Please reach out with any questions or concerns.

🩷🐶 Trixie #A2097595

9/23 Stray  | American Staffordshire Mix | Spayed Female | 1Y 1M | 53.2 lbs | HW Negative

💜 Volunteer Notes:

📝 Shelter Notes:

10/1: Trixie was nonstop vocal in her kennel, pulling the cover in and jumping on the kennel door. Her pupils were dilated and staff noted that she appeared very stressed. Multiple enrichment items were offered, but nothing lasted to help her settle. She also caused other dogs to become stressed.

9/30: Trixie was moved to adoption in the morning. She was placed into an outside run and was nonstop vocal in her kennel. Once leashed, she walked out on a loose leash. After being placed into her kennel, she was jumping up and knocking over her water bowl and continued vocalizing. Staff covered her kennel and offered a rawhide, which helped briefly, but she resumed vocalizing once she finished.

9/29: Trixie was high-pitch barking in her kennel and tapping her feet. Staff opened the kennel and leashed her as she exited. She walked on a semi-tense leash. In the runs, she continued high-pitch barking and jumping up on the run door.

9/26: Trixie was described as very friendly. When petted, she leaned into the person. She greeted staff with a wagging tail and loose, wiggly body. She was very vocal in both her kennel and the runs and walked on a semi-loose leash.

9/25: Trixie was forward barking, panting heavily and pacing back and forth. When her kennel was opened, she ran out very forward. Outside, she continued forward barking and pacing. Staff covered her kennel, but she pulled the blanket and shredded it. She was offered a rawhide but was not interested.

9/24: Trixie greeted staff at the front of her kennel with a relaxed body, soft eyes and a softly tapping tail. She was easily leashed, walked on a loose leash outside to the runs and was easily returned to her kennel.

🩺 Medical Notes:

9/23: Trixie weighs 53.2 lbs. Her medical exam was documented as normal. She is heartworm negative.

💖 Trixie is a young, friendly girl whose notes show a striking difference between her social behavior with people and the distress she is experiencing in the kennel. She has repeatedly been described as loose, wiggly, affectionate and friendly, even leaning into pets, and she has demonstrated that she can walk nicely on a loose or semi-loose leash. As her stay has continued, however, she has become increasingly overwhelmed—vocalizing constantly, pacing, jumping on the kennel door and struggling to settle despite attempts at enrichment. Her dilated pupils and escalating behavior suggest the shelter environment is extremely stressful for her. Trixie would likely benefit tremendously from a home where she can decompress, get away from the constant stimulation and show more of the affectionate, wiggly young dog staff have already seen. 🩷

📌 Please contact BARC if you are local and can help! Neither BARC nor this page can assist with out-of-state adoption or foster offers. We are NOT the shelter.

text:
Susan Collins's odds jumped 10 points in a week
Democrats' Senate odds didn't drop

On Polymarket, Collins has climbed from 31.5¢ to 41.5¢ in Maine since Sep 25

Democratic control of the Senate sat at 62.5¢ all week, then ticked up to 64.5¢ today

Count the seats

Republicans hold 53, and Vance breaks ties, so Democrats need 51

If every market favorite wins, Alaska's Mary Peltola included, they get 52. Lose Maine, and it's exactly 51

Treat the races as independent, and Democrats take the Senate about 73% of the time if Jackson wins and 48% if Collins does. If her win signals a bad night for Democrats everywhere, it's lower. A swing this size in Maine alone is worth about 3 points of Senate odds, at most

The other close races ended the week about where they started: Ohio, Texas, Alaska, Michigan. Only Iowa moved toward Republicans, by 2 to 3 points.

The control market's book is lopsided. There's about $620k bid at 62¢, while the offers just above are far thinner. The price has drifted up two cents today

Polls still lean Jackson, up 2 in the FiftyPlusOne average

Two polls out this week split: Republican-leaning co/efficient has Collins up 2, and AARP has Jackson up 3. In 2020, Collins trailed in nearly every public poll and won by 8.6 points

The first debate is Oct 6

Is Maine local news, or the first sign of a national shift?

text:
Building Lead Lists:

I have found very few business owners who have I spoke with that actually know how to build lead lists, and for the ones who do make an attempt, at least for more start ups, it was evident to see they were not even thinking about building a list properly.

I have made the same mistake, so if you are an SDR, this is something I would consider thinking about.

The majority of bad lead lists usually come from not understanding the offer properly and not targeting the right people.

So how do you target the right people?
Good question

It starts by the offer. Who would benefit the most from your companies product/service?

This is where is its important to have your ICP dialed.

Bad lead list: lawyers with less than 50 employees
Good lead list: Attorneys who focus on Personal Injury, between 1-10 employees, only in the state of Texas, who are doing more than 20 cases a month

Why does this work? - because have a very specific persona that allows you gather proper research and feedback. Necessary in order to make proper adjustments.

This is why its important to know the offer well and the persona.

If you start building leads around the wrong title, the wrong size company, etc. You are wasting your time making any calls and decisions. You may get lucky, and still book a meeting.

Learning this concept is more important than how to use the tools.

And I made the mistake of doing the former without the latter. Save yourself the headache.

For the 13th consecutive year, Texas' Governor Greg Abbott has declared October to be "Careers in Construction Month" at the request of the Texas Association of Builders. We are pleased to share the signed proclamation here:

STATE OF TEXAS
OFFICE OF THE GOVERNOR

Texas is proud to lead the nation with a robust economy and excellent business climate, and that economy is complemented by a construction industry that upholds an exceptional standard of quality. The contributions of construction workers have laid the literal foundation for the Texas that we know and cherish today. In a state characterized by economic prosperity with a strong emphasis on quality of life, the construction sector remains essential to sustaining the demands of continued growth.

The Lone Star State's construction workforce remains steadfast in meeting this challenge. As our population and economy continue to expand at an unprecedented rate, so does the need for skilled professionals in the industry. Our state stands ready to meet the demand by preparing for the necessary workers who will be required to support this ongoing development in the coming years.

Civic groups and industry professionals have admirably prepared for this demand by standardizing training and providing the next generation of construction workers with the necessary tools to thrive in this industry. With an eye to the future, these groups host job fairs, panel discussions, and community events to develop aspiring construction workers.

Each year, the month of October is set aside to increase public awareness and appreciation of the construction industry. During this month, employers, trade associations, and schools promote the industry's many career opportunities. By retaining and growing the number of skilled construction workers, we will ensure an even brighter future for the Lone Star State.

At this time, I encourage all Texans to learn about our construction industry, to appreciate the work that these dedicated professionals do, and to explore the numerous opportunities that this important sector offers. Together, we can and will build a bigger, better Texas.

Therefore, I, Greg Abbott, Governor of Texas, do hereby proclaim October 2026 to be Careers in Construction Month in Texas and urge all Texans to observe the occasion with appropriate ceremonies and activities.

In testimony whereof, I have hereunto affixed my signature this the 24th day of August, 2026.

Greg Abbott
Governor of Texas

text:
Would you rather have $70 million or $52.5 million?

I was doing some research on NFL contract structures, after the Joey Porter Jr. issue with the Steelers. I cover baseball, where there is no salary cap, and where all contracts are guaranteed, outside of option years. I wanted to better understand the NFL structure.

The common trend and understanding of NFL contracts is to cite the total potential contract value.

For example, I see people mentioning that Le'Veon Bell was offered $70 million over five years by the Pittsburgh Steelers, which he turned down. The $70 million figure is the only figure I ever see mentioned.

At the same time Bell rejected that deal, the Rams signed Todd Gurley to a four year, $60 million deal. This was a higher AAV than Bell was offered. However, there was a massive difference in the two deals.

Gurley received $22 million guaranteed at signing, along with $45 million total guaranteed. That means 75% of his total contract was guaranteed.

By comparison, Bell received around $10-17 million guaranteed at signing, along with about $33 million guaranteed over two years.

Even these numbers are a bit misleading. Here's what I learned...

If Bell and Gurley both sign in 2018, they're only really guaranteed the total at signing. That's the signing bonus total, plus their 2018 salary. For Gurley, this was around $22 million. For Bell, this was to be $10-17 million, reported.

Even though the rest of the contract has a salary structure, the players are still effectively year-to-year. A serious injury in 2018 would have severely affected future earnings.

This happened with Gurley. His knee began acting up in 2018, right at the start of his deal. His deal was structured in a way where the Rams had to pay him his full 2019 salary, due to him being injured in 2018. This bumped his total earnings up to $34.5 million. After this, the Rams cut him ahead of the next guaranteed roster point in 2020.

Gurley signed a four year, $60 million deal. His deal came with the key injury guarantee that made his 2019 salary guaranteed in the event of an injury. He got injured in year one, and received $34.5 million of his deal through two seasons.

Bell's $33 million guaranteed was a "rolling structure", which didn't provide the same injury guarantees as Gurley. Had Bell suffered the same injury in 2018, the Steelers could have cut him in March 2019. At that point, the $10-17 million would have been the only thing Bell would have received.

It also makes sense that Bell sat out in 2018. The franchise tag salary of $14.5 million would have been very little difference from the extension. He only would have been guaranteed money in the same $10-17 million range, with no future guarantees.

Bell signed with the Jets in 2019. This was a four year, $52.5 million deal. That's not much difference in AAV from the Steelers offer. The Jets offer also had $27 million guaranteed at signing.

His first two seasons were guaranteed. Even though Bell struggled with the Jets, he was paid around $27 million for his 2019-2020 salaries, despite being released in 2020.

After being released by the Jets, Bell signed smaller deals with the Chiefs, Ravens, and Bucs, making a little over $1 million extra in 2020-2021. He signed a four year, $52.5 million deal with the Jets, but only ended up making around $28 million over the next three seasons.

If Bell was franchised by the Steelers in 2018, or even if he signed their $70 million offer, he would have been at risk of making only ~$14 million guaranteed, had his production fallen off like it did with the Jets. His decision to sit out, then sign with the Jets likely made him an extra $13 million.

And if he received a deal like Gurley's, he would have been guaranteed around $35 million in 2018-2019, regardless of injuries in 2018 or performance issues.

It doesn't matter that the Steelers offered Bell $70 million over five years. That's a best case scenario, and the best case in the NFL rarely happens.

What I learned in this research is that while the $70 million figure makes media headlines, the guaranteed amount is far more important.

Joey Porter Jr. was reportedly offered $27 million in average annual value. This would have made him the 7th highest paid cornerback in the league, from an AAV standpoint. Porter reportedly wanted at least $30 million per year, putting him among the highest paid.

Again, these are the headline prices.

The reported guaranteed structure for Porter would have placed him 18th in guaranteed money among cornerback deals. Even with the $27 million AAV, he was only guaranteed a little over one year of that salary. Any injury or poor performance in 2026 would have left him at risk of having the rest of his contract voided, with a lower guarantee than most cornerbacks receive.

There's a scenario where Porter could be worse off with Dallas than signing the Steelers extension. If he plays well this year, but doesn't agree to an extension with Dallas after the season, they could give him the franchise tag. His total earnings across the two seasons would be around $26 million, which is less than the reported $33 million the Steelers were offering in guaranteed money.

On the flip side, the gamble by Porter is that he performs well this season, and is more likely to get a higher guaranteed amount with Dallas versus what the Steelers typically offer with their habit of avoiding guarantees beyond the first year of a contract.

There are a few exceptions for the Steelers.

T.J. Watt signed a three year, $123 million extension. This had a massive $108 million fully guaranteed. Unlike Bell's rolling structure, the Steelers locked in the 2025, 2026, and 2027 base salaries for Watt at signing. Their only potential savings from the $123 million is a $15 million roster bonus at the end of the deal.

DK Metcalf signed a four year, $132 million extension. His deal included $60 million in fully guaranteed money. The Steelers guaranteed his first two seasons. They even maintained this after his suspension in late 2025, which could have allowed them to void future guarantees.

Watt is a rare situation where nearly the entire contract was guaranteed. Metcalf received almost 45% of his deal guaranteed. Bell's guarantee would have been around 20% of the total value.

By comparison, Gurley's deal in 2018 guaranteed him 36.6% on day one, along with 57.5% after two years due to his structure that still paid him despite an injury. That's a massive guaranteed increase over what Bell was offered.

Porter's issue likely comes down to guaranteed amounts. Here are some of the highest contracts at cornerback around the league:

-Christian Gonzalez: 4 years/$135 million, 75.56% guaranteed
-Derek Stingley Jr.: 3/$90, 98.89%
-Devon Witherspoon: 4/$132, 76.52%
-A.J. Terrell: 4/$81, 81.23%
-Jaycee Horn: 4/$100, 70%
-Patrick Surtain II, 4/$96, 80.73%

Porter was reportedly offered 4/$108 with 30.56% guaranteed. That's less than half the guaranteed money that most cornerbacks make. Even if the Steelers doubled the guarantee, they'd still be below the common 70% or higher rate of guaranteed pay that cornerbacks receive.

I mentioned a scenario where Porter could end up making less guaranteed money with Dallas than he would with the Steelers offer. I think there's a better chance he ends up making more guaranteed money by getting away from the Steelers and their refusal to pay guaranteed money beyond the first season. Most teams guarantee a majority of cornerback contracts, and the Steelers were only offering a high potential with the headline-grabbing AAV.

Terrell's contract best displays the issue. He was given a lower AAV than the reported offer to Porter ($20.25 M vs $27 M AAV), but his guaranteed structure was more than double. He was given $42.34 million guaranteed at signing, which locked in his 2024 and 2025 salaries.

The Falcons also included guarantee triggers a year in advance for 2026 and 2027. Terrell's 2026 salary was guaranteed on March 17, 2025. His 2027 salary was guaranteed on March 15, 2026. They ended up reworking his deal earlier this season, converting $12 million of his 2026 salary into a signing bonus.

What's interesting about Terrell is that his numbers dropped after the extension. His completion percentage against was a career-worst in 2024. The Falcons had a decision in early 2025: Cut Terrell and avoid guaranteeing more money, or keep him and guarantee his 2026 salary before he even played a game in 2025.

They kept him. His 2025 season was better, with his second lowest completion percentage against of his career. So, it made sense that they decided to keep him again in March 2026, guaranteeing his 2027 salary.

Terrell also has a lot of dead cap space that locks him on the roster. When the Falcons gave him $42.34 million guaranteed up front, a big portion of that was a $25 million signing bonus. They prorated those payments at $5 million per year across five years. Had the Falcons cut Terrell in March of this year, they would have had to pay all of that upfront, along with his 2026 guaranteed salary from their March 2025 decision. He also had an injury guarantee of $18.5 million for his 2027 contract. If he couldn't pass a physical on the day he was released, that 2027 money would have been guaranteed.

He performed well in 2025, so it's not a surprise the Falcons kept Terrell in 2026, guaranteeing his 2027 salary. The alternative would have been at least $30 million in upfront payments and dead cap space, and potentially up to $48.5 million in dead cap space. There is a stipulation where a team can cut a player after June 1st and spread the dead cap hit across two seasons. But Terrell's deal is structured in a way where the team would need to guarantee an extra season before getting this cap benefit.

The guarantees of Terrell's contract are structured in a way that the Falcons can't easily get rid of him, while also having to make a decision on retaining him nearly two years in advance. They don't even get the post-June 1st benefit until next year.

All of this illustrates the massive gap between the cornerback market and what the Steelers offered Porter.

If you're focusing on the AAV across four years, you're ignoring that a down season from Porter in 2026, or an injury, could allow the Steelers to easily cut him with very little future cost due to the low guaranteed amount.

From an organizational standpoint, this makes sense. The approach by the Steelers minimizes risk in a game filled with risk. The team isn't seen as the bad guy when they cut an underperforming player who doesn't have guaranteed money in the future.

On the flip side, the player is seen as a bad guy if he wants to renegotiate the deal. This happened with Cam Heyward, who I remember being vilified for holding out in 2026.

The Steelers signed Heyward to a three year, $45 million deal in September 2024. This lowered his cap hit by $10 million at the time, while introducing the rolling structure that was part of Bell's offer. Heyward was coming off an injury in 2023, and was in the final year of his deal. His value wasn't as high at the time, and the Steelers benefitted from the lowered cap hit.

After his 2024 season, the Steelers had to decide on a $13.45 million roster bonus in March 2025 for the upcoming season. They brought Heyward back. In 2026, the same rolling structure would have hit, with $12.95 million due. This is when Heyward was looking for a new deal, after reviving his value the previous two seasons from when he signed in September 2024.

What he ended up signing was a two-year deal that would pay $32.25 million total. He received $14.95 million upfront for 2026, which also provided the Steelers with $5.5 million in cap room. Heyward went from a $12.95 million roster bonus under his original deal to $16.25 million guaranteed under the new deal.

Part of this guarantee was due to the 2027 season spreading out his new bonus. Heyward was given the $14.95 million signing bonus, with around $7.5 million paid in 2026. That's a drop from his previous $12.95 million roster bonus that would have been paid this year.

If the Steelers cut Heyward ahead of March 2027, they would save $16 million in cap space next season, compared to his max $23.47 million projected cap hit. This would remove his 2027 salary, while still leaving the Steelers on the cap hook for his bonus portion that was shifted to 2027.

Despite all of the outcry during the negotiations, this deal worked out for both sides. Heyward received $3 million more in guaranteed money, plus the chance to make an additional $16 million if the Steelers keep him in 2027. The Steelers received $5.5 million in cap savings this year as part of the restructuring, and they aren't on the hook for much next season if Heyward has a career-ending injury this year.

Going back to Porter, if he had signed with the Steelers for 4/$108 million, he's still at a disadvantage. Say Porter becomes one of the best cornerbacks in the game in year one, increasing his value from when he signed. That only gets him a second year guaranteed, with the Steelers almost certainly picking up his 2027 salary. However, if he gets seriously injured in 2027, the Steelers can cut him for the final two years. In that scenario, he only receives $60 million of the $108 million he was reportedly offered.

When you compare that to Terrell, it's not a good deal for Porter. The guaranteed percentage, and the path to guaranteed money, are both considerably worse. And when you compare Porter's offer to Stingley and Witherspoon, who both received injury guarantees at signing, Porter's contract structure doesn't compare. Both of those players were protected from the team cutting them due to injuries. Their teams can still cut them if they play poorly, but they have financial injury protection.

It makes sense why the Steelers continue to have contract issues with their players.

The media and fans focus on the AAV and total potential money. That's best-case scenario.

The players focus on guaranteed money. They know that if they get injured, or their performance slips in a single year, the team can easily cut them and their high AAV goes away.

The Steelers structure their deals to give easy escapes for injuries or poor performance. Yet, when a player like Heyward performs as one of the best in the league, and massively increases his value from when he signed, the Steelers would have to break their self-imposed traditions to give him a new deal.

The renegotiation demands from Heyward put him in a negative light with the media and fans, who say that he agreed to a deal and should play out that deal.

And that's a one-way street.

The Steelers set up their contracts in a way where they agree to a deal, but can easily avoid honoring that agreement if the player's value declines. Why wouldn't the player have the same right to want to alter the deal when their value increases?

My assessment of Porter is that the guaranteed structure was the sticking point. If he signs a 4/$108 deal, and becomes one of the best cornerbacks in the league, the Steelers get a discount on his AAV by paying him less than $30 million per year. And if he gets injured or struggles in 2026, the Steelers can escape while paying Porter a much smaller guaranteed amount than most corners receive when they sign.

This is also why it makes sense that Porter would be fine playing under the same rookie contract with Dallas, with no extension. It's not about his pay this year. It's about the potential to be paid after this year. By getting away from the Steelers, Porter also gets away from an organization that heavily avoids guaranteed money. He has a better chance signing a deal with Dallas that pays more guaranteed money, even if the AAV is the same or lower.

That gets back to the original question: Would you rather have $70 million or $52.5 million?

The Steelers offered Le'Veon Bell $70 million. He ended up signing a year later with the Jets for $52.5 million. The difference is that Bell made $27 million after one bad season with the Jets. He would have made about half that guaranteed amount if he signed with the Steelers and had a similar result in his first year.

It's a trick question. The real question is would you rather be guaranteed $14.5 million or $27 million?

That's much easier to answer. And when you start to view NFL contracts in that light, you see why the Steelers keep running into disputes.

The Steelers set up their contracts in a way to display lottery potential with high AAV totals. However, they are also set up to allow the team to escape the deal at the first sign of trouble. Meanwhile, the players are locked in to the original structure, no matter how well they play.

To put it another way:

"The thing is, Bob, it's not that I'm lazy, it's that I just don't care... It's a problem of motivation, all right? Now if I work my ass off and Initech ships a few extra units, I don't see another dime, so where's the motivation?"

The Steelers are the Initech of the NFL. Unfortunately, I don't know their roster well enough to know their version of Milton.

I hope you found this valuable. I enjoyed researching NFL contract structures this morning, and I wrote this up while doing the research, to hopefully provide insight to others on questions that I had when seeing the Porter news.

text:
People do not behave the way they behave because they thought it through. They are not sitting there, weighing your proposal, and choosing. Most of the time they are unconscious. They are following the flow — the flow of life, the flow of energy, the animal body underneath. And that animal is steered by fear.

That is what I understood after talking to thousands of people.

So when you ask for something and they refuse, the usual move is to take the refusal as the answer. Okay, it doesn’t work. Next. But why did they reject it? Most of the time it is not because the proposal is bad. It is not because they are dumb or bad people either. It is because they are not operating consciously. They are in defense. If you address the fear, you get agreement far more often than you think.

A good proposal is not the ask. A good proposal prepares the person first. It names the pain. It takes the fear off the table. Then it makes the offer. That gets results. A bad proposal walks in cold and hopes logic will do the work. It usually doesn’t.

And if the thing you are selling is actually bad, or the exchange is not fair, that is a different problem. Fix the product. This is about the other case — the case where the offer is sound and they still shut the door. That door is defense, not judgment. They did not sit down, list the advantages, list the disadvantages, and decide. They flinched.

This is why reacting to their behavior is a waste. You are dealing with the animal part, and that is not always the part you want to deal with.

It depends what you want. If you want to exploit someone, the animal is a gift. Fear, status, rejection, resentment — weak points. Attack those and people move. If you want a smart decision, if you want to cooperate, if you want to build something and pull the best out of them, you have to reach the conscious part. And you only reach it by addressing the fear first.

Fear of rejection is the common one. You start talking and they are already braced for you to dismiss them. Leave that untouched and they stay defensive no matter how good the offer is. Show that you accept them. Show that you came to cooperate. Give a real compliment. Show a little of your own weakness. The fear disappears in that moment, and the conversation moves to a layer where something can actually be built.

You will not know every fear in a new person. You don’t need to. Most people run the same few. Start there and you will be right more often than not. That is why the old Carnegie books still work. They are not magic. They address the fears almost everyone is carrying.

The rest you learn by watching. You propose something. They close. They reject. That is not a verdict on your idea. That is a defensive state. From the situation and from what you asked, you can usually see which fear is driving it.

Don’t take their first behavior as the final fact. Work on it. You can influence almost everyone, and almost every decision they think is already made.

Do not let your life or your business drift with the current. Do not swim with the flow. Control it. Swim the direction you chose, even when the water is against you. You are building this on purpose. Be proactive. Do not react to other people’s fear and resentment as if those were the weather. They are not the weather. They are a state. States can be addressed. This is your world, act like it.

text:
If EBONYI, A poor state in south-eastern Nigeria, is known for anything, it is for the paucity of its development efforts, from reducing poverty to improving literacy. That may be because the state government has been pursuing higher ambitions: it has been trying to build an airport. It says it spent some 50bn naira ($38m) on it between 2020 and 2023 alone, more than half of what it spent on education in the same period. The project has been marred by corruption allegations and vandalism. After a few flights, air traffic stopped because of a defective runway. Undeterred, Ebonyi’s government is mulling the next step: launching its very own airline.

Nigeria’s state-run airlines have a modest record, to say the least. The state carrier, Nigeria Airways, went bust in the early 2000s amid tales of unpaid salaries and rat-infested cabins. Of those run by state governments, three at least still operate (though only one is profitable). Ebonyi’s proposal is a “joke”, says Chris Aligbe, an aviation analyst. Yet state governors present plans to start their own carriers with some regularity. In July the governor of Kano, a northern state, said a local airline would start operating within the year “by the grace of God”.

State governments are not best placed to run airlines, but a logic of sorts exists for their lofty plans. Nigeria is vast and has terrible road and rail networks, plus a big problem with bandits. Being accessible by air could be a boon for isolated states, especially if it makes them more appealing to rich investors and tourists from Abuja, the capital, and Lagos, the commercial centre.

Map: The Economist
Such hopes needn’t be pie in the sky. Akwa Ibom, a state in the south, launched an airline in 2019. Ibom Air has helped turn the regional airport into an economic hub and claims to have boosted tourism. It now connects to six destinations outside the state, including Accra, the capital of Ghana, and is building a repair and maintenance facility for west Africa. The aim is to offer the sort of specialised repairs for which African airlines currently have to fly overseas. It is also profitable, bringing in 7bn naira ($5.3m) in profits in 2025. Officials in neighbouring Cross River state hope that their local carrier will tempt tourists to try the state’s seafood and attend its annual carnival.

Yet the economic case for a local airline run by the state government is, in general, hard to fathom. Ebonyi’s struggling airport is an hour’s drive from the terminal in neighbouring Enugu state, which has ample capacity (and its own fledgling airline). Bayelsa, another state in the south, also wants to launch an airline, even though flights from Port Harcourt, 45 minutes across the border in Rivers state, serve it well enough (see map). Though airline capacity is rising, domestic air travel grew by a modest 4% last year. The market remains small, as few Nigerians can afford to fly.

Yet officials have reasons for their obsession with air travel. One is politics. Ebonyi’s airport may be unusable, but the governor who had it built apparently impressed the president enough to be appointed infrastructure minister. Another is money. The federal government sometimes takes over failing regional airports and pays states generous compensation. Spending on airports and airlines is little scrutinised. Ebonyi’s government says it has paid 50bn naira for three planes for its proposed airline. So far, there is no sign of any of them being delivered. ■
@TheEconomist

Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary

FRIDAY

Morning Prayer
God, come to my assistance.
- Lord, make haste to help me

Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit
as it was in the beginning, is now, and will be forever.  Amen.

Virgin of virgins,
I choose you today
as my sovereign, my queen, my empress,
and I declare myself, as I am in fact,
your servant and your slave.
I invoke your royal name of Mary,
that is, sovereign Lady,
and beg of you with all my heart
to admit me into the privileged circle¡
of your family
as one of your servants,
to do your will
as a humble slave and a loving child.
As a sign of your acceptance
engrave on my heart
with the fire of your love,
not the brand of an unwilling slave,
but those two gracious words of the angel:
Ave Maria.
As long as I draw breath
may your burning love ensure
that I bear these words
in my heart and in my memory,
and that until my dying breath
my will may be always on fire
with my great desire to serve you,
my sovereign and my queen,
glorious in your majesty.
Though I am in every way unworthy
of so honorable a title,
I resolve sincerely to be your slave,
to serve you wholeheartedly,
to protect your name,
and that of your Son,
against every insult,
as far as it may rest with me,
and never to allow anyone in my charge
to offend your Son in any way.
By your tender love for your Son,
by the glories you have received
from the Most Holy Trinity,
do not reject me from your service
but as my sovereign and my queen
preside over all my actions,
command whatever you will,
direct all my work,
remedy all its defects.
During my whole life
rule over me
as your servant and slave.
At the hour of my death,
as I hope for
at the end of my loving servitude
among the privileged members of your family,
receive my soul and escort it
into the presence of God.

St Bartolome de Los Rios(1580-1652)

Ant.1 My soul clings to you, Lord Jesus Christ.

Psalm 51
O God, have mercy on me
Your inmost being must be renewed, and you must put on the new man. (Eph 4:23-24)
Have mercy on me, God, in your kindness.
In your compassion blot out my offense.
O wash me more and more from my guilt
and cleanse me from my sin.
My offenses truly I know them;
my sin is always before me
Against you, you alone, have I sinned;
what is evil in your sight I have done.
That you may be justified when you give sentence
and be without reproach when you judge,
O see, in guilt I was born,
a sinner was I conceived.
Indeed you love truth in the heart;
then in the secret of my heart teach me wisdom.
O purify me, then I shall be clean;
O wash me, I shall be whiter than snow.
Make me hear rejoicing and gladness,

From my sins turn away your face
and blot out all my guilt.
A pure heart create for me, O God,
put a steadfast spirit within me.
Do not cast me away from your presence,

Give me again the joy of your help;
with a spirit of fervor sustain me,
that I may teach transgressors your ways
and sinners may return to you.
O rescue me, God, my helper,
and my tongue shall ring out your goodness.
O Lord, open my lips

For in sacrifice you take no delight,
burnt offering from me you would refuse,
my sacrifice, a contrite spirit,

In your goodness, show favor to Zion:
rebuild the walls of Jerusalem.

Point 1: "War is Hell" and the 1948 account.

- The timeline refutes the framing. Deir Yassin was April 9. Haifa and Jaffa emptied in April. Roughly 300,000 Palestinians were displaced before the first Arab army crossed the border on May 15. The expulsions preceded the invasion you say caused them.

- What distinguishes policy from hell: the villages were razed afterward and return was permanently barred by law. Fog of war ends when the war ends. Bulldozers and absentee-property statutes are peacetime decisions.

- The AOC comparison fails on power. She is one legislator of 435 with no executive authority. Ben-Gurion ran the executive, and Weitz chaired the actual Transfer Committee. The test for whether "radical statements" were policy is whether the stated outcome occurred. 750,000 expelled. It occurred.

- On "UN sanctioned": the partition allotted 56% of the land to a third of the population, over the objection of the two-thirds who lived there and had no meaningful say. An authority's stamp is not consent, and you of all people should distrust an appeal to it.

Point 2: Dresden, and "they could have firebombed Gaza."

- They dropped at least 70,000 tons of explosives on Gaza's 141 square miles. Dresden, Hamburg, and the London Blitz combined: about 30,700 tons. More than double the tonnage of your own worst-case examples, on a sealed territory the size of Philadelphia, destroying 69% of all buildings. You chose the comparison. Gaza loses it.

- "Tons of food, stolen by Hamas": USAID's internal analysis and Israeli military officials quoted in the NYT found no evidence of systematic Hamas diversion. What is confirmed: famine, and at least hundreds of starvation deaths, in a territory whose every calorie Israel controls.

- "Did far more to protect civilians than any military in history" is empirically inverted. The UN commission found the rate of child deaths "unparalleled across modern conflicts globally." Israel's own leaked military database listed 17% of the dead as fighters. And even granting your claim: protection is measured by outcome. The outcome is 20,179 dead children. If that's history's best protection, the word has no meaning.

Point 3: "Covered by points 1 and 2."

- It wasn't. The mirror went unanswered: prisoners raped at Sde Teiman with the indicted soldiers defended by ministers, UN-documented use of Palestinians as human shields, crowds shot at food lines, soldiers posting their own demolition videos. That list was your hypothetical's conduct, drawn from the record. Declining to grade it is an answer of its own.

Your bottom line: "if they disarm, there's peace" has a control group. The West Bank fires no rockets and its security forces cooperate with Israel. It received record settlement expansion and the deadliest year on record before Oct 7. Where Palestinians hold no weapons, the land shrinks anyway. Disarmament into occupation is not an offer of peace, and 1948 proved the opposite of what you think: the expulsions came first.

"War is Hell" appears four times in your reply, and each time it does the same work: converting decisions into conditions. Hell doesn't bar refugees from returning. Hell doesn't announce a siege on camera. Those are choices, and choices have authors.
