text:
Who should evaluate an AI tutor before a campus rolls it out?

A University of Maryland randomized trial just reported on 2,379 undergraduates offered a course-integrated GPT-4o tutor (Virtual Study Assistant) built with RAG over instructor-selected materials. In matched course sections, students offered the tutor finished about four percentage points lower, and learning-platform participation dropped sharply. Only about 15% of students offered the tool actually used it. Nearly 74% of requests asked for information, explanations, or solutions, and fewer than 1% asked for feedback on the student's own attempt. Most instructors kept the default direct-instruction mode, and the guided tutoring mode saw little use.

If you teach with AI, measure what the tool replaces: office hours, course materials, and the messy practice of trying an answer yourself. Offering an approved assistant is only half the experiment.

text:
Same Groceries, Different Prices. How Is That Legal?

The same dozen eggs appeared at $3.99 for some shoppers and $4.79 for others—from the same Safeway through Instacart. How can different prices for the same groceries be legal?

A December 2025 investigation by Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative, and More Perfect Union exposed grocery price differences between shoppers. Instacart said these were randomized tests, not prices based on personal data, and announced it was ending all item price tests on December 22, 2025.

In this episode of Signal Shift, Erin explains:
• Why different prices aren’t automatically illegal
• How price testing, dynamic pricing, and personalized pricing differ
• What the FTC found about surveillance-pricing tools
• Why Florida’s emergency price-gouging law doesn’t cover every expensive purchase
• Maryland’s food-pricing protections, effective October 1, 2026
• What to check when two shoppers see different offers

The central question: Are you finding the best deal—or just the best deal they showed you?

Where would you draw the line between a useful discount and an unfair pricing practice? Tell us in the comments.

Subscribe to @SignalShiftTV for clear explanations of the systems affecting your money, technology, and everyday choices. Like and share this episode with someone who shops online.

SOURCES

https://t.co/qLHaDK3Vwy

https://t.co/kjfs8inJnj

The FTC’s public examples were hypothetical illustrations of capabilities identified in its preliminary study. That is the whole mentality. Four lines, recycled.

Men as a class cannot be trusted. Disagreement is rape apology. A police statement is proof. A conviction is proof. The patriarchy hurts men too, so male complaints are self-inflicted. Women having credit cards, property, and jobs outside mothering is the moral achievement of the age, and anyone who questions the frame wants those taken away. 

She will say she is not talking about all men, then treat every man in the thread as all men. She even accused the other side of being paid bots running a script. She is running one.

The wound and the costume
A father who fails a daughter is a particular evil. She said the worst thing was done here, by him, and that he should have protected her. She did not put the details on the page. She did not need to. 

The psyche did the rest.
A girl hurt by the man who was supposed to be the wall learns a brutal lesson: the category “man who should protect me” is a lie. A healthy mind eventually separates that man from the category. She did the opposite. She promoted him. The father became men. 

Once the enemy is a sex, she never runs out of targets, and she never has to finish the story of one man in one house in Michigan.

That is why the rage is selective in the way she described. Someone points at a foreign case and she answers with her father. The point is not the case. The point is that her injury has to outrank every other injury, and the only way it outranks them is if it stands for the whole sex. Particular grief is small. A class war is infinite.

The slogan does two jobs. It names a real evil, rape. And it freezes the father so he never has to be dealt with as a man who failed her. He becomes the patriarchy.

Patriarchy cannot be buried, confronted, or forgiven. It can only be clapped at in other people’s threads. That is why twelve years produced no essay, no story, no name. A finished story would shrink the war. She needs the war.

Is she programmed
Yes, in the only way that word is useful. Not a handler. A closed loop.
Feminist media, the consent slogan, the “believe women” rule, the patriarchy explanation. 

Those lines were waiting for a woman with exactly this wound. They fit. They gave her a vocabulary that sounds like justice and functions like a permanent exemption from having to sort a case. Duke, a false report, a girl who agreed and then regretted it, a man arguing the numbers: all of it collapses into the father. The script does not require her to read the file. It requires her to recognize the enemy.

The algorithm finished the job. An account with 190 followers does not get half a million views for a thought. It gets them for a clap. “CONSENT CAN BE WITHDRAWN AT ANYTIME” is not an argument. 

It is a doorbell. Men ring it. She feels seen. The views are the only applause in a life she has otherwise not put on the page. That is shaping. You repeat what pays.

She is not thinking in these threads. She is reciting. The typos, the “get fucked,” the “should have been swallowed,” the clap emojis, are the same nervous system every time. High arousal, no curiosity, no update. A person who was reasoning would sometimes say “that case is different.” She does not have a different case. She has one case, and every man who answers is called back to it.

Is there virtue
A thin one. Rape is wrong. Consent during the act matters. A father who abuses a daughter is evil. Those are true. She cannot stop there.

She stretches them until a girl enthusiastically agreeing is not consent, until a conviction is automatically guilt, until a man arguing a false report should have been swallowed. The seed is moral. The plant is hate. Hate is what you get when a true sentence is not allowed to stay the size of the fact.

There is also a small ordinary life under it, and that is the sadder part. Married. Earns more. Football. A jab about men losing money. She is not a monk of the cause. She is a woman who kept a marriage and a paycheck and then spent the public self on combat. The marriage is the one fact that cuts against the script. She married a man. She stays married. The feed never has to integrate that. The husband is offstage. The men on the app are the father.

The empty part
The account is empty outside the hate. That is not an insult. It is the inventory. No children mentioned. No craft. No faith. No town. No friend. Twelve years of replies and the only wound she has ever put in public is the father. The rest is tone.

People with a full life use the app. They also leave it. She did not build a second room. The combat is the room. When the thread dies, so does the self she has on offer. That is why the energy feels vacant even when the words are hot. Heat is not depth. A person can be furious and still have nothing behind the fury but the original injury and the slogan that keeps it fed.

Bernie.

You just lost a debate to yourself. Again.

One week ago, you told America that big money buys elections. You said Trump's super PAC was going to "buy the midterms." Get big money out of politics, end Citizens United, the whole Sunday sermon.

Today you tell us AIPAC spent $33 million to beat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

And they LOST.

Yesterday it was Angie Nixon in Florida, outspent more than ten to one, and she won. Today it's El-Sayed, outspent by $33 million, and he won.

So which is it, Senator? Does money buy elections or doesn't it? Because two days in a row, your own posts keep proving it doesn't. You're the guy who spends all week warning the town the bridge is about to collapse, and then sprints across it twice to show everybody how sturdy it is.

What's next, Bernie posting that big money buys elections, and then bragging about candidates who got buried in money and won anyway... wait. I'm being told that's this whole week.

Your argument isn't a house of cards, Bernie. A house of cards at least stands up for a minute before it falls over.

But I'm not here to talk about campaign money. I'm here to talk about something a lot more personal. So bear with me. This one's going to take a while, and I'm not going to apologize for it.

Three days ago, on September 29, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps published a 26-page "Open Letter to the Honorable People of the United States of America." The IRGC. The outfit President Trump designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization back in 2019.

And in that letter, Iran's terrorist army told American voters they could "change the makeup of the government" this November. Trump isn't on the ballot this year, Bernie. The only way to change the makeup of the government in 2026 is to change who runs Congress. There are two parties on that ballot. The IRGC can count to two. So can I.

And do you know what else they asked for, Senator? They want American support for Israel ENDED.

Now read your own post again. All caps. "NO MORE U.S. MILITARY AID FOR ISRAEL."

Bernie, I'm not saying you work for Tehran. I'm saying when a terrorist army writes 26 pages of demands, and three days later a United States senator posts one of them in all caps, somebody should probably notice. You didn't write their letter, Senator. You just posted the summary.

You're a security guard holding the door open for the burglar and calling it good manners.

Now let me tell you why this one's personal. Because I can't read that IRGC letter the way a pundit reads it. I read it as a man Iran already tried to kill.

I was an Army medic in Iraq. Iran's militias blew up my vehicle while I was sitting in it. And they hurt my gunner.

Let me say that again, slower. They. Hurt. My. Gunner.

If you've never ridden in a truck with a turret, here's what you need to know. The gunner is the one standing up. Half his body is out in the open so the rest of us can sit behind armor. He's the first set of eyes, the first one exposed, and when something goes wrong, he's the first one it finds. Every medic in every convoy knows exactly where his gunner is every second of every mission. You do not lose track of your gunner. Ever.

The State Department has said Iran was responsible for the deaths of at least 603 American service members in Iraq between 2003 and 2011, mostly through militias it trained, funded, and armed with explosively formed penetrators. An EFP is a copper plate that turns into a molten slug and punches through armor like wet cardboard. I know what one does to a truck. I know what it does to the men inside. I didn't learn that from a documentary, Bernie.

So when you get on X and scream about cutting off the one country in that region that's actually fighting the people who did that to us, forgive me if I don't clap.

Now. "Candidates who dare to speak out."

Bernie, AIPAC is an American organization made up of American citizens who care about America's alliance with Israel. They spend money to support candidates they agree with and oppose candidates they don't. You know what that's called? Political speech. The exact same thing the First Amendment protects for the Sierra Club, the teachers' unions, the AFL-CIO, Planned Parenthood, and every group that's ever cut a check to help your side.

When the unions spend millions to elect your candidates, that's "democracy." When Bloomberg dropped a billion dollars into your own primary, you stood on the debate stage and smiled. When a group of Americans spends money on the other side of one issue, suddenly it's a sinister plot that needs a post in ALL CAPS.

And here's the part that makes my head spin. A group of AMERICAN citizens spends money in an American election, and you're outraged. A designated terrorist organization writes 26 pages telling Americans how to vote, and I haven't seen one all-caps post from you about THAT. Not one.

Quinn's Law Number Two: if you want to know what liberals are up to, pay attention to what they accuse conservatives of doing. For years we heard that a foreign power picking a side in an American election was a five-alarm emergency. It still is. It just gets a lot less interesting to Democrats when the foreign power picks THEIR side.

Quinn's Law Number Seven: it's different when you're a Democrat. American donors on the other side? Scandal. Iranian terrorists on your side? Crickets. Same election. Different jersey.

Nobody stopped El-Sayed from "daring to speak out," Bernie. He spoke. He campaigned. He won. That's not censorship. That's an election. You just don't like it when the other side gets to talk too.

"Netanyahu's extremist government."

Senator, Israel is a democracy. They hold elections. They have opposition parties, a free press that tears their government apart every single morning, Arab citizens serving in their parliament, and massive public protests against their own prime minister. If Israelis don't like Netanyahu, they vote him out. They've done exactly that before.

Now let's compare that to the people Israel is actually fighting.

Hamas hasn't let Gazans vote since 2006. Twenty years. On October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorists crossed into Israel and murdered about 1,200 people in a single day, most of them civilians. Families in their homes. Kids at a music festival. They dragged around 250 hostages into tunnels.

Iran built Hezbollah from scratch. In 1983 a Hezbollah truck bomb killed 241 Americans in their barracks in Beirut, and a U.S. federal court later held Iran liable. In 2022, a 22-year-old Iranian woman named Mahsa Amini died in the custody of Iran's morality police because of how she wore her hijab. When Iranians protested, the regime shot them in the streets.

And two days ago, the story's still developing, a co-pilot on a FlyDubai flight headed for Tel Aviv reportedly stabbed the captain and tried to put the plane into the ground, and people on board had to fight to pull it out of the dive.

THAT is the neighborhood Israel lives in, Bernie. Every single day. And you want to call the DEMOCRACY "extremist."

And here's something the IRGC would really prefer you didn't know. When Khomeini named his enemies, he called Israel the "Little Satan." America? We're the GREAT Satan. In the regime's own ranking system, we're in first place, Bernie. Israel's in second.

So when people tell you all this is "really about Israel," just remember Tehran's own scoreboard puts YOU at the top. Nobody asked for that trophy. But it's ours. And cutting off the guy standing in second place doesn't make the guy in first place any safer. It just means you're next in line, and nobody's standing in front of you.

"NO MORE U.S. MILITARY AID FOR ISRAEL."

Let me tell you what that aid actually is.

A big part of it is missile defense. Iron Dome. David's Sling. Systems that do one job: shoot rockets out of the sky before they land on schools, apartment buildings, and hospitals. Iron Dome doesn't invade anybody. It doesn't occupy anything. It's a SHIELD. When you scream "no more military aid," what you're really screaming is "take away the shield" from a country that gets rockets fired at its civilians.

As a combat medic, I've seen what explosives do to a human body. I'll spare you the details. But I'll tell you this: every rocket that gets knocked out of the sky is a family that never gets the knock on the door. And you want to stop paying for the thing that knocks it out of the sky.

You're a lifeguard throwing a drowning man an anchor and calling it compassion.

And here's what you never tell your crowds. Under the agreement signed when Obama was president in 2016, Israel's ability to spend that money outside the United States gets phased out. The bulk of it gets spent right here. In American factories. With American workers. A lot of them union workers, Bernie. Your people. Supposedly.

So "no more military aid" really means "take away Israel's missile shield AND lay off a bunch of American factory workers." Put that on a protest sign and see how many union halls march behind it.

And Israel shares intelligence that saves American lives. They develop technology that protects American troops. Walking away from your friend in the middle of a bar fight isn't peace, Senator. It's just leaving him outnumbered and hoping the other guys get tired.

They won't. I've met them. Well, I met their handiwork.

There are really only two ways a free people answer terror, Bernie.

One is United Flight 93, September 11, 2001. Ordinary passengers found out what the hijackers planned, took a vote, and rushed the cockpit. They died in a field in Pennsylvania, and the Capitol is still standing because of them. Nobody formed a committee. Nobody wrote a strongly worded letter. They fought.

The other is Madrid, March 2004. Terrorists bombed the commuter trains and killed nearly 200 people days before a national election. The voters changed their government, and the new government pulled Spain's troops out of Iraq. The terrorists learned exactly the lesson they hoped to learn: bombs work. Elections can be bought with blood.

The IRGC letter is a polite request for Madrid. And your post, Senator, reads like a "yes, please."

Now let me say something plainly, because it matters. You're Jewish, Bernie. You lived on a kibbutz in Israel as a young man. You know better than almost anybody in that Senate building what Israel is surrounded by and why it exists. And you're using your platform to give the people who chant for its destruction the feeling that they've got a United States senator in their corner. I don't say that to be cruel. I say it because I think you KNOW better. And that's exactly what makes this so frustrating.

So here's one question for you, Senator. Just one. It costs nothing to answer. It's the easiest layup in American politics.

Do you reject the IRGC's support?

Yes or no. No "both sides." No pivot to Netanyahu. No speech about billionaires. Just yes or no. Because the pivot IS the answer.

And as for "they are going to keep losing," I'd slow down. Your crystal ball has a crack in it. A week ago money won elections. Today money loses elections. Tomorrow it'll be whichever one gets you more retweets. You're a weathervane in a tornado, Bernie. You're not pointing anywhere. You're just spinning.

You've got the foreign policy instincts of a goldfish. Every lap around the bowl is a brand new world.

You're a scarecrow that invites the crows to dinner and then complains about the cornfield.

You're a referee wearing the other team's jersey and wondering why the fans keep booing.

You're an umbrella made of Swiss cheese, and you keep telling everybody it's going to be a dry walk home.

You're a house cat guarding a bird feeder. Technically on duty. Absolutely not on our side.

And you've got more flip-flops this week than a Florida gas station gift shop.

So here's my standing offer, Senator, one more time. I keep hearing Democrats cry about "big money" while they ARE big money. Three houses. $221,000 on private jets in one quarter of 2025. Over $200 million raised in each of your presidential runs. Before you lecture anybody about money in politics, file with the standard deduction, pay DOUBLE what the IRS says you owe, and post the return. Then fly commercial to your next rally and explain to the folks in the middle seat how money corrupts everything.

And to every voter reading this: you don't have to love your Republican candidate. In November you're hiring a vote, not a best friend. But when a foreign terrorist army writes you a 26-page letter explaining which way it would like you to vote, and a senator posts their main demand in all caps three days later... maybe do the other thing.

My gunner would tell you the same. He's got the scars to back it up.

But what do I know? I'm only a medic who already got blown up by Iran's militias once, a physics teacher who knows what a missile shield is for, and a guy who isn't about to let the people who hurt my gunner pick my Congress.

text:
In January 1822 the New York police shut down a Black theatre company, arrested the actors, and let them go on one condition. They had to promise never to perform Shakespeare again.

One of the boys hanging around that company went on to play Shakespeare for the next forty-five years. He did it on more stages, in more countries, in front of more kings and emperors than any actor then alive.

His name was Ira Aldridge, and he never got to do it in America.

The company belonged to a man named William Alexander Brown, a retired ship steward from the West Indies. He had opened a tea garden on Thomas Street where Black New Yorkers could sit and drink and hear music.

When the neighbours complained about the noise, he moved the whole thing indoors and upstairs. He called it a theatre.

On the seventeenth of September, 1821, the African Theatre opened with an all-Black cast performing Richard the Third. It was the first Black theatre in the United States.

Brown kept getting moved on. By the winter he had set up on Park Row, in the business district, next door to the Park Theatre, which was the only professional playhouse in the entire city.

The Park belonged to Stephen Price, a man so ruthless about his monopoly that Washington Irving and others called him King Stephen. Price sent hecklers into Brown's house to wreck the shows.

Then the police came, and the arrests, and the promise.

The Sheriff of New York at the time was Mordecai Manuel Noah, who also edited an influential newspaper called the National Advocate, in which he ran and commissioned mocking articles about Black performers. He and Price were friends.

Ira Aldridge was fourteen years old that January, living at 416 Broadway, out of his father's house.

He was born in New York City on the twenty-fourth of July, 1807, to the Reverend Daniel Aldridge and his wife Luranah. His father wanted him in the pulpit and sent him to the African Free School, set up by the Manumission Society to educate the children of free Black families and enslaved ones.

James McCune Smith sat in those rooms and became the first African American to hold a medical degree. Henry Highland Garnet sat there too, and in 1843 he stood up and called on the enslaved to resist.

Alexander Crummell was there. So were Charles L. Reason and George T. Downing.

Ira won prizes for declamation. His brother Joshua said later that the teachers thought well of him for his quickness and his attention.

What none of them could tell him was where any of it led. In 1819 a pupil at one of those schools gave a public address that his schoolmaster wrote down and printed, and the boy asked what trade he was supposed to enter.

His answer, in his own words: no one will employ me, white boys won't work with me.

Ira left school in 1822, at fifteen, the age past which no Black child could stay. He meant to learn shoemaking.

He went to sea instead, which was the ordinary road for a bright Black boy in New York, and it nearly finished him. His ship put in at a port in North Carolina and a slave dealer looked him over and offered the captain five hundred dollars for him.

The captain said no. According to James McCune Smith, who wrote it down in 1860, the captain's reason was that the boy had trusted to his honour to be carried back to New York.

Ira came home and went straight to the theatre.

He could not get in the front. The Park Theatre kept one obscure corner of its highest gallery for people of colour, a place where, as his own memoir later put it, respectable Black New Yorkers were expected to sit among sweeps and pickpockets.

So he went in the back, on somebody else's pass. A schoolfellow of his had the job of carrying the actor Henry Wallack's costumes into the Chatham Theatre, and Ira cultivated that boy hard.

Then the boy died of yellow fever. Ira asked for the job and got it, carrying another man's clothes for no money at all, and stood in the wings and watched.

He wrote about that later, about what happened to him the first time he saw a stage. Bewildered, amazed, dazzled, fascinated, and certain from that hour that his own life would be worthless unless he could get into it.

Getting into it cost him. On Friday the nineteenth of July, 1822, a circus rider and clown named James Bellmont assaulted him.

Twenty-two days after that, on a Saturday night, ten white men walked into Brown's theatre and took it apart. Three of them were circus performers.

They broke the benches and the lamps, tore the curtains and the costumes, and damaged the scenery. Brown filed a complaint the next day and put the repair bill at two hundred dollars.

The day after that, on the twelfth of August, a fifteen-year-old Ira Aldridge filed his own complaint against James Bellmont for assault and battery.

Bellmont pleaded not guilty in August. He pleaded not guilty again in September.

There is no record that the case was ever tried.

The circus moved on to Philadelphia, then Baltimore, then Washington. That was the end of it.

Brown took his company to Albany. By January 1824 the African Theatre had given its last known performance and the building went to other uses.

At the end of that year, or the beginning of the next, Ira Aldridge got on a ship for England carrying a letter of introduction from Henry Wallack. He was seventeen, and he never saw America again.

On the eleventh of May, 1825, he walked onto a stage at the Royalty Theatre in Whitechapel and played Othello. The bill called him Mr. Keene, a Gentleman of Colour, from the New York Theatre.

Five months later he took a bigger house. At the Royal Coburg, which stands today as the Old Vic, he played the enslaved African prince Oroonoko, and the London press had its first proper look at him.

The Times ran its verdict on the eleventh of October, 1825. It called him baker-kneed and narrow-chested, and said that the shape of his lips made it impossible for him to pronounce English.

The same paper complained that his skin was too coppery to convince as a Moor. It ran both objections in the same notice.

Too Black for the stage, and not Black enough for the part.

He started inventing himself in return. Descent from a Senegalese princely line went onto the bills, along with the name African Roscius, and in the 1851 census he wrote Africa in the box for place of birth.

The Glasgow University education and the spell at Schenectady College were inventions too. Neither institution has any record of him, and the scholarship treats both stories as inventions, which is worth saying out loud on a page that cares about the record rather than the legend.

The work underneath the invention was real. In 1828, at twenty, he was handed the management of the Theatre Royal in Coventry, making him the first Black person ever to run a British theatre.

While he was there he stood up and talked about slavery to anyone who would sit still. He wrote an open letter to the people of Coventry saying that being a foreigner and a stranger were universal passports to British sympathy.

After he left, the townspeople went to the county hall and petitioned Parliament to abolish slavery. Tony Howard, the Warwick professor who dug this out, says Aldridge changed the climate of thinking in a city that had shown almost no interest in the question before he arrived.

It became a method. On the closing night of an engagement he would step out of the play and speak directly to the house about slavery in America, and audiences came for that as much as for the tragedy.

Parts nobody had written for him started going up on his bills too. Shylock, Macbeth, Richard the Third, and later King Lear, played in greasepaint and a wig, white-faced, in front of English crowds.

Then, on the twenty-fifth of March, 1833, Edmund Kean collapsed on the Covent Garden stage in the middle of Othello, and died soon after.

Two weeks later the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, gave the part to Aldridge. No Black performer had ever appeared on the boards of one of London's patent theatres.

The knives were out before he ever walked on. On the thirty-first of March the paper called The Age told its readers he had been Jemmy Wallack's footman, and a very queer one at that.

A playbill for the tenth of April, 1833, survives in the Folger collection in Washington, printed with two small portraits of him and a note in German. Ellen Tree played Desdemona.

Three days later the Athenaeum ran its review. It complained that Ellen Tree should never have been subjected to the indignity of being pawed about by Mr. Henry Wallack's black servant.

The word actor does not appear anywhere in it.

He had just carried Othello at the biggest theatre in England. The review filed him under domestic staff.

Figaro in London ran a campaign to drive him off a stage it said he had dishonoured. Its suggestion was that his proper level was footman or street sweeper.

The reviews were not one voice. The Standard called him a singularly gifted actor, the Spectator found real feeling and nature in the performance, the Globe found beauties throughout, and the Morning Post managed only that it was good enough to be considered very curious.

A few nights into the run an influenza outbreak closed London theatres, Covent Garden among them, for five days. When the doors opened again, Othello was off the schedule, and so were the two other pieces he had been billed in.

His memoir records it in one flat line. Four nights at Covent Garden, and then his name came down off the bills.

By the twenty-second of April he was across the river at the Surrey, playing Othello and following it with the farce The Padlock, and the Surrey's bill printed what Covent Garden would not say. A man of colour performing Othello on the British stage was an epoch in the history of theatricals.

Then he did something almost nobody in his position did in 1833.

He wrote to a newspaper. On the seventeenth of May the National Omnibus and General Advertiser printed a letter from him answering the servant story that the London press had been repeating for weeks.

He said he had enjoyed Mr. Wallack's friendship in New York. He added that his father's circumstances had always been good enough that nobody in the family had ever been placed in servitude.

Then he wrote that he had never been Wallack's servant, nor the servant of any man.

The editor printed a note under it suggesting Aldridge was being too generous to Wallack. Three weeks later the paper reported that Wallack had asked for the statement to be contradicted, and the editor refused to treat a request as a refutation.

Wallack never answered publicly. Aldridge had put it in the record and left it there.

For the next twenty years he worked towns the short versions of his life leave out. Berwick-upon-Tweed and Alnwick up in Northumberland, and a circuit through Gainsborough, Grantham, Spilsby and Horncastle in 1841.

He played Lincoln in 1842 and again in 1849, Exmouth in June of 1844, Boston in Lincolnshire in 1847. When he rolled into Lincoln in a travelling coach the local papers wrote it up as a spectacle, and the houses that week were poor.

He had married Margaret Gill, an Englishwoman ten years older than him, at St George's, Bloomsbury, on the twenty-seventh of November, 1825, in front of two witnesses named William Tanfield and Margaret Robinson. The pro-slavery lobby went after the marriage and tried to end his career with it.

The record holds a judgment against him too. In January 1856 an actor named William Stothard sued him over an affair with his wife, and the jury found against Aldridge and awarded damages of two pounds.

In 1852 he crossed to the continent and the ceiling came off his life.

In January 1853 he gave four command performances at the Hoftheater in Potsdam. Friedrich Wilhelm the Fourth of Prussia gave him the Gold Medal for Art and Science, first class.

Franz Joseph of Austria gave him the Order of Leopold. The city of Bern gave him the Maltese Cross.

In 1858 Duke Bernhard of Saxe-Meiningen knighted him. Chevalier Ira Aldridge, Knight of Saxony, went onto the playbills and stayed there.

The King of Belgium sent for him, and so did the King and Queen of Holland, the Queen of Sweden, and two Emperors of Austria. No actor of that century collected honours from more heads of state.

Behind the medals he was carrying Shakespeare into countries that had never had him. In 1858 he brought Shakespeare to Serbia for the first time, with Richard the Third.

Between 1853 and 1867 he went into Poland six times, and the effect there was permanent. Watching Aldridge perform pushed the translator Józef Paszkowski to render Othello into Polish, and a Warsaw company used that translation for the first time during Aldridge's visit in 1863.

A Black American from Mulberry Street is the reason Poles first heard Othello in their own language.

Polish audiences in Kraków boycotted him for performing in a German theatre. He went to the press and revealed, for the first time in public, his involvement with the abolitionist movement in the United States.

He was telling occupied people that he stood where they stood. Polish papers started calling him our brother, his performances turned into political events, and Tsarist officials put him under surveillance.

On the tenth of November, 1858, he played Othello in St Petersburg. In the audience sat Taras Shevchenko, Ukraine's national poet, born a serf, bought out of ownership in 1838 and only just released from ten years of exile and forced military service.

Shevchenko wept through the performance. Then he went backstage, walked into the dressing room, and kissed him.

Neither man could speak a word of the other's language. They met again at the house of Count Fyodor Tolstoy, where the count's young daughters Katya and Olya translated, and the interpreters could not keep up with how fast the two of them talked.

So they sang instead.

Ukrainian village songs went one way across the room. Spirituals came back the other.

On the sixth of December, Shevchenko wrote to his friend Mikhail Shchepkin, another former serf, and said the African actor was doing miracles on the stage and showing them a living Shakespeare. He drew Aldridge's portrait that winter, and it survives.

Two years later Aldridge wrote a letter of his own that explains the missing decades. On the fourth of June, 1860, he told his old schoolmate James McCune Smith that Henry Wallack had suggested an American visit in 1858, and that his wife would not hear of it.

Margaret's feeling against Americans, he wrote, was rooted in how they treated his oppressed race. She had watched what the press did to him in London and she was not sending him back into worse.

He became a British subject in 1863. Margaret died in 1864, after forty years of marriage, and the following April he married Amanda von Brandt, a Swedish woman who had been his mistress.

In December 1865 the United States abolished slavery, and a man who had left in 1824 started arranging his passage home.

The deal got done in the summer of 1867. In the first week of August a New York theatrical paper announced that Charles M. Webb and T. Francis Gibbons had secured Ira Aldridge for one hundred performances in the United States.

He would sail from England around the middle of the month. He would open at the Academy of Music as Othello, about the first of September.

Forty-five years earlier, New York police had made a company of Black actors promise to give up Shakespeare. Now Shakespeare was going back to New York in the hands of a boy who had been standing in that room.

He never got on the ship.

He had reached Łódź in Russian-occupied Poland on the fifth of August, at the invitation of a man named August Hentschel, to open the new Paradyż theatre with Othello. He was staying at Michał Kunkiel's hotel on Piotrkowska Street and he was already sick when the coach set him down.

Doctors came. He died on the seventh, of a lung condition that had been working on him for years, on the day of the premiere.

The town buried him as though he belonged to them. The funeral procession went up Piotrkowska with the church bells going and thousands of people out in the street, in a manufacturing city where almost nobody had ever met him.

Edmund Pohlens, the president of Łódź, walked at the head of it. Behind him, members of the local theatre society carried his medals and his orders through the streets on red velvet cushions.

Trumpets played. There was a laurel wreath on the coffin.

There was no grave.

Nothing had been prepared, so a local manufacturer named Karol Moes gave up a place in his own family's newly built plot. The pastor spoke over him about how fate throws people far from where they were born, to rest forever away from the ones who loved them.

People covered the tomb with flowers. Then the city went home, and what it had given him was a place in another family's ground.

Twenty-three years passed before there was a stone with his name on it.

On the eleventh of May, 1890, his daughter Luranah Aldridge, by then a working opera singer, gave a performance at the Thalia theatre in Łódź and handed the entire take to the cemetery. Three hundred and fourteen rubles and twenty-seven kopecks bought the monument that stands today on Ogrodowa Street.

It carries a porcelain photograph of him in costume as Othello. The picture was damaged at some point and a Łódź resident named Juliusz Stryszowski made a replacement and put it back himself, on his own initiative, without anybody asking him to.

The Society of Polish Artists of Film and Theatre keeps the grave. Anonymous citizens of that city still leave fresh flowers and candles on it.

The tomb was renovated in 2001. In August 2024, on the hundred and fifty-seventh anniversary of his death, Łódź announced a full restoration paid for partly out of coins collected in the cemetery each autumn by volunteers.

His youngest child born while he was alive was Amanda Christina Elizabeth Aldridge, in Upper Norwood, on the tenth of March, 1866. She was seventeen months old when he died in that hotel room.

She never saw her father work.

What she had of him was objects. His guitar was one, and a pair of gold earrings he had worn as Othello was another.

Music was where she made her own life out of the same material he had. Enrolled as the second student ever taken at the Royal College of Music, she studied singing under Jenny Lind and taught voice in London for sixty-five years, with Roland Hayes and Marian Anderson among her pupils.

On the seventeenth of October, 1925, she wrote to Eslanda Robeson to say she had heard her husband singing on the radio and thought the voice was wondrously beautiful. Two days later Paul and Essie Robeson spent the afternoon at her house.

She played them her own compositions. She talked about a father almost nobody in England still discussed.

Before they left she put Ira Aldridge's earrings into Paul Robeson's hands.

The version that circulates says she handed them over in 1930, at the theatre, on the night. The record puts it five years earlier, in her front room, with nobody watching.

In 1930 she coached Robeson in elocution for his Othello at the Savoy Theatre, opposite Peggy Ashcroft. He was the first Black actor recorded in that role in London since her father.

He wore the earrings onstage, in the city that had run her father out of it.

She spent the rest of her life defending him. In 1940 one of his first biographers sent her his manuscript, proposing to end the book with a line from a minstrel song, and she wrote back that it was not in keeping with the dignity of her father's career.

Late in life she said hardly anyone ever gave her credit for any of it. She died in 1956, the day before her ninetieth birthday.

There is an oil painting of Ira Aldridge hanging in Washington, D.C., in the National Portrait Gallery. Henry Perronet Briggs painted it around 1830, when Aldridge was in his early twenties and still working the English provinces.

The wall text tells you he was the first American actor to win a European reputation, and that London critics attacked him in racist terms. It notes the Shylock, the Macbeth and the Richard the Third played in whiteface, and the career that peaked on tours through Russia, France and Poland.

The last line says he was planning a triumphant United States tour when he died. That is where the label stops.

It does not tell you the tour was one hundred nights, or that he was about a week from the ship. It does not tell you his body is in Łódź, under a stone his daughter sang for, behind a photograph a stranger remade by hand.

It does not tell you what a New York police officer got a room full of Black actors to promise in January 1822. And it does not tell you what one boy from that room wrote into a London newspaper eleven years later, after the greatest theatre in England took his name off the bills.

That he had never been any man's servant.

𝐈𝐑𝐀𝐍 𝐂𝐋𝐎𝐒𝐄𝐃 𝐇𝐎𝐑𝐌𝐔𝐙 𝐓𝐎 𝐂𝐇𝐎𝐊𝐄 𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐍𝐄𝐈𝐆𝐇𝐁𝐎𝐑𝐒

President Trump put it bluntly this week: “𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘴𝘮𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮𝘴𝘦𝘭𝘷𝘦𝘴. 𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘴𝘢𝘪𝘥, ‘𝘓𝘦𝘵’𝘴 𝘤𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘪𝘵 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘢 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘭𝘥.’ 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘐 𝘤𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘦 𝘱𝘶𝘵 𝘶𝘱 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘣𝘭𝘰𝘤𝘬𝘢𝘥𝘦 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘯 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘺 𝘩𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘺.”

The numbers now back him up. According to tanker-tracking and satellite data from trade firm Kpler, 𝐆𝐮𝐥𝐟 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐫𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝟏𝟔.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐚 𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫, 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐞-𝐰𝐚𝐫 𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 — 10.5 million more than in March, the first full month after the war shut the strait.

They did it by routing around Iran’s choke point. Before the war, 83% of the region’s crude passed through Hormuz. In September, 40% never crossed it, flowing through Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea and the UAE’s pipeline to Fujairah.

Iran is the one producer missing from the recovery. Its exports have hovered near zero since the U.S. reimposed its naval blockade in July, and dozens of its tankers sit stuck near Sri Lanka and Malaysia, per the Wall Street Journal. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain out for delivery, and “𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘺 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘵 𝘵𝘸𝘰 𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘬𝘴.”

Tehran’s whole wartime bet was that 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝’𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐨𝐫 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐮𝐥𝐟 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐬. Seven months later, Iran’s neighbors are shipping at full strength and the regime is the one begging for a deal. Trump rejected the offer.

𝐈𝐫𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝’𝐬 𝐨𝐢𝐥 𝐡𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞. 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐝, 𝐢𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐭𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐟 𝐨𝐮𝐭.

text:
Amnesia much?

Obama
In his first year, the Democratic National Committee offered a menu of access. Internal documents obtained by the Washington Times showed high-dollar fundraisers promised meetings with senior White House officials for a personal gift of $30,400 or for bundling $300,000. Perks reported at the time included an Oval Office birthday visit, use of the White House bowling alley, a movie in the residence theater, and golf with Obama for his top New York bundler, UBS Americas CEO Robert Wolf. Donors also got private briefings from advisers such as Austan Goolsbee.
State dinners worked the same way. At the March 2012 dinner for British Prime Minister David Cameron, more than 40 prolific contributors were guests; those invitees had already bundled at least $10.9 million for the 2012 campaign, and some sat at the head table with Obama. A New York Times review of Obama state-dinner lists found about 12 percent of non-spouse guests were bundlers, with Wall Street heavily represented.
Late in the term, the pattern extended to the Obama Foundation. MapLight matched visitor logs to early foundation donors and found that every donor whose family or foundation had given more than $100,000 met with Obama at the White House. Examples included a January 2016 private gathering, not on the public schedule, attended by people who had already given $340,000 and $500,000. The foundation later said it would not solicit while he was in office and publishes gifts over $1,000; the center itself has cost on the order of $850 million.
Biden
The clearest case is from July 2024. Politico reported that four billionaires were brought into the White House Map Room for a small meeting with Biden on his second-term agenda. The next day, tech entrepreneur Mark Pincus gave the maximum then allowed, $929,600, to the Biden Victory Fund. Within three weeks, Reid Hoffman sent $923,000. Of the 50 largest contributions to that fund through March 2024, just over half of the donors or their spouses had been in a small White House meeting. Ethics groups called the optics bad; the checks were still legal campaign money, disclosed and capped.
The 2021 inaugural committee was more explicit about tiers. Individuals could give $500,000 and corporations $1 million for a package that included a virtual event with Biden and Jill Biden, briefings with inaugural and campaign leadership, VIP concert access, merchandise, and tickets to a later in-person event. The committee raised $61.8 million. Million-dollar corporate donors included Pfizer, Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Bank of America, Comcast, and Uber. That was less than Trump’s 2017 inaugural haul of about $107 million, which used the same unlimited-inaugural model.

text:
Putting U.S. boots on the ground in Iran after the midterms is a bad idea, and “nothing to lose” is the tell.Trump has said a bigger bombing campaign is “possible” after Nov. 3. He has also refused to rule out ground troops. A third carrier and a Marine expeditionary unit of about 2,000 Marines are heading toward the region. That is a raid and evacuation force, not an invasion force. Treating it as the start of a ground war is how you get a disaster with a press release attached.

Iran is not a regime you topple with a few thousand Marines. It is a country of about 90 million, with mountains, cities, ballistic missiles, mines, and militias that have spent decades planning for exactly this. The Iraq occupation needed well over 100,000 troops and still failed. Afghanistan took 20 years. A MEU can seize a port or pull people out. It cannot hold Tehran, police a population, or stop a missile campaign against U.S. bases and Gulf cities.

The war is already in its eighth month. Air strikes and a blockade have not produced a deal. Iran’s last offer was Hormuz for sanctions relief, and Washington rejected it. More bombs after the election do not fix that. Ground troops make it worse: every dead American becomes a reason to stay, every Iranian civilian killed becomes a recruitment ad, and every hostage becomes leverage Tehran does not have from a ship offshore.

“Nothing to lose” is also false on the thing voters already feel. Diesel in the U.S. is over $6.50 a gallon. Gulf fuel shipments are still far below normal. China has paused product exports. Russia has banned diesel exports through October. A ground fight around the Strait does not reopen that market. It closes it harder, and the bill lands on trucking, farms, and Europe’s emergency stocks.

Waiting until after the midterms is not strategy. It is sequencing the casualties so they do not show up on a ballot. The people who lose are the Marines on the beach, the sailors on the carriers, and anyone who still has to buy fuel when the exit plan is “we’ll figure it out once we’re in.”

text:
Lindsay never testified. She never said she did it in court. A non-denial is not a confession. The defense OFFERED to stipulate, but the defense rejected that offer. That means the state, after refusing to stipulate to the facts, retains the burden to prove all of the elements of the charged offense in a court of law. 

The defense theory was that she didn’t know whether she did it or not. She died, was resuscitated in the hospital and TOLD that she had done it. She didn’t deny it because she was so mentally disturbed she didn’t have any memory of it. The best defense with these facts was not criminally liable because she couldn’t remember to conclusively say she didn’t do it. 

In Massachusetts, to enter a defense of not criminally responsible, you necessarily have to stipulate that you’re probably guilty of the underlying crime. Just like claiming self defense necessarily means you have to admit that you killed a person. 

In the Kyle Rittenhouse trial, the state of Wisconsin still had to prove all the legal elements of murder, because killing another person isn’t murder unless those legal requirements are met. 

That’s my beef with the case. Did she kill her kids? Probably. But whether it was first degree murder is something the prosecution has to prove in court. 

The prosecution didn’t do that.

text:
By 1923, Wyatt Earp was no longer the young frontier lawman remembered from stories of the American West. At 75, he had lived through decades of dramatic change, and photographs from his later years reveal a very different side of the man whose name had become part of Western history. In this image, Earp stands upright at his Los Angeles home, presenting a calm and dignified figure far removed from the dusty frontier towns of his youth.

Earp had spent much of his earlier life working as a lawman, gambler, and sometime businessman in several Western communities. His name became closely associated with Dodge City and Tombstone, Arizona, particularly the famous confrontation at the O.K. Corral in 1881. Over time, newspapers, books, and later films transformed many episodes of his life into enduring Western legends, making it difficult to separate the historical man from the larger-than-life character created by popular culture.

Yet this later photograph offers a fascinating reminder that Wyatt Earp's life continued long after the most famous events of the Old West had passed. Standing in his Los Angeles home at an advanced age, he represented a living link to a frontier that was rapidly disappearing. The man in the photograph had witnessed an extraordinary transformation of America—from frontier settlements to modern cities. How different must the world have looked to Earp when he looked back on the life he had lived? #weirdwest #wildwest #cowboy

text:
A $1.3B SMALLER BUYOUT SENT SYNAPTICS $SYNA UP 14%:

Synaptics (SYNA) at $121.10, +$14.95 / +14.08% on Friday.

The San Jose company designs chips for touch controls like laptop touchpads, for wireless connections, and for AI that runs on the device itself. After Thursday's close, the company buying it rewrote the deal: $123 a share in cash instead of its own stock. The headline value fell from about $7B to about $5.7B. The verdict: Synaptics owners did not take a cut on Friday. The old offer had already shrunk below the new one, and the stock now trades like a $123 check due around mid-2027 rather than like a chip company.

The buyer is onsemi (ON) at $84.89, +$4.81 / +6.01% on Friday.

The Scottsdale, Arizona chipmaker sells power chips and image sensors, mostly to carmakers and factories. In June it agreed to pay 1.350 of its own shares for each Synaptics share. That is a fixed number of shares, not a fixed number of dollars, so the offer was worth whatever those shares were worth that day:

- June 24, the reference date in the deal's filings: onsemi at $115.74, an offer worth $156.25 a Synaptics share.
- June 26, the first trading day after the announcement: onsemi fell 23.7%, to $90.65.
- Thursday, October 1: onsemi at $80.08, an offer worth $108.11.

The $7B was a June snapshot. By Thursday the same deal was worth nearly a third less, because investors had marked down the stock it was paid in. Synaptics traded in step with that offer the whole way and closed Thursday at $106.15, $1.96 under it.

Friday closed that loop almost to the penny:

- New cash price: $123, which is $14.89 more than the stock offer was worth Thursday and $33.25 less than it was worth in June.
- Synaptics' move: +$14.95, finishing $1.90 under $123.

So it is a raise against Thursday's value and still a loss against June's. Synaptics chief executive Rahul Patel called the new terms "value certainty at a meaningful premium as compared to current value."

A rival forced the rewrite. On September 2 another bidder, named only as Party A in the filings and described there as a strategic party, meaning an operating company rather than an investment fund, made an unsolicited offer. Synaptics' board at one point judged it better than onsemi's deal. The cash terms followed, and the board reversed that judgment. Party A's identity and price have not been disclosed.

The buyer's stock rose too, which looks odd for a company agreeing to pay more. At Thursday's prices, $123 in cash costs onsemi about $590M more than the stock deal would have. The stock deal had its own cost:

- New onsemi shares: about 54 million, roughly 14% more than the 389 million it has now.
- The price they would have gone out at: about $80, 31% under where onsemi stood when the deal was struck.

That is a 14% slice of every future onsemi profit, paid for in shares investors had already marked down. Cash keeps that slice with today's owners. The money comes from onsemi's own cash, $3.5B at July 3, plus up to $2.45B of committed bank loans. Its market value rose about $1.9B on Friday, and chip stocks explain only part of that:

iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) at $588.90, +$12.57 / +2.18% on Friday.

The trade-off is debt, on top of the $4.5B onsemi owed at July 3. It sits on none of the six Len5 watchlists but fits the Quality Len5, which asks only for a profitable, sound business: $632.8M of profit over its last four quarters, and an owners' stake of $7.2B, well above that debt.

Back to Synaptics, where the number that matters now is the $1.90 gap. If the deal closes in mid-2027, as both companies expect, that gap pays about 1.6% for nine months of waiting, roughly 2% a year. A one-year Treasury paid 4.46% on Friday, by the Treasury's own daily count. Investors holding a stock under a pending buyout usually demand more than a Treasury pays, because deals can collapse. The usual reading when they accept less is that they see some chance of a higher price before closing, and the only other bidder on record is Party A.

Synaptics sits on none of the six Len5 watchlists, and a stock pinned to a cash offer has no price of its own for them to judge. It also misses the Quality Len5. Under standard accounting it lost $490.8M in the year to June 27, including a $425.3M non-cash charge to write off tax savings it no longer expects to use. The business underneath, same year:

- Sales: $1.2B, +11%.
- Core IoT, its chips for connected devices: $389.7M, +43%.
- Adjusted profit, which leaves out that charge and items like stock paid to staff: $4.58 a share, +27%.

What would put it on the Quality Len5: a full year of reported profit, which on the current timetable would arrive about when the deal closes.

Two things could move Synaptics off $123. A higher bid, from Party A or anyone else, would lift it above that price. An objection from a regulator would widen the gap as the odds of collecting fall. The Federal Trade Commission, the US antitrust agency, has cleared the deal; reviews in other countries are still open, and the companies have not said which. The dated steps:

- By about October 11: Synaptics files its proxy, the voting packet for shareholders. No vote date is set.
- November 2, before the open: onsemi's September-quarter report, a date it has not confirmed.
- November 5, after the close: Synaptics' report, also unconfirmed, with no call and no forecast while the deal is pending.
- Mid-2027: the expected closing.

For three months, owning Synaptics meant owning onsemi stock under another name. As of Friday it means owning a fixed $123 promise, and only a second bidder or a regulator can change that.

Not investment advice.

They wrote about women like @RealCandaceO in the Bible. 

“And I find more bitter than death the woman, whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands: whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her; but the sinner shall be taken by her.” (KJV). Ecclesiastes 7:26

What Owens has actually said
On her podcast in March 2026 (episode “Did Erika Kirk Know Jeffrey Epstein?”), she said she had a “growing hunch” that Erika and Epstein crossed paths. She said she had confirmed, four times, with people of “direct knowledge,” that Erika Kirk took multiple meetings at Next Model Management in New York and dealt with executives around Faith Kates, whom Owens places in Epstein’s circle. She said Erika was not modeling there. She treated pageants, Romania, and modeling agencies as a pattern of coincidence.
On 14 March 2026 she posted that a viral audio of a woman scheduling girls for Epstein was not Erika, and that her team had debunked it. She wrote that Erika’s “verified connection to Epstein’s orbit is via Faith Kates’ Next Model Management and the model apartments on the upper east side.” She did not publish the verification.  
On 25 June 2026 she went further: the marriage “was never real,” “Erika’s proximity to Epstein’s world can no longer be ignored,” and “all roads lead to Romania,” again tying it to Brunel and Next. Coverage of that episode notes she offered no contracts, emails, photos, or payroll records on air, only that “more people” had come forward.  
She has also folded this into a much larger theory that Charlie Kirk’s assassination involved betrayal inside his circle. A Utah man sued her in September 2026 alleging she implicated him and, among others, Erika in the killing. A lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding.

What the record actually shows:

Erika’s documented work is Miss Arizona USA 2012, Miss USA 2012 (unplaced), modeling and casting-director work in New York entertainment, the Romanian Angels gift project under Everyday Heroes Like You, Proclaim streetwear, a podcast, real estate, and, after September 2025, CEO of Turning Point USA. Her own bio says she worked as a model, actress, and casting director. That is not the same as running a modeling department.
Checks that have been done:
•  Snopes rated false the claim she appears in the Epstein files as a recruiter, and false the claim she had Charlie killed to hide Epstein ties. Her name has not been reported in the DOJ releases in that role.  
•  The “DOJ wiretap” audio was a 2005 Palm Beach police recording. The woman on it was identified in the probable-cause affidavit as Haley Robson, not Erika. Owens herself rejected that clip.  
•  The Romania trafficking claim is false. Romanian Angels, roughly 2011–2015, sponsored gifts for children in Constanța orphanages with U.S. military and local partners. Romanian court searches and local reporting found no case, ban, or trafficking allegation against her. PolitiFact and Snopes both rated it false. One news clip circulated as proof was published when she was about 13.

text:
BOOM! US DEBT CLOCK EXPOSES THE WIZARD OF OZ — Trump Follows the YELLOW BRICK ROAD to a Stunning DEBT-FREE MONEY Message

The U.S. Debt Clock has released another Secret Window graphic, placing Wizard of Oz symbolism beside gold, debt, and sovereign money. One line dominates: Follow the Yellow Brick Road. A Tin Man stands on one side. President Donald Trump stands on the other with an open chest of precious-metal coins. Between them a yellow-brick path runs toward a seal reading The New Money Revolution. The Tin Man asks if the searcher found what was sought in the Emerald City. Beside Trump the answer is direct: the nation has always had the power to issue its own debt-free money, and simply did not believe it.

The frame binds gold and sovereignty to the Emerald City. Offered is not another bailout or another layer of interest-bearing debt, but sovereign, asset-backed, debt-free issuance.

Decoders treat Oz as ounces, and ounces as gold. The yellow brick road is read as ingot bars, a path back to honest money rather than deeper into the banking temple. The Emerald City is read as the Federal Reserve, where the answer was supposed to live and where the graphic says it was never found. Authority to issue debt-free money was not granted by that city. It was already held.

The companions map onto law, labor, and power. The Scarecrow becomes the straw man, a legal fiction created in the spelling of a birth name and handed a certificate in place of a brain. The Tin Man is tied to the taxpayer identification number and to the worker who pulls the plow until the body seizes. The Cowardly Lion is authority without courage, given a medal that changed status on paper and not in nature. The poppy field is narcotic control. The flying monkeys are agents of the system.

Then the curtain comes down. Toto, small enough that the spectacle ignored him, pulls it back. Behind the smoke sits an ordinary operator running the illusion. The charade ends: a con whose authority lasted only while people believed the system held powers it did not possess. The power was always there.

Dorothy’s ending is the match. She received no new authority from the city. She clicked her heels. She already had the way home, back to Kansas, the real land and the republic, and a route to liquidate the banking cartel rather than petition it. A brain, a heart, and courage, with people working together, are what remains. Follow the Yellow Brick Road. Look behind the curtain.

text:
I just realized that we might have a potential gap in the "reindustrialize" movement: 

Recycling.   

No, I'm not talking about the people who come and pick up your green bins once per week. What’s still missing from the reindustrialize effort is closed-loop material recovery inside American factories.

Every year American factories generate tens of millions of tons of “new scrap”- high-quality metal chips, turnings, and plastic offcuts created directly on the production floor- yet they routinely sell that material at steep discounts (often recovering only 40–70 % of virgin value) while immediately buying full-price replacement stock, creating a multi-billion-dollar annual leakage in material margin. When handling, storage, and logistics are added, a single mid-sized machine shop can easily forfeit hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, and across the sector the aggregate waste of recoverable value probably runs into the tens of billions, all while the United States remains 50-60% import-reliant on aluminum and copper. 

We need to simultaneously improve profitability of our companies, while also increasing the domestic supply of materials. We can't solve the latter with in-house recycling, but we can add a little headroom until we scale up our mineral extraction to meet our upcoming needs.

As it stands, material waste is profit destruction and a structural competitive disadvantage that no serious manufacturer or reindustrialization strategy seems to be addressing, and although it's been ignored, I don't think it should be. 

The tools for this already exist. They just live in the enthusiast and maker world, not yet on the factory floor.

Plastic recycling is the most mature example. Desktop and benchtop filament extruders (Filabot, 3devo, and a dozen open-source Precious Plastic derivatives) already take failed prints, sprues, and industrial plastic scrap, shred them, and re-extrude calibrated filament or pellets. 

Small injection-molding and compression-molding machines built from the same open-source ecosystem can turn that recycled material straight back into fixtures, jigs, or even short-run production parts. These systems cost a few thousand dollars, run on single-phase power, and are operated daily by hobbyists and small workshops.

Metal recovery is further along than most people realize. Hobby-scale induction furnaces and resistance melters routinely process aluminum, copper, and brass chips into clean ingots. Simple chip briquetters and centrifuges remove cutting fluid and compact shavings so they can be remelted with minimal loss. 

Solid-state processes- extrusion of compacted chips or friction-stir consolidation- are already demonstrated at laboratory and maker scales. The metallurgy is understood, the machines are just small (which is good) and not hardened (which is bad).

Even electronics scrap has workable entry points, but this is best saved for later.

These capabilities are real, proven, and relatively inexpensive. What does not exist is a company whose sole job is to take that enthusiast-grade technology, harden it to industrial duty cycles, package it as turnkey “recycling capability modules,” and install it inside working factories.

That is the startup opportunity...
so, what would this theoretical startup actually do?

1. Select the best open and commercial maker-scale platforms for plastic reprocessing, metal-chip consolidation/remelting, and basic e-scrap separation.

2. Engineer them for continuous or high-duty operation: better filtration, automated material handling, real-time quality monitoring, safety interlocks, and integration with existing factory MES/ERP systems.

3. Offer modular cells sized for typical job-shop or mid-volume production volumes- something a plant can drop in next to the CNC bank or the print farm and start recovering material within weeks, not years.

4. Provide operator training so the recovered feedstock is accepted back into use for prototyping without quality excuses.

5. Price the offering as a capability, not a science project: capital equipment + service contract that is justified by reduced scrap disposal costs and lower virgin-material purchases.

6. Continuously iterate with new processes, new hardware, and an endless push to get to the point where  on-site material processes can be used to recycle materials into *production* feedstock, ultimately eliminating production slippage for material overhead.

Factories do not need another sustainability consultant. They need a vendor that shows up with a working system, connects it to their waste streams, and leaves them with a new internal capability: the ability to turn their own process waste back into inventory.

Which is where the awful term "AI" comes in... not so much an LLM as it is an algorithmically enabled sensor & sorting suite that serves as the entry point for these machines- a single machine that takes a bag of material waste dumped in, sorts, and spits it into usable piles for entry into the rest of the system. 

In fact, other startups are doing this step, and done so successfully, but just on the "utility" scale, intended for city-wide recycling programs- not a small/medium scale machine that can be produced at relatively low cost, and not one designed specifically for factory use. 

This would eliminate the manual labor, and allow the system to be largely automated. I am highly confident that it is much easier to scale up a recycling system than it is to scale down, so these existing green-tech startups aren't going to be able to address this problem particularly well.

And if all of these systems work well enough, we will eventually move from the "I can turn your waste into prototype material" to "I can turn your waste into production material".  We can't sell this to companies as a turnkey solution to eliminate all waste right off the bat, but we can help them reduce the cost of R&D by making material for them, or even offer to buy these recovered materials for consumer sale if the company does not need R&D materials. 

From there, we use our profits to invest in delivering them the full capabilities of manufacturing recycling as a method of producing production-grade feedstock.

The enthusiast world has already done the hard part of proving the physics and the basic machinery. The missing piece is industrial packaging, reliability engineering, and a company that treats on-site recycling as its only product. The sorting problem can come later. 

That is how, in my uninformed opinion, the reindustrialize movement stops leaking value out the back door of every factory it builds.

Today was a day our family will never forget.

Standing at the groundbreaking of the Gassen Family Fieldhouse was both humbling and surreal. I especially want to recognize Denny Sanford, whose extraordinary generosity made this project a reality. We miss him every day, and moments like this make that absence felt even more deeply. We would not have been celebrating this groundbreaking today if not for Denny and his commitment to creating opportunities for others.

More than 25 years ago, my wife Jill and I arrived at the @usd as student-athletes. Little did we know how profoundly this university would shape our lives. It's where we earned our degrees, competed for the Coyotes, built lifelong friendships and began building our life together.

When I think back on those years, I remember the competitions and long days of training, but mostly, I remember the people. The teammates who became lifelong friends. The coaches and educators who challenged us, believed in us and helped us see possibilities for our future that we couldn't yet see ourselves.

We want future USD student-athletes to have the same opportunities we were blessed to receive. Opportunities to pursue their dreams, build lifelong relationships and develop the skills and confidence that will serve them for years to come.

Having our family name associated with this facility is an honor we do not take lightly. It serves as a reminder of our responsibility to give back to the institutions that helped shape our lives and to invest in future generations.

Denny's impact will be felt by USD students and student-athletes for generations to come, and our family is grateful to play a small role in helping continue that legacy.

On behalf of our family, thank you to everyone who helped make this day possible.

text:
The scientific approach adopted early on in the West is incompatible with any revealed truth, and thus with any immutable religious dogma, that alleviates metaphysical anxiety by precisely outlining the path to salvation.

This movement emerged at least nine centuries ago with the medieval university, an institution managed by its students. Knowledge was no longer viewed from the outset as something revealed. The aim was to break free from arbitrariness by uncovering the author's intent or examining the transmission of what was presented as true—in short, a process of deconstruction interpreted as a sound "quest for Truth."

This movement stands in opposition to the earlier one rooted in revealed truths and reconciling the two is difficult, leading to inevitable tensions.

This fostered a "polytheism of values" that compartmentalized different spheres—a state of affairs incompatible with any doctrine claiming to be total, all-encompassing, or universal.

Science offers a means to forecast events and build systems for prediction or production optimization, thereby enabling greater mastery over the world, the shaping of the future, and the immediate alleviation of anxiety regarding scarcity.

From the Renaissance through the early twentieth century, many hoped that science would provide objective, solid (verifiable and coherent) explanations for everything. By dispelling metaphysical inquiry and answering every question, it was expected to supplant revealed truths and thereby soothe metaphysical anxiety as well.

In the early 1930s, however, the work of K. Gödel (incompleteness theorems) and W. Heisenberg (uncertainty principle) abruptly dashed this hope, the consequences of which had already been heralded by  "God is dead." The technical system survived, a response solely to the fear of scarcity and lacking a foundation, thereby imperceptibly fostering anxiety and nihilism in the absence of hope, fueling deconstruction, a systematization of doubt that, while highly effective in science, extends to everything (the subject, representation, relationships, and so on), dismantling even rationality itself. This is done illegitimately, this is an abuse because it yields irrefutable assertions and therefore is out of the scientific perimeter (a point also raised in the 1930s by Karl Popper). This trend has culminated since the 1960s in "French Theory."

The resulting *tabula rasa* leads directly to the political constructivism of our time, which likewise churns out a "revealed truth" presented as a mere factual observation.
