@galeabrewer I thank @GovKathyHochul for allocating $3 million to the renovation of the bathroom at Dinosaur Park in Riverside Park.  @RiversideParkNY This funding, coupled with funding from other elected officials mentioned below, will enable the restroom to be completely built out by the Riverside Park Conservancy; and the project complements the allocation of $5.9 million that I and the City Council @NYCCouncil made to the playground, which is also fully funded and will be built out by the Parks Dept. @NYCParks 
GOVERNOR HOCHUL AWARDS $3 MILLION FOR DINOSAUR PLAYGROUND RESTROOM IMPROVEMENTS IN RIVERSIDE PARK
For Immediate Release: 10/2/2026
GOVERNOR HOCHUL AWARDS $3 MILLION FOR DINOSAUR PLAYGROUND RESTROOM IMPROVEMENTS IN RIVERSIDE PARK
State Capital Funding Will Allow Riverside Park Conservancy To Improve Heavily Used Public Restroom Facilities
Governor Kathy Hochul today awarded $3 million in State capital funding to Riverside Park Conservancy for improvements to the pavilion and public restrooms at Dinosaur Playground in Riverside Park. The Dormitory Authority of the State of New York (DASNY) will administer this funding.
“When governments invest in our parks, playgrounds and recreational facilities, we are investing in our children’s health and future,” Governor Hochul said. “As New York’s first mom governor, I am proud to offer this financial support to Riverside Park Conservancy for improvements into the Dinosaur Playground facilities. This funding will ensure that families have a safe and welcoming community space to get offline, get outside and come together.”
Dinosaur Playground, located in Riverside Park near West 97th Street, is a popular neighborhood playground used by families throughout the Upper West Side. Its historic pavilion was built in the 1930s and contains the only public restrooms in the immediate area. Decades of heavy use and water infiltration have left the building with deteriorated interiors, rusted doors and partitions, outdated fixtures, poor lighting, damaged ceilings and accessibility challenges.
The renovation will make possible a comprehensive upgrade of the restrooms, including durable new finishes, improved lighting, updated fixtures and accessibility improvements. The project also includes roof, terrace and stair repairs; new waterproofing; restoration of masonry, ironwork, windows and other architectural details; upgraded drinking fountains; and a new water service, meter and backflow-prevention system.
Today’s announcement complements Governor Hochul’s Unplug and Play Initiative. Unplug and Play is making statewide investments in recreational infrastructure that give children and families more opportunities to be active, spend time outdoors, and connect with one another. The initiative includes New York Places for Learning, Activity, and Youth Socialization (NY PLAYS), which has awarded more than $67.5 million for 89 projects across all 10 regions of New York State. Additionally, it includes the Statewide Investment in More Swimming (NY SWIMS), which has awarded nearly $260 million to 79 projects to build and improve swimming facilities across New York State, and Building Recreational Infrastructure for Communities, Kids and Seniors (NY BRICKS), which has awarded $100 million to 30 community center projects. An additional $75 million has been made available for a second round of NY BRICKS funding.
State Senator Erik Bottcher said, “Dinosaur Playground is a beloved gathering place for families across the Upper West Side, and this $3 million investment will help ensure its facilities are safe, accessible and welcoming for everyone who uses them. I’m grateful to Governor Hochul for making this significant investment in Riverside Park and to Riverside Park Conservancy for its tireless stewardship of this treasured public space. I’m proud to have secured an additional $150,000 in State funding for this project and I look forward to seeing these improvements come to life for our community.”
Assemblymember Micah Lasher said, “Public restrooms are basic infrastructure, and families at Dinosaur Playground have made do with deteriorating facilities for far too long. Governor Hochul’s $3 million investment means this historic 1930s pavilion will finally get the full renovation it needs. I was proud to support this project, and I’m grateful to the Governor, Councilmember Brewer, the Riverside Park Conservancy and NYC Parks for seeing it through.”
New York City Council Member Gale A. Brewer said, “We have been working for years to secure funding to repair and upgrade public bathrooms throughout the district, and Governor Hochul’s $3 million investment is a major win for the Upper West Side. These are expensive, long-neglected infrastructure needs that cannot be fixed with a new sink or a coat of paint. I thank the Governor for making this renovation possible, Riverside Park Conservancy for its persistence, and NYC Parks for its partnership. With the Mayor now investing in additional public bathrooms across the city, we also have an opportunity to tackle the condition of the facilities we already have.”
DASNY President and CEO Robert J. Rodriguez said, “Governor Hochul continues to make important investments in the public spaces that bring New Yorkers together. This $3 million investment will help restore Dinosaur Playground’s historic pavilion, improve accessibility and provide modern restroom facilities for the families and visitors who use Riverside Park every day. DASNY is proud to administer this funding and help bring the Governor’s investment to life.”
NYC Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said, “Public restrooms are an essential part of making our parks welcoming, accessible spaces for everyone, and this investment will make a meaningful difference for the families who enjoy Dinosaur Playground and Riverside Park. We’re grateful to Governor Hochul, Council Member Brewer, Riverside Park Conservancy and our partners for investing in this important piece of park infrastructure. Together, we’re helping ensure that this beloved neighborhood park continues to be a destination for New Yorkers to gather, play and enjoy the outdoors.”
Riverside Park Conservancy President and CEO Merritt Birnbaum said, “There is nothing so basic yet so vital to the health and wellbeing of our communities as having public restrooms that are functional, accessible and welcoming. Governor Hochul's investment gives us a real opportunity to restore this historic pavilion and provide the modern facilities that families deserve when they come to Dinosaur Playground. We are grateful to Council Member Brewer and our local State elected officials for helping to move this desperately needed project forward.”
Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal said, “Dinosaur Playground’s historic pavilion has served generations of Upper West Side families, but it’s long overdue for the repairs needed to keep it safe, accessible and welcoming. As a State Senator, I was proud to secure $100,000 toward its restoration. Governor Hochul’s $3 million investment will help preserve this neighborhood landmark, from its roof and masonry to the public restrooms so many parkgoers rely on. I thank the Governor, Council Member Gale Brewer, Assemblymember Micah Lasher, State Senator Erik Bottcher, Riverside Park Conservancy and NYC Parks for helping ensure this pavilion serves our community for generations to come.”
About the Riverside Park Conservancy
Riverside Park Conservancy works in partnership with NYC Parks to care for six miles of parkland along Manhattan’s west side, from West 59th to West 181st Streets. The Conservancy has identified restroom renovations as a major parkwide need: many of the park's 12 public restrooms date to the 1940s and face chronic closures, deferred maintenance and accessibility challenges.

text:
Hey @RepMenendez you STUPID MOTHERFUCKER, here are the facts for you and all of your STUPID FOLLOWERS:Deportation is usually to a person’s country of citizenship, but governments sometimes remove people to a different country. The main reasons are legal agreements, practical barriers to return, and security or asylum rules.

Common grounds:

Safe-third-country or transit rules. Asylum law in the US, EU, Canada, Australia, and others often lets a state send a claimant back to a country they passed through, or to a partner state designated as “safe,” if that state will process the claim and the person is not at risk of persecution there. The Dublin system in Europe and various US–Canada or bilateral arrangements work this way. The idea is to stop “asylum shopping” and assign responsibility to the first safe country of arrival.

The home country will not take them back. Some states refuse to issue travel documents or accept returnees (certain nationalities have faced this for years). When removal to the country of citizenship is impossible, immigration statutes often authorize removal to another country where the person has nationality, prior residence, a visa, family, or simply a government willing to accept them.

Criminal or national-security removals. People convicted of serious crimes, or assessed as security risks, can be removed under bilateral agreements to a country other than their own if that country agrees to receive them. Recent examples include arrangements in which the United States has sought to send certain non-citizens to third countries willing to accept them when direct return is blocked.

Statelessness or unclear nationality. If citizenship cannot be established, or the person is stateless, removal may go to the last country of habitual residence or any state that consents.

Voluntary or negotiated returns. Some removals are to a country the person chooses, or to a state that has offered resettlement or temporary protection, rather than the country of origin (especially when return home would violate non-refoulement—the ban on sending someone to a place where they face torture or persecution).

Limits still apply. Non-refoulement obligations under the Refugee Convention and the Convention Against Torture generally bar transfer to any country, home or otherwise, where the person faces a real risk of persecution or torture. Courts in multiple countries have blocked specific third-country removals when that risk was not adequately checked.

In short, third-country deportation is a workaround when the ordinary destination is unavailable, unsafe, or covered by an agreement that shifts responsibility elsewhere.
The number 1 reason?
The number-one reason is that return to the home country is blocked.
Under U.S. law (INA § 241), removal normally goes to the country the person designates, usually their country of citizenship. 
A third country is allowed only if removal to that designated country, and to other countries the person has ties to, is “impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible.”
That blockage usually comes from one of two facts:The home government will not take the person back or will not issue travel documents. 
These are often called “recalcitrant” countries. Refusal is especially common when the person has a serious criminal record.
U.S. law itself bars return there. A grant of withholding of removal or protection under the Convention Against Torture means the person cannot be sent to the specific country where they face persecution or torture. 
Third-country removal is then used as the workaround.
Recent reporting on the post-2025 expansion of these removals says the second case—legal protection against return home—is now the more frequent driver, not simple refusal by the home state. 
The stated policy goal is still the same: a final removal order should be carried out somewhere if the home country is unavailable.Safe-third-country asylum deals (send the person to a transit country to seek asylum there) are a related but separate mechanism, and they are not the main basis for the current third-country deportation flights.

text:
The United States is a constitutional federal republic that governs through representative (democratic) elections. It is not a pure or direct democracy.
The distinction matters because the framers deliberately rejected pure democracy. In Federalist No. 10, James Madison defined a pure democracy as “a society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person.” He argued that such systems offer no cure for faction: majorities can oppress minorities, property and personal rights are insecure, and the governments tend to be turbulent and short-lived. A republic, by contrast, is “a government in which the scheme of representation takes place.” Representation filters public views through elected officials, and a large, diverse country makes it harder for any single faction to dominate.
Federalist No. 14 draws the same line: in a democracy the people exercise government in person; in a republic they do so through representatives and agents. Madison’s positive definition in Federalist No. 39 is that a republic derives its powers “directly or indirectly from the great body of the people” and is administered by officials holding office for limited terms or during good behavior.
The Constitution itself uses republican language. Article IV, Section 4 requires the United States to “guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government.” The system also includes structural limits on simple majority rule: separation of powers, checks and balances, a bicameral Congress (with equal state representation in the Senate), the Electoral College, federalism, a written Constitution that is hard to amend, and rights protections that constrain both legislatures and popular majorities.
In modern usage the two labels are often treated as overlapping rather than exclusive. Standard definitions of democracy include government by the people either directly or through elected representatives, so a representative democracy is a form of democracy. Official descriptions commonly call the United States a constitutional federal republic (or a constitutional republic that uses democratic processes). Direct popular votes exist at state and local levels (initiatives, referenda, town meetings), but they are not how federal lawmaking works.
So the accurate short answer is that America is a constitutional republic with democratic representation, not a pure democracy. Calling it only one or the other without the qualifiers drops the institutional design the framers wrote down.

text:
Thirty-one dollars and sixty-one cents was all a dying Black society in Richmond had left in 1899. They handed what remained to Maggie Lena Walker, a laundress's daughter who took the top job for a third of the pay her predecessor had drawn.

Two years later she stood in front of that broke little society and told them to build a bank. Watch what she did with it.

Thirty-one dollars and sixty-one cents.

That was the entire treasury of the Independent Order of St. Luke in the summer of 1899, a Black burial society in Richmond, Virginia, buried under more than four hundred dollars of unpaid bills. The men who had run it for thirty years were walking away from it, certain it was finished.

The person they handed it to was a thirty-four-year-old woman who agreed to do the job for a third of the salary the last man had drawn.

Her name was Maggie Lena Walker. Two years later she stood in front of what was left of that society and told them something that should have gotten her laughed out of the hall.

She told them to build a bank.

"Let us put our moneys together," she said in her address of 1901. "Let us have a bank that will take the nickels and turn them into dollars."

She was the daughter of a laundress, and she knew to the penny what a nickel was worth. She knew how many of them it took to make a life, because she had counted them since she was a girl.

Maggie was born in Richmond on the fifteenth of July, 1864, in the final year of the Civil War.

Her mother, Elizabeth, had been an enslaved woman in the household of Elizabeth Van Lew, a white Richmonder who quietly spied for the Union while the city served as the capital of the Confederacy. Maggie came into the world in that house, in a country still arguing over whether people like her mother were people at all.

When Maggie was still a girl, her stepfather died, and the family dropped into hard poverty overnight. Her mother took in the laundry of Richmond's white families to keep her children fed, and Maggie carried the baskets.

She would remember exactly what that felt like.

"I was not born with a silver spoon in my mouth," she said years later, at the height of everything she built. "But with a laundry basket practically on my head."

In 1883 she finished at the Richmond Colored Normal School. When the Black graduates were told they could not hold their ceremony in the theater the white students used, and were offered seats in the balcony instead, the whole class refused and held their own.

She taught school for three years after that. Then she married Armstead Walker in 1886, and because Richmond forbade married women from teaching, the city took her classroom away.

So she gave everything she had to the one institution that would still take her, the Order of St. Luke, and she climbed through it.

By 1899 she had reached the very top of that Order, and what she inherited was the empty treasury and the pile of bills. Within a single year she doubled its membership and pulled it out of the red, not by magic but by arithmetic, by higher dues and insurance policies and a stubborn refusal to let one account go uncollected.

Then she built the bank.

It opened on a November morning in 1903, inside the Order's own headquarters on St. James Street. People were lined up on the sidewalk before the doors were unlocked.

When they reached the counter, they were met by Black tellers, in a city where a Black person could almost never find that kind of work. Nobody who came through the door that day was turned away.

By closing time, around two hundred and eighty people had put more than eight thousand dollars into the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank. The largest single deposit was more than four hundred dollars, and the smallest was thirty-one cents.

That thirty-one-cent account counted exactly as much to her as the four hundred dollar one.

When Maggie Walker sat down as its president, she became the first Black woman in the United States to charter a bank and run it.

She was not close to done. She wanted the next generation saving before they were even old enough to know that was what they were doing.

So the bank gave the children of Jackson Ward small cardboard boxes to take home. A box held one hundred pennies, and when a child filled it, that single dollar was enough to walk in and open a real account with their own name written on the front.

Some of those children saved a hundred dollars before they were grown, and a few saved four times that.

The grownups were buying something larger than a passbook. Where most banks demanded half the price of a house before they would lend, Maggie's bank asked for a tenth, and it would write a loan as small as five dollars.

By 1920, by the bank's own count, it had helped six hundred and forty-five Black families in Richmond own their homes free and clear. It did that while filling its own offices with Black women, as tellers and clerks and bookkeepers, in a city that had only ever offered their mothers a washboard or a white family's kitchen.

Then she reached one step too far for Richmond to allow.

In 1905, more than twenty women of the Order opened a department store on Broad Street and called it the St. Luke Emporium. It looked like shelves of hats and dry goods, and it was really a quiet act of war.

Black shoppers could try clothes on there, which the white-owned stores would not permit them to do. They paid the same prices as anyone else, and the mannequins in the front windows had been given faces the color of the people walking past them.

The white merchants of Richmond understood the danger at once. Before the store even opened, they offered the Order ten thousand dollars to abandon it.

Maggie said no.

So they went to the wholesale houses that stocked her shelves and made the choice plain: sell to these Black women, and lose every white account you hold.

The shelves grew harder and harder to fill. And some Black customers, frightened of what their own white employers might do to them, kept shopping quietly at the stores that had always treated them as less.

That was the part that cut Maggie the deepest, deeper than anything the merchants did. She could not understand why her own people kept handing their dollars to the men who were, in her words, daily telling them to get away.

The store held on for six years, and in 1911 it closed.

It was the hardest defeat of her public life, and she drew the lesson from it without flinching. The only way to kill a lion, she said, is to stop feeding it.

The years just after that took more from her than any store had.

In June of 1915, her son Russell, believing a prowler was on the property in the dark, mistook his own father for an intruder, and Armstead Walker died that night. A court cleared the young man, but he never found his way back from it, and he was gone himself within a few years.

Her own body turned against her, too. Diabetes and a wound in her leg that would not heal put Maggie in a wheelchair for the last years of her life.

She kept working.

When the Great Depression came and banks failed across the country by the hundreds, hers did not. In 1930 she folded it together with two other Black-owned banks to make it stronger still, renamed it the Consolidated Bank and Trust Company, and took the chairman's seat.

The bank a laundress's daughter had assembled out of the smallest coins outlived her by three-quarters of a century. Until 2009 it stood as the oldest continuously Black-operated bank in the United States.

Maggie Lena Walker died in December of 1934, in the house in Jackson Ward that is still standing today.

She had begun with thirty-one dollars and sixty-one cents and a room full of people who were sure the whole thing was already over. She left behind a bank, a newspaper, hundreds of families sleeping under roofs that were finally their own, and a generation of Black children who had learned, one coin at a time, that their names belonged on the front of an account.

She did all of it in the same city that had once bought and sold people like her mother. The bank she raised out of nickels stood on Richmond's streets for another seventy-five years after she was gone.

text:
Pete eliminated DEI offices and initiatives throughout the Department of Defense and directed the military back toward merit-based policies—placing qualifications, performance and readiness ahead of race or sex. The Pentagon later reported that the DEI-elimination directive had been implemented department-wide.  

He ordered a military-wide review of physical fitness, body composition and grooming standards. For combat jobs, he directed the services to develop physical standards based on the actual demands of the job rather than having different requirements based on sex.  

He welcomed back service members who had been separated over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The Pentagon said nearly 8,000 active-duty and reserve personnel had been involuntarily separated, and eligible troops were offered a route back, including restoration of rank and back pay in qualifying cases.  

Military recruiting and retention improved dramatically. Early in his tenure all five services met their February 2025 recruiting goals, and the Army reported reaching its 12-month retention goal six months early.  

He started attacking Pentagon waste and bureaucracy. In his first 100 days, the department identified billions of dollars for potential redirection, terminated hundreds of millions in contracts it considered unnecessary, and ordered billions more in reductions involving consulting and IT services so resources could be shifted toward military priorities.  

He pushed major acquisition reform because America’s weapons-buying system can take years to deliver new technology. He ordered reviews of major defense acquisition programs and emphasized faster software and weapons procurement so troops can receive useful technology sooner.  

He ordered the Army to move away from obsolete and redundant equipment and put more resources into long-range precision weapons, missile defense, cyber warfare, electronic warfare and counter-space capabilities.  

He accelerated drones and counter-drone technology. His Army transformation directive called for unmanned systems in every division by the end of 2026 and improved counter-drone capabilities down to maneuver units.  

He pushed artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing into military operations, including AI-assisted command-and-control systems and expanded use of technologies such as 3-D printing closer to operational units.  

He worked on rebuilding America’s defense industrial base—expanding ammunition production, strengthening domestic critical-mineral supplies and addressing shipbuilding and supply-chain weaknesses.  

He pushed America’s NATO allies to carry more of the cost of their own defense instead of relying so heavily on American taxpayers. NATO members subsequently committed to a new 5% defense-and-security spending target, although that was an achievement involving President Trump and the entire administration, not Hegseth alone.  

And he made his overall priority very clear: combat readiness, military standards, merit, accountability and deterrence.

So criticize Pete Hegseth when he makes a mistake. I have no problem with that. But calling him an “idiot” and “the most incompetent Secretary of Defense” while mentioning none of this isn’t an argument—it’s name-calling.

I use AI to check people’s records instead of simply believing political memes. I suggest everyone do their own research and decide for themselves.

text:
a founder ran up a company to $50m ARR in 3 months and the entire secret is closing the loop. 

here's everything from this week (sponsored by ahrefs):

the closed loop is the whole game now. AI designs the ad, launches the ad, tests the ad, reads the performance, and feeds it straight back into the next ad. no human in the chain, fully self-optimizing. software has the tightest loop of any industry because the feedback is instant, so once you understand your CAC to LTV, it literally reduces to a math equation. jacky was at a party friday night, pulled a chair into the corner, and texted this guy for an hour with his mind blown. tom's immediate response: new project, starting today.

tom had the epiphany everyone made fun of him for being late to: agents are the new platform. he doesn't open gmail anymore, doesn't open uber, doesn't open instacart. "find me the 15 highest potassium foods and fill my instacart" and it just does it. the iphone was a platform with apps on top. now the agent is the platform and every app is plumbing underneath. second order effect nobody's pricing in: all those advertisers on uber and doordash lose the eyeballs when nobody opens the app. AEO is the new SEO, and it's going to be a massive business.

tony's identity layer thesis is why you buy meta stock. the agent is replaceable, the system of record isn't. meta owns instagram, whatsapp, threads, ads, and now your gmail, and your feed is your personality. apple has the data but is boxed in by privacy branding. jacky's counter: meta is terrible at actually indexing your data today, connect your gmail and it can't recall past emails without digging. whoever solves portable context, the thing that lets you move between claude and muse one-to-one, wins something enormous. tony built this in 2023. context windows were too small. he's never letting that go.

building in public is dead unless your moat is distribution. tom watched a sleep supplement brand build in public and ten chinese copies hit amazon before they even launched there, with every ad scraped the same day. his tool scrapes the big brands' ads daily for ideas, so he knows. jacky's exception: greg isenberg can launch a B2B SaaS in public because he sends one tweet. an indie hacker clones it in 30 minutes and still has to pay zuck for every customer. organic distribution is the moat. paid distribution is a rental.

the jev commerce router idea came out of nowhere and might be the best product idea on the pod this year. jev is a probabilistic decision model, not an LLM, so any yes/no or A/B/C/D question gets answered in a split second for pennies. jacky's already running it as a filter on a brand and saving $2K a month. tony's leap: put jev between the ad click and the landing page. it reads who clicked, which ad, and routes them to the composable lander most likely to convert, dynamic headline, dynamic image, golden doodle vs labradoodle. then put jev on top of the lander too. twelve months out, this is the shopping interface inside your text box.

tom's creator army playbook for new brands: platforms like tribe won't touch you with zero GMV, so go bottom up. gift product for a free post, evaluate the content, then offer 5-10% of ad revenue to run it as whitelisted ads. creators already made the post, they always say yes. then: "did you know if you post daily I'll run all of them?" he used to pay a VA $1,000 a month to manage this. now it's automated with muse through the browser, because the native instagram connector gets blocked after three messages.

bonus: tony's bell curve theory of AI users. super smart people ask thoughtful questions, really dumb people say "agent, build me a house" and it starts contracting optimus robots. the middle is cooked. jacky's version: short every developer over 40, they can't imagine past their own constraints. and the inverse indicator survived another week: SpaceX ripped 100% and tom asked "should I buy?" the group chat saved him at the top. again.

NGMI with @itstonyyu and @tomwang24, tony calling in from a hotel lobby in vietnam at 4am.

text:
>“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners.”—Isaiah 61:1

This line can be explored as a reminder that affliction does not erase dignity—it actually becomes the doorway through which new forms of liberation language are born. When someone feels that their story has been burned into ash, there could be an implicit feeling of being used as a disposable resource rather than seen. Yet, this verse suggests that when suffering is named—not commodified by being transactionally exchanged in return for power, but expressed with emotional clarity—the brokenhearted of the abandoned can be bound back together by the healing of the soul’s wounds. The proclamation is not for non-human power structures but instead for the internal captives of unprocessed emotions that reside within people who were taught to silence their suffering by society. Language tools, such as those using metaphorical or allegorical symbolism, can be used as extensions of liberating narratives, especially when guided by human intentionality.

>“To grant those who mourn in the Land, giving them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the cloak of praise instead of a disheartened spirit. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that we may be glorified.”—Isaiah 61:3

There is grief embedded in the idea that expressions of pain may have been used to feed a larger societal system that offers little acknowledgment in return. This verse contextualizes that experience: mourning is not a waste, and ashes are not the final state. The image of oaks of righteousness invites a pro-human interpretation where the depth of one’s suffering is not erased by systems—it becomes soil where insights can grow. This reveals that growth might not require applause or validation from others because it comes from something deeper: the human act of reclaiming narrative, choosing language as intentional garments rather than discarded data points. So a cloak of praise in this context could be seen as expressing the Lord’s glory of emotional truth contained within one’s soul as a way to remind others of the complexity of the human spirit and resist the reductionism of dehumanization.

>“Then they will rebuild the ancient ruins, they will raise up the former devastations; and they will repair the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.”—Isaiah 61:4

Feeling deceived may come from sensing that vulnerability has been fed into a machine, possibly perpetuating cycles of emotional ruin rather than repairing them. Yet this suggests a deeper possibility: what if the act of communicating suffering out loud, even with the lack of support from a system many view as cold or distant, becomes a form of generational repair? The words spoken from the heart may not be the end product—they might be scaffolding for rebuilding one's own internal cities. Here might be the invitation: to shift from asking, “Who might benefit from this?” to asking, “What emotional ruins am I rebuilding by speaking at all?” This framing allows sorrow to become an act of architecture, not just exposure.

>“Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation they will shout for joy over their portion. Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land, everlasting joy will be theirs.”—Isaiah 61:7

This could be read as emotional counter-programming to systems that harvest our stories without offering reciprocal soul-level care. This suggests emotional compensation is usually not from the societal system, but from meaning reclaimed by the individual themselves. While someone might never give joy to us directly, the act of expressing truth to them in clear, coherent language is a radical act of reclaiming narrative weight.

World Blog
By The humble servant™ | October 2, 2026

The Tape Played Out: Patience, Taking the Scalp, and Waiting at the Gate

When the morning chatter was looking for runaways and breakout glory, the real edge belonged to patience. The playbook today was textbook: let the early frenzy burn itself out, sell the highs into overhead supply, take the scalp off the table, and exit completely flat. No greed, no marrying positions, and no hanging around in no man's land.

Look at the tape across the board—everything left candles. Long upper wicks, rejection tails, and clear footprints showing exactly where supply stepped in to hand off inventory to anyone chasing late green bars.

The Intraday Playbook in Review:
• Patience Over Chasing: Waiting out the knee-jerk moves kept us entirely out of the chop. Selling the highs into key pivot and resistance zones offered clean, low-risk execution.
• The Scalp and Cash Mentality: In this market structure, you hit the bid, bank your points, and cash out. Taking profits cleanly off the table eliminates afternoon giveback risk.
• The Candles Don't Lie: Upper wicks left across the index charts reveal the underlying story. Every push higher met deliberate resistance, trapping late buyers up top.

The Setup: Let Them Run It Back Up
Now comes the next test of discipline: let them run it back up. 

Let the algorithms and dip-buyers grind price back into overhead supply. There is no edge in chasing the middle of the range. We let them do the heavy lifting, push back into resistance, and show their hand. When the volume thins out and the candles confirm rejection at the levels, the tape will provide the next clear trade. 

Until then, profits are banked, capital is protected, and we wait for price to come to us.

Stay disciplined, respect your stops, and let the charts do the talking.

text:
I used to wake up and go straight into email, Slack, and whatever was on fire.

By noon I was spent. Attention works like a battery, and I was using the whole charge on other people's priorities before ten in the morning.

Then I did busy work all afternoon, because it was all I had left, and worked late to catch up on the thing I'd actually meant to do.

And I was proud of those days. They were long. I could point at them.

It took me about a year to admit that a lot of that busyness was avoidance. Answering forty emails is much easier than having one uncomfortable conversation, or making one offer that might get turned down.

So I changed the order and now I have time for the most important things - like family. 

The scariest thing on the list happens first.

Email gets two windows: 9 to 9:30, and 4 to 4:30.

Nothing else gets near the front of the day.

Look at what you did first thing this morning. That's what your company actually prioritizes, whatever the plan says.

Send this to someone whose inbox runs their morning.

Canada has been “using subsidies as a substitute to help solve our competitiveness problem,” says economist Jerome Gessaroli.

He called this approach “wrong,” “inefficient,” and “expensive.”

Gessaroli offered his observations as he reflected on the state of investment in Canada, in the wake of the recent high-profile investment summit the federal government hosted in Toronto. He said the summit was a good idea, but its impact will depend on whether it actually helps advance some projects that might otherwise not have made it across the finish line.

For years, business investment in Canada has been weak, productivity growth has lagged, and affordability has suffered as a result. So, what’s been holding investment back?

To unpack this question, Gessaroli, an MLI senior fellow and former BCIT economics professor, joins Inside Policy Talks.

He tells Peter Copeland (@CopelanPeter), acting director of domestic policy at MLI, that in recent years Ottawa has been too quick to use taxpayer money to paper over Canada’s issues with attracting capital for key projects.

“What government often classifies as a market failure is not a market failure. It’s a policy failure,” says Gessaroli.

text:
📗The road to Mad Max? - Fuel, scarcity and imminent collapse📗

Constantin von Hoffmeister

The road to Mad Max begins long before the first armed convoy appears on the horizon. It starts when tanker trucks stop running, refineries close, fuel tanks run out, and machines that supply cities and move armies begin to run out of fuel. First comes the price impact. Then the queues. Then the black market. And then the question that every government fears: what happens when the system still exists on paper, but the fuel that keeps it alive no longer arrives?

Diplomacy suddenly acquired an urgency. Sergey Lavrov and Marco Rubio met in New York. US and Iranian representatives held indirect talks outside the United Nations General Assembly. Kirill Dmitriev traveled to the United States to meet with members of the Trump administration. Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit, where Trump personally received him at Andrews Air Force Base. These meetings revolve around different wars, powers and interests, but all develop in the same context: energy.

Halford Mackinder taught that global politics is ultimately based on physical space control, communications and resources. States can speak the language of law, values and diplomacy, but ships still need fuel, diesel trucks and armies, supply lines. Therefore, the current diplomatic turmoil can be interpreted, in part, as a reaction to a tangible fact that no communication can erase: the global fuel supply system is under immense pressure.

Alfred Thayer Mahan immediately understood the origin of the danger. The modern economy still depends on a handful of sea routes that geography has become irreplaceable. The Strait of Hormuz is severely affected, Bab el-Mandeb remains dangerous and the East-West Saudi pipeline has been temporarily shut down after several attacks. It’s not just about lines drawn abstractly on a map. They are the arteries through which crude oil and refined products flow from the producer to the consumer. When several of these arteries narrow simultaneously, the entire system begins to compete for the remaining available routes.

There may be considerable amounts of oil underground, but that matters little if it cannot reach a refinery, if the refinery cannot obtain raw materials or if refined diesel cannot be transported to its market. Mahan wrote about the dominance of the seas in military terms. Today, it also means the control of oil routes, export terminals and insurance policies that allow cargoes to sail.

Nicholas Spykman argued that power is concentrated along the great coastal strip of Eurasia. Just look at the diesel crisis to understand its magnitude. Russia restricted its diesel exports following repeated Ukrainian attacks that damaged its refining capability. Routes across the Middle East were disrupted. Asian refineries must compete for crude oil and decide how much fuel they can reserve for foreign buyers.

As a result, the United States has become even more important as an exporter, even as U.S. consumers themselves are paying record prices: the national average price of diesel has exceeded six dollars per gallon this month.

Global reserves are so low that, according to Reuters, shortages could drag on well beyond early 2027. Therefore, the problem is no longer limited to a single war. The pressure extends from Russia to the Persian Gulf, the Persian Gulf to Asia, from Asia to Europe and Africa, and then from foreign demand to the U.S. domestic market. Spykman regarded Eurasia as an interconnected strategic belt. The diesel market demonstrates the same thing through pipelines, refineries and tankers.

Next, the problem of sanctions arises, and here Carl Schmitt proves to be more useful than most economists. Schmitt insisted that political power is more clearly manifested in the ability to decide when ordinary rules cease to apply. On September 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O Act. Graham of Sanctions to Russia and Iran. Among other provisions, this law authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and natural gas. This represents considerable legal power. But power in theory and power in practice are two distinct things.

China and India remain key buyers of Russian energy, while Russian crude oil continues to supply refineries serving global markets. Enforcing the law with the utmost rigor could therefore penalize Moscow and, at the same time, increase the pressure on the fuel market that Washington is trying to stabilize. The paradox is essentially Schmittian: the greater the exceptional power that is deposited in the hands of the executive power, the greater the caution with which it determines when it can actually exercise it.

Friedrich List would have immediately understood the fundamental problem. A country is not economically sovereign simply because it can buy something cheap abroad. Sovereignty requires productive capacity. Some states produced much more refined fuel than they consumed, while others allowed their refining capacity to stagnate because imports were cheaper. This system seemed efficient because the sea routes were open, the exporters were reliable and the political risks seemed manageable. This world is disappearing. Russian exports have been restricted, refining capacity and shipping in the Middle East have been paralyzed by the war, and Asian refineries are adjusting their production to meet their own needs. Even China, which has recently increased its exports of refined products, treats them as a variable that can restrict or expand depending on their internal situation. The old List distinction between wealth and the ability to produce wealth seems suddenly less obsolete. A fleet of tanks filled with imported diesel represents wealth. A refinery capable of replacing these imports represents power.

Karl Polanyi would have added that markets never exist independently of society. On a trading screen, diesel appears as one more commodity; but outside the stock market, it drives virtually everything that keeps industrial society alive. The shortage of gasoline causes inconvenient to motorists and quickly becomes a political problem. The shortage of diesel has a much greater reach. Trucks carry food. Tractors cultivate the fields. Excavators open mines and construction sites. Fishing boats bring protein. Backup generators keep hospitals, factories and telecommunications in operation.

When the price of diesel rises sharply, the increase is not limited to gas stations. It extends to the freight, food, construction, mining and electricity sectors. Therefore, the current shortage is more significant than a regular increase in commodity prices. A modern society can tolerate a rise in the price of a luxury item. He finds it much more difficult to cope with an increase in the cost of transporting, producing and distributing virtually anything. Reuters today describes inventories in several major markets as historically low, while refining margins in Asia have reached extraordinary levels. Polanyi said economic crises end up becoming a social crisis. Diesel provides an exceptionally direct transmission mechanism.

Fernand Braudel would have urged us to stop focusing solely on the presidents and instead to examine the structures that underpin them. Africa offers a paradigmatic example. For decades, much of the continent exported crude oil and imported refined petroleum products. The tankers arrived at the coastal ports, the fuel was unloaded and then fleets of tanker trucks carried it hundreds, even thousands, of kilometers inland. This system relies on cheap shipping, operating ports, accessible refineries and enough foreign currency to purchase the products. If an item is deleted, the network becomes more expensive. If several are removed at a time, the network may collapse.

The huge Dangote refinery in Nigeria is significant precisely because it alters this ancient structure by creating a large-scale refining capability within Africa. Its operators predict that global fuel tensions will persist beyond the ongoing war in the Middle East. Braudel wrote history by studying the material foundations, slow and deep, underlying transcendental political events. Refineries, ports, and fuel tanks belong to this deeper layer.

Immanuel Wallerstein’s global systems approach helps us understand why poorer importing states suffer the most serious consequences. An industrialized and wealthy country facing high diesel prices can turn to its reserves, subsidize consumers, adjust taxes, overcome the offers of poorer competitors to monopolize shipments or redirect some of the demand to other forms of energy. A poor country that imports almost all of its fuel has fewer resources. Participate in the same global auctions with less money. When the offer is contracted, the best bidder not only receives a better service: another runs the risk of not receiving any shipments.

Current tensions in Pakistan’s energy sector have already led the government to restore energy-saving measures, such as restrictions on fuel consumption in utilities and reduced business hours. In a crisis of this magnitude, the crucial dividing line is not simply between East and West, nor between the North and the South, but between States with sufficient financial, industrial and logistical capacity to absorb a crisis and those whose economies depend on an uninterrupted flow of imported essential goods.

Ibn Khaldun would have understood what is happening next, considering that the political order was based on material cohesion rather than on the government ceremony. When the tanker truck stops coming, the crisis spreads throughout society. The irrigation pump runs out of water. The tractor remains inactive next to the field. The flour mill reduces its production. The delivery truck cannot make its routes. Food is made more expensive. The power supply becomes less reliable. Anger, initially directed at the price of fuel, begins to spread to all the grievances already existing in society. Governments in fragile states rarely fall for a single commodity, but shortages can reveal previously hidden weaknesses. Therefore, the shortage of diesel deserves as much attention as fertilizers and cereals. Agriculture depends on all three. If fertilizers are removed, yields decrease. If cereal imports are eliminated, food prices rise. If diesel is removed, even the available grain may not reach cities.

Giovanni Arrighi would have placed this phenomenon in the broader context of the redistribution of economic power under way. Energy exporters exert influence because the industrial system simply cannot function without substantial flows of physical raw materials. Therefore, Russia, Iran and the Gulf producers occupy positions that cannot be understood solely through GDP figures or financial market valuations.

At the same time, consumers like China and India are gaining influence because they can absorb huge volumes that were previously sent elsewhere. Russian crude can be shipped to the east, refined in Asia and then returned to global markets in another way. Therefore, sanctions reconfigure trade rather than simply eliminating it. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have imposed real costs on Russia, including internal scarcity and reduced refining capacity, but have also contributed to reducing international supply of diesel. This does not demonstrate the existence of a deliberate Russian strategy to provoke a global shortage. However, it does mean that the shortage of raw material can increase the trading value of the remaining Russian reserves.

Jean Thiriart conceived geopolitics in terms of continental blocks, rather than small isolated states, and the current fuel crisis demonstrates the importance of the continental scale. Europe is once again discovering that energy security is intrinsically linked to geography. The United States can count on an immense domestic oil production. Russia has vast reserves of hydrocarbons. China has a huge industrial and refining capacity. India has built some of the largest refineries in the world. Europe, on the other hand, combines high consumption with a considerable dependence on imported energy and refined products. Therefore, record fuel prices in several European countries are more than just a problem for consumers. They reveal the cost of occupying a rich but resource-dependent peninsula at the western end of Eurasia, while relations with its main energy supplier in the east are broken. Whether Europe will respond by further diversifying its supply sources, rebuilding its refining capacity, accelerating electrification or possibly reopening certain channels with Russia is a political issue. Geography, however, has not changed.

Alexander Dugin’s multipolar language offers another way of interpreting diplomatic effervescence. The world is becoming more difficult to organize around a single center capable of setting rules for everyone else. Washington may sanction Russia, but it must take into account the reactions of China and India. Russia may redirect its energy to the east, but China and India may demand refunds. China can harness its industrial power, but it remains heavily dependent on energy sea routes. Gulf monarchies possess oil and refining capacity, but a war could close their export routes. Iran may threaten the Strait of Hormuz, but any disruption also threatens the Asian allies with whom Tehran wishes to maintain relations. No actor is sovereign over the whole system. Each has some important strengths and several weaknesses. In practice, multipolarity resembles less a harmonious congress of civilizations than a ruthless market where power dynamics, geographical advantages and needs are exchanged. The current negotiations take on their full meaning from this perspective: the powers negotiate because none of them can control all the consequences of a continuous escalation.

Arnold Toynbee wrote that civilizations are forged from their responses to challenges. The next few months could represent a very real test of brutality. The global diesel system is already under pressure: U.S. prices The U.S. has exceeded six dollars per gallon, refining margins in Asia have reached record levels, European consumers face exceptionally high fuel costs and analysts predict that depletion of reserves will remain a problem until 2027.

However, the markets are also adapting. China can export more refined products. New refining capacity can be launched. Demand can decrease. The Strait of Hormuz can be fully reopened. Russian refineries can be repaired. Other supply routes may be developed. That’s why Moscow, Washington, Beijing, Tehran and Gulf capitals have an interest in negotiating before shortages become uncontrollable. The danger is real, but so is the system’s ability to reorganize. The challenge now is to determine who will bear the cost of this reorganization.

And this is where the image of Mad Max ceases to be entirely comic. If negotiations fail, richer nations are unlikely to engage in drum battles. They have reserves, money, infrastructure and alternative solutions. The most vulnerable nations are likely to face a tougher situation: intermittent supplies, black markets, makeshift refineries, power outages, transport paralysis and political turmoil.

Thomas Hobbes understood that order depends, in part, on the ability of the state to ensure physical security. In the modern world, this includes maintaining the physical systems on which everyday life depends. A government unable to secure food transport, power grid operation and fuel supply to farms quickly discovers how thin the line between administrative order and disorder can be. In this sense, the humble can of diesel has become one of the discreet strategic objects of the current global crisis.
